News.title: Noel Edmonds faces backlash after he ‘condemns two farm shop bought lobsters to death’ after releasing them into the sea
News.content:
NOEL Edmonds has been accused of condemning to death two lobsters he bought from a farm shop to release into the sea.

The former Deal or No Deal host and his wife Liz returned the pair to the water on the Isle of Man.



Noel said they were uncomfortable seeing them confined in a tank and decided to buy them to release them.

In a social media clip, he said: “Nice clear water in Peel Harbour; there they go.



“And we know this is nice fresh water because a moment ago a seal went past.

“Wonderful place.”

But the 77-year-old was told his act of kindness was likely to backfire as the lobsters would not survive their return.

One web user said: “They didn’t have a chance the moment he removed them from tank.”



Another posted: “A lovely sentiment, but from a marine biologist perspective it’s best not to release captive lobsters.”

Meanwhile Matt Harrison, the owner of the farm shop from which Noel bought the lobsters, said he had moved their tank in response to the controversy — and was thinking of getting rid of it altogether.



He said he bought the lobsters to support a young local fisherman, adding: “The tank is still in the shop but we’ve moved it.

“I am sensitive to people’s feelings, but the vast majority want us to keep it.”

News.title: Four injured in shooting in major European city after argument breaks out as cops rush to scene
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GUNFIRE SHOCK Four injured in shooting in major European city after argument breaks out as cops rush to scene

FOUR people have been injured in a shooting on a street in Germany.

Cops have been deployed to the area of Berliner Straße in the Mülheim, Cologne, after shots rang out on Monday around 10pm.



Police say a dispute “between several people” sparked the incident, though full details have not yet been released.

Rescue workers have taken four people – some seriously injured – to hospitals.



Witnesses alerted the police after hearing gunshots in the street.

The operation is ongoing with the area under police cordon.



Numerous officers are currently on the scene interviewing witnesses and securing evidence.

It was also not yet known who fired the shots or how many shots were fired.

News.title: Tragedy as animals die in fire at Britain’s ‘2nd-best zoo’ with staff ‘devastated’ as two people also rushed to hospital
News.content:
ANIMALS have been killed after a fire ripped through the office at Britain’s “second-best zoo” leaving staff “devastated”.

Two owners of Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World in Hadley, near Telford in Shropshire, were also taken to hospital as a precaution.



The Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service were called to the attraction on Monday morning, August 3, after a fire was discovered in the zoo’s office.

One of the zoo’s owners Will Dorrell said in a video statement posted on Facebook on Monday evening that some animals had perished in the blaze.



He said: “We are saddened to announce that several stick insects, a snake and a hedgehog have died as a result of this morning’s fire at the zoo.

“These animals were privately owned by the zoo’s owners and have never been on display to the public.



“The owners are devastated at the loss of these animals but would like to thank Shropshire Fire and Rescue for all of their efforts in trying to extinguish the fire.”

Thanks to the speedy response by the fire crews, they were able to prevent the fire from spreading to other wooden buildings surrounding the office.



Mr Dorrell did though confirm the office had been “gutted” by the fire.

The attraction has been closed all day but it intends to re-open tomorrow, August 4.

Mr Dorrell asked that visitors “please bear with us and sort of excuse the mess” as they try to clear up and cordon off the area affected.

An earlier statement had said: “Our team have been monitoring the animals across the site to ensure that they all remain safe and well.

“If you had booked tickets or an animal experience for today, then please email info@hoo-zoo.com to re-arrange your visit for an alternative date.



“Please quote your order reference number and preferred new date in your email. Thank you for your support and understanding.”

Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World was rated the second best in the UK by users of travel website Tripadvisor.

It’s the second year running Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World had been able to claim the runner-up prize.

Earlier this year it was also voted the ninth-highest rated zoo in Europe.

The site, which used to be a farm, had been in the hands of the Dorrell family since 1988.



Chester Zoo was rated the top-rated zoo in the UK by Tripadvisor users in the same survey.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Dorrell said the achievement was surprising because there were “some fantastic zoos in the UK and in Europe”.

The ratings are based on customer reviews on the tourism website.

News.title: Lucy Powell’s anti-Tory obsession is no substitute for a serious education policy
News.content:
Loopy Lucy

IF Westminster gossip is to be believed, Lucy Powell was Andy Burnham’s THIRD choice to be Education Secretary.

The new PM may already regret not having a fourth option.



Powell’s claim that ex-Tory minister Michael Gove’s drive to raise academic standards in schools contributed to more than one million young people being out of work or training is as dangerous as it is patently wrong.

The Sun has argued for years that there needs to be better apprenticeship opportunities for kids, especially with AI radically changing the world of work.



But that CANNOT come at the expense of dropping standards and abandoning any ambition to give ALL pupils the best possible chances in life.

Not only is there NO evidence for Powell’s claims that Gove is responsible for leaving teenagers on the jobs scrapheap.

But in Wales and Scotland — where Labour and SNP-led governments refused to follow his methods, which later made English classrooms world leaders in maths and science — youth unemployment is HIGHER.

Labour’s catastrophic tax rises on business have done the real damage to young people’s prospects.

Allowing a ballooning of mental health benefits claims has only made that worse.

Powell’s depressing diatribe is rooted solely in her tribal hatred of Tories rather than educational fact.



Our kids will pay a high price for her wilful moronism.

Zero clue

ANDY Burnham says he “cannot ignore” the impact of Labour’s Net Zero policies on the cost of living.

So why is new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh insisting that green levies don’t increase bills for households, when they so obviously do?

Fanatical Fahnbulleh, a disciple of Ed Miliband, also downplayed the prospects of significant new drilling in the North Sea.

The lack of honesty over the estimated £40billion a year cost of Net Zero has been staggering.



It seems there’s also not much chance of a straight answer about what, if anything, the Government is going to do about it.

Liddle giant

ROD Liddle knew what Sun readers’ lives were like – and they loved him for it.

Proud of his working class roots and his country, Rod wasn’t afraid of laying bare the hypocrisy of left-wingers spouting concern for ordinary folk while being firmly part of the Establishment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Funny, fearless and staunchly committed to a free Press, no topic was off limits — he knew exactly what he thought, and did not hold back.

One of a kind and one of our own, he will be sorely missed.

News.title: Incel or blood lust? What was ‘puppet master’ Bryan Kohberger’s real motive & how appeal shows Ted Bundy-style craving
News.content:
DEPRAVED murderer Bryan Kohberger may have wanted to emulate infamous serial killer Ted Bundy — and is now struggling with losing control behind bars, a violent crime expert has claimed.

Kohberger, 31, admitted to the brutal slayings of four University of Idaho students on November 13, 2022, as part of a plea agreement that spared him the death penalty.



But despite sitting silently through hours of emotional victim impact statements and admitting to the murders, Kohberger has now made a dramatic U-turn and is seeking to withdraw his plea and face trial.

The move comes as the Netflix documentary The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare reaches number one on the streaming platform.



The one question that still hasn’t been answered is why he targeted victims Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Madison Mogen, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20.

The U.S. Sun spoke with Dr. Gary Brucato, a clinical psychologist, researcher and author who helped profile the person responsible for the murders before Kohberger was identified and arrested.

Brucato, who specializes in early psychotic illness, violent crime and mass or serial murder, believes Kohberger’s actions may have been influenced by notorious killers such as Ted Bundy.

Bundy, a rapist and necrophile, kidnapped, sexually assaulted, and murdered dozens of young women and girls across the US between 1974 and 1978.

Dr. Brucato believes Kohberger’s crimes had a sexual component, despite there being no evidence that he sexually assaulted any of the victims.

He said the killings may have been driven by a desire to imagine himself as “a powerful, virile figure” acting out a psychologically exciting scenario, possibly inspired by violent offenders he had studied.



“I have a very strong sense that Kohberger was so much like a serial offender rather than a mass murderer, where you do something once and either take your own life or get incarcerated and that’s the end of it.

“I think this is somebody who was sort of trying to master it and lost control the first time he did it.

“I think it’s possible that if he hadn’t been caught, [he] might have thought about doing it again.”

Prosecutors alleged Kohberger entered the King Road home intending to attack specific targets, but encountered more people than expected, including Ethan.

Digital forensics experts previously hired to examine the case have said Kohberger had researched Bundy, along with Danny Rolling, known as the Gainesville Ripper, and other serial killers.



His reported porn search history also included terms such as “raped,” “forced,” “passed out,” “sleeping” and “voyeur.”

Dr. Brucato believes Kohberger’s alleged fascination with notorious killers may reveal a desire for recognition and control — traits often seen in offenders who seek to build a notorious legacy.

While there is no public evidence that Kohberger stalked the victims in the traditional sense, prosecutors alleged he had visited the King Road home area before the murders, including cellphone data that placed his phone near the residence on multiple occasions.



Dr. Brucato said, “I was fascinated by the alibi that was given by Kohberger because he claimed that he was looking at the stars at Wawawai Park.

“First of all, on a psychological level, this notion of studying something that you can never touch the way an astronomer studies a star, but he can’t touch it.”

Dr. Brucato suggested Kohberger may have approached his victims in a similar way — observing and studying them from a distance.

He also pointed out that Wawawai Park is near the site where the remains of Joyce LePage, a Washington State University student whose 1971 disappearance has been considered by some as a possible Bundy case, were discovered.

Bundy was never charged or confirmed as LePage’s killer.



The documentary also explores the suggestion that Kohberger, who appeared to have no close friends and struggled with romantic relationships, may have identified with the incel movement (involuntary celibate).

The term refers to people who say they are unable to find a romantic or sexual partner, and some online incel communities have become known for promoting misogynistic and extremist views.

However, Dr. Brucato doesn’t believe Kohberger fully fits that profile.

“I had an issue with that from the beginning, because Kohberger, we know, was somebody who did have some date experiences,” he said. “He was just extremely weird on them.

“For example, the date that he reportedly had where he told the woman that he wanted to tickle her or that she had, you know, nice birthing hips.



“He was a sort of weird person, more than somebody who couldn’t get a date.

“And so I don’t think of him so much as an involuntary celibate.

“I think of him more as a person whose detached, peculiar mechanical quality and his desire to render relationships predictable, almost like a scientist thinks, weirded people out.”

Dr. Brucato also recalled how Kohberger had few contacts saved in his phone, which included impersonal labels like “girl I ran with” and “second girl I ran with.”

“I think that this is precisely the kind of person who would have been frustrated that he couldn’t make a science out of women and other people, and how to get people to like him and so forth,” he said.



Dr. Brucato believes Kohberger’s frustration at being unable to shape how others saw him may have contributed to his decision to become violent.

Bundy famously pleaded not guilty and represented himself during his trial, turning the courtroom into a stage as he fought to control his own narrative.

Dr. Brucato believes Kohberger has felt powerless since he was sentenced to life behind bars, and is the reason behind him suddenly seeking a trial.



He said, “If he is found guilty, what will he do? Probably write a book or start telling the story to manipulate the public that way.

“I think ultimately, one way or another, he always seems to be the puppet master.”

He went on, “I’m sure he feels extremely out of control in prison.

“I know he’s been upset over silly things like not getting the bananas he wants and things like that. And I’m sure he’s probably being picked on.”

But Kohberger will have a legal mountain to climb to try and get a trial.



Ada County District Judge Steven Hippler previously asked him in court, “I want to make sure that your plea is given voluntarily.

“I want to make sure that you actually committed the crimes to which you’re pleading guilty, because I don’t want you to plead guilty to a crime you didn’t commit.”

Hippler then asked, “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?” before reading out the murder charges tied to each victim.

Kohberger stood up and replied confidently, “Yes.”

Despite this, Kohberger’s request for new court-appointed counsel has been granted and a new filing shows he will be represented by public defender Gregory Rauch.



Kohberger filed a handwritten petition seeking to withdraw the guilty plea, which was entered to escape the death penalty.

He alleged that he was subjected to “coercion, disinformation, false promises” and the withholding of evidence he considered favorable to his defense.

Kohberger also claimed he was told that whether he was actually guilty was “not an important factor” when considering the deal.

Dr. Brucato worries about Kohberger getting pleasure out of having a trial.

“Let’s say he gets rid of all his attorneys and he wants to represent himself, that’s a little too Bundy-like for my taste,” he said.



“But then he’s allowed to have access to all kinds of evidence and think about the perversion of this person having crime scene photos and information and so forth.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“You almost wonder if, in some twisted way, there’s also an element of reliving [the murders] and then the family being dragged back and having to listen to it.”

To watch the full interview with Dr. Gary Brucato, visit The U.S. Sun’s YoTube channel.

News.title: Labour sparks ‘dumbing down’ row as Tories blast plans to make schools less academic
News.content:
LABOUR wants to dumb down classrooms while refusing to take the blame for the youth jobless crisis, Tories say.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell was criticised for saying the “one-size-fits-all” approach to learning has led to a million UK youngsters not being in training or in work.



She was attacked for taking a “fresh look” at what children were being taught as she tried to walk back reforms by Michael Gove, who ran her department in the 2010-14 coalition years.

Ministers are considering curriculum changes so teenagers take fewer GCSEs to stop them becoming stressed.



Ms Powell says schools have been stuck in a straitjacket of prioritising academic subjects for pupils.

She said: “We can no longer ignore that too many get left behind or are turned off by an education system that’s become too single-minded.”



She went on: “One million.

“That’s how many young people from the education system Michael Gove presided over who are now left outside education, not in employment and not training.”

“That is not a coincidence – it’s a consequence. It’s his legacy.”

But Laura Trott, the Tories’ Shadow Education Secretary, said: “Labour is using education as a smokescreen for its failures on tax and welfare.



“Labour is ignoring both recent history and the evidence.”

Tory peer Baroness Spielman, former head of schools watchdog Ofsted, said Ms Powell is trying to “deflect responsibility” from tax and minimum wage rises which have reduced job prospects for youngsters.

News.title: PC Harper’s ‘disgusted’ widow’s fury as hero cop’s killers WILL be released early despite PM’s pledge to keep them caged
News.content:
FURY erupted as it emerged two killers of hero PC Andrew Harper WILL still get early release.

Soft-justice plans to free Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole halfway through 13-year jail terms were paused last month.



But following a review, there will be no change to manslaughter cases, which means the two thugs could be out in months.

Furious widow Lissie Harper, 35, said: “This is disgusting.



“I’m beyond appalled and bristling with anger to hear Andrew’s killers are soon to be free.

“The level of disrespect the Government are showing to Andrew and other victims, and their loved ones such as me, is beyond contempt.”

“What abhorrent message does this send?

“How dare ministers say the killing of a police officer isn’t enough of a ‘sickening crime’ that deserves the stiffest of punishments.

“Andrew’s killers have shown no remorse.

“To release them early from their already pitiful sentences is an affront to justice.



“The Government and justice system have not just let me down, they have added insult to injury.

“This is an utter betrayal, one I will not be able to forgive or forget.”

In 2019 PC Harper, 28, was fatally dragged by a car driven by Henry Long, 18, as it towed a stolen quad bike.



Long, Bowers and Cole, then 17, were found guilty of manslaughter. The younger pair got 13 years’ jail, Long got 16 and will stay in prison.

Mr Burnham, who is taking a holiday after two weeks in No 10, launched an urgent review of Sir Keir’s plan which aimed to ease pressure on packed jails.

Early releases will begin in October.

Mr Burnham said: “I wanted to go even further as I know there will still be concerns about other offenders having their sentence shortened.

“But it’s not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing, which would put public safety at much greater risk.”



Tiff Lynch, National Chair of the Police Federation of England and Wales, branded the pairs release as “deeply disappointing” and “impossible to justify”.

“The Government has recognised that some offenders are simply too dangerous to benefit from early release, yet those convicted of killing police officers have been left off that list”, she said.

“We recently spoke out against the early release of the men responsible for PC Andrew Harper’s death, and officers, their families and the public will be asking why those who murder police officers can still qualify for reduced time behind bars.”



Freeing the two prisoners early “gravely risks undermining not only public safety but public confidence”, Lynch added.

She urged the government to “rethink” the decision in the face of “real distress” it will cause to bereaved families.

The decision has also come under fire from Thames Valley Police Chief Constable Jason Hogg’s, who described the decision as “demoralising” for emergency service workers.

“It is simple: if Andrew’s killers were convicted today, they would receive life sentences due to the law that was created in his name”, he said.

“We stand with Andrew’s family, the Police Federation, our Police and Crime Commissioner in our dismay and we will continue to lobby the Government to make the right decision.”



There will be an extra 14,000 new prison places by 2031 with the fastest prison building programme since the Victorian era.

Beefed-up community monitoring will help probation staff track movements and see random drug testing for 1,000 offenders every month.

The number of regions using chemical suppression to manage sexual offending will be doubled.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch condemned the PM’s move, which adds to the 70,000 who have been released early under various Labour schemes.

She said: “Andy Burnham wants a round of applause for agreeing not to release rapists and child sex offenders.



“He’s not getting one. This is only a partial climbdown.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Killers, violent offenders, men who have terrorised their partners and more will all still walk out of prison in October.”

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy added: “Burnham must go further and block the early release of killers too.”

News.title: ‘Precious angel’, 5, who was ‘found dead in water’ after going missing is pictured as ‘devastated’ family pay tribute
News.content:
'UNIMAGINABLE LOSS' ‘Precious angel’, 5, who was ‘found dead in water’ after going missing is pictured as ‘devastated’ family pay tribute

A FIVE-year-old “precious angel” who was “found dead in the water” has been pictured as her devastated family pay a touching tribute.

Little Letti Cole was discovered dead in a body of water in Badsey, Worcestershire, on July 29 after a desperate search by the cops.



Many villagers came out to help with the search for the youngster, who her family described was their “most precious angel”.

The family have set up a GoFundMe page with the aim to create a memorial for the young girl.



Letti’s aunt Hayley Cole said: “On Wednesday evening, we lost our most precious angel in the most tragic circumstances.

“Our family is completely heartbroken, devastated, and still in shock. No family should ever have to go through such an unimaginable loss.



“The kindness, compassion, and support shown by the people of Badsey has restored my faith in humanity.

“I want to thank every single person who gave up their time and made every effort to help look for our beautiful Letti.

“Your love and support will never be forgotten.”

The idea to set up a memorial came from a person on Facebook who got in touch with the family and suggested the tribute.



So far, more than £7,000 has been raised.

Hayley said: “I thought perhaps people would donate a few hundred, but I never expected anything like this.

“These are people we don’t even know.

“I mean Badsey Butchers; as soon as I set it up, they donated £1,000.

“We are in complete shock at everyone’s kindness and grateful to everyone who gave up their time to help in the search.



“There is a memorial set up at Badsey Church, which is beautiful. Badsey is an amazing village.”

Writing on the GoFundMe page, Hayley added: “Please don’t feel under any obligation to donate.

“Your love, prayers, and support have already meant the world to our family.

“Thank you from the bottom of our hearts.”

West Mercia Police have said there was no third-party involvement in Letti’s tragic death and warned the public not to speculate online.



A spokesperson for the force said last week: “Sadly, the child was found unresponsive in a body of water, and a short time later was pronounced dead.

“There is no third-party involvement in the child’s death, and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

“This is an incredibly tragic incident.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We ask the public to avoid speculation online as this is incredibly distressing to the family, and we ask that their privacy is respected at such a difficult time.”

Anyone who wants to donate to the appeal can click here.

News.title: Met Office issues rain update for Tuesday - but three UK regions still face drought
News.content:
Met Office issues rain update for Tuesday - but three UK regions still face drought

Half of England was declared a drought zone last week, and with a new heatwave seeing Britain enjoy its 20th day of 32C-plus sun, farmers are warning of food shortages to come

View 3 Images Dry grass at Kempton Park Racecourse in Surrey, on July 31 (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

Rain is on the way for parts of the UK after the driest July in England and Wales since records began, but some of southern England may still not see a drop, forecasters said.

‌



Another record tumbled on Monday (August 3) when the temperature reached 33.5C in Wisley in Surrey, marking the 20th day of 2026 when 32C or higher was recorded in the UK and exceeding the previous record of 19 days set in 1995, the Met Office said.

‌



In the latest heatwave, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has amber health alerts in place for the East Midlands, East of England, South East and London until Wednesday morning.

‌



There are also yellow heat health alerts for the North West, South West, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber, as the agency warns the latest high temperatures could put extra pressure on the NHS, with more vulnerable people likely to require medical treatment.

View 3 Images A drought has been declared across half of England and all of Wales (Image: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Outbreaks of rain and showers are forecast on Tuesday in Northern Ireland, Scotland, western England and Wales – but the Met Office has forecast a dry day for much of the Midlands, the east and south-east of England with warm sunshine and high humidity.

‌



Temperatures are expected to decrease gradually in the second half of the week, and there is some more unsettled weather forecast for parts of the UK including a yellow warning for thunderstorms in Northern Ireland. But the South East will continue to see little in the way of desperately needed rain, the Met Office has warned.

July was southern England’s driest month ever recorded, with the whole of Wales and half of England plunged into drought. Farming leaders have warned it is “one of the most severe droughts many farmers and growers have lived through”, with poor yields, struggles to access water for fruit and vegetables and livestock keepers using winter feed for their animals.

The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has demanded urgent action to secure water supplies for homegrown food production.

‌



View 3 Images An aerial view shows smoke rising from wildfires near Dunwich Heath (Image: TOLGA AKMEN/EPA/Shutterstock)

In July, 19 counties across England recorded effectively no rainfall – 1mm or less – across the whole of the month, the Met Office figures show. The summer of extreme weather has seen two record-breaking heatwaves, in May and June, that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths, and two more heatwaves in July which have fuelled drought and wildfires.

Firefighters remained at the scene of a heathland blaze in Dunwich, Suffolk, on Monday, and crews declared a major incident as they tackled a huge wildfire in the Rhondda valley in South Wales.

Article continues below

Drone footage showed blackened ground and smoke billowing metres into the air over the valley, where South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said the fire had affected 150 hectares of land, including forest, scrubland and vegetation.

News.title: Body found in month-long search for kayaker, 19, who capsized off Northumberland coast
News.content:
Body found in month-long search for kayaker, 19, who capsized off Northumberland coast

Michael Henry, 19, went missing after the kayak he was in capsized near Boulmer on Tuesday, July 7, and his body was later found off the coast of Blyth

View 2 Images Michael Henry, 19, from Rothbury in Northumberland (Image: Northumbria Police)

A body has been found after a month-long search for a 19-year-old lost at sea.

‌



Kayaker Michael Henry is thought to have died after the two-man canoe he was travelling in capsized off the coast of Northumberland.

‌



The second man on board the kayak managed to swim away when disaster struck on July 7. He managed to swim to a buoy which he was able to cling to before being rescued by the Coastguard.

‌



Despite the best efforts of search and rescue teams, which quickly dispatched lifeboats to try and locate the lost teenager, the search was called off on July 15. He was presumed to have died at sea.

Now Northumbria Police have confirmed that a body has been recovered after it was found in the water off the coast of Blyth on July 26.

‌



View 2 Images A Northumbria Police vehicle [file image] (Image: Newcastle Chronicle)

Formal identification has since taken place and a report has been prepared for the coroner. Michael's family had previously paid a heartfelt tribute to him, describing him as a "marvellous person", reports Chronicle Live.

On 15 July, they said: "We would like to thank everyone for all their love, kindness and support now and throughout Michael's life; it was that love and kindness that made him the marvellous person he was.

Article continues below

"Michael was a much-loved son, brother, grandson, nephew, team-mate and friend; a keen sportsman who loved the outdoors. Michael was preparing to go travelling this summer and hoping to start university next academic year.

"Michael will be forever in our thoughts, and we will miss him. Our thanks go to the emergency services and everyone who is helping to search for Michael."

News.title: Mum of Norwegian 'hitman' says he's treated 'like animal' in prison and 'keeps his head down'
News.content:
Mum of Norwegian 'hitman' says he's treated 'like animal' in prison and 'keeps his head down'

The mother of Johannes Natland hopes that her son can be transferred back to his homeland to serve his sentence as she shares an insight into his life behind bars

View 3 Images Johannes Natland has been found guilty and will be sentenced in October

The mother of 19-year-old Johannes Natland, who travelled to Britain from Norway to carry out a "hit" for a Swedish gang, has opened up about his time behing bars.

Natland was thwarted when police swooped to arrest him in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, after being found to be in possession of two firearms and 19 rounds of ammunition. The Old Bailey heard how the talented footballer, 19, had been tasked by organised crime group Foxtrot Network to carry out criminal activity on behalf of the Iranian regime.

The murder target of the Scandinavian group, which has been sanctioned by the UK government, has never been identified. Following a retrial, Natland heard the jury's unanimous guilty verdict today after they deliberated for more than 17 hours. He showed no emotion in the dock as the decision was read out.

View 3 Images He is due to be sentenced in October (Image: Metropolitan Police/AFP via Getty Images)

Teen girl forced into car by men as Essex Police launch manhunt READ MORE :

Widow of PC Harper shares disgust as hero cop’s killers WILL be released early READ MORE :

Natland pleaded guilty to possession of the firearms and ammunition, but had denied the conspiracy charge. CTP London officers uncovered a significant amount of evidence demonstrating that he was fully aware he was being asked to kill someone in the UK.

Giving evidence, Natland claimed that he was not intending to carry out the assassination but was instead intending to ‘shoot himself in the foot’, as a way to avoid repercussions if he refused the mission. However, after hearing the evidence throughout the trial, the jury found him guilty of conspiracy to commit murder.

Natland will be sentenced at the Old Bailey in October.

Natland's mum, Ellen, hopes that her son can be transferred back to his homeland to serve his sentence. She told MailOnline: "The [prison] conditions [in the UK] are very different from in Norway. Johannes keeps his head down and has spent a lot of time saying, "I'm Norwegian," so not a part of any of the [English] gangs.

"He didn't believe he would survive a year in prison. I don't think he would have if we hadn't been there every other week."

View 3 Images The arrest of Johannes Kongsnes Natland. (Image: Metropolitan Police / SWNS)

Johannes is 'scared to death' of a potentially lengthy sentence, Ellen said. She added: "Johannes is treated more like an animal already. It is crazy. All of us are crushed. Our son is not a violent person, he has no criminal record, he has never harmed anyone and would never do so."

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of CTP London, said: “Due to the swift and professional work of CTP London officers, supported by officers from West Yorkshire Police and CTP North East, Natland was arrested before he was able to carry out a murder in the UK.

Article continues below

“This investigation highlights the importance of the strong links with our international law enforcement partners to counter the very real threat of criminal organisations across European borders. We’ve worked particularly closely with colleagues from Norwegian law enforcement authorities and as a result, we have stopped somebody from being assassinated here in the UK.

“Our investigation, which remains ongoing, has also resulted in two lethal weapons and ammunition being taken out of criminal hands and off the streets of the UK which has undoubtedly made the public safer.”

News.title: PC Harper's mum says family 'will pay the price' as killers eligible for early release
News.content:
PC Harper's mum says family 'will pay the price' as killers eligible for early release

Debbie Adlam, mother of PC Andrew Harper, says her family will "pay the price" after learning that killers Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers remain eligible for early release

View 4 Images Deborah Adlam, mother of Pc Andrew Harper (Image: PA)

The mother of Pc Andrew Harper has said her family will "pay the price" after discovering that her son's killers remain eligible for early release under the Government's proposed sentencing reforms.

‌



Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Monday that rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming would be excluded from the scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.

‌



The proposals have drawn fierce criticism after it emerged that two of Pc Harper's killers would still qualify for early release.

‌



View 4 Images The Thames Valley Police traffic officer was just 28 when he was killed (Image: PA)

Teen girl forced into car by men as Essex Police launch manhunt READ MORE :

Widow of PC Harper shares disgust as hero cop’s killers WILL be released early READ MORE :

The 28-year-old police officer sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his mother Debbie Adlam said: "It feels like we're letting Andrew down again. We've been through the justice system, we thought we'd done as best as we could. Now we're standing up to fight again with this evening's announcement, so I just feel really let down, for Andrew's sake as well as ours."

‌



Pc Harper died after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary.

The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not have been eligible for the Government's scheme.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter following a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020, would become eligible for release after serving half of their sentences. Ms Adlam confirmed that Justice Secretary Alex Norris had contacted her by phone to explain the situation.

‌



View 4 Images (left to right), Henry Long, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers. (Image: PA)

She said: "Apparently, the situation is, if nothing was done, then the prison system would fall completely. But we're paying the price for it. It's Andrew and his family, and many others like us, we're paying the price."

When asked whether she accepted Mr Norris's apology, Ms Adlam said: "I do know that he was sorry, but there surely has to be other answers, other ways to look at and other things to explore. This decision was made very quickly."

‌



Thames Valley Police Chief Constable Jason Hogg said: "I am beyond disappointed the Government is continuing to allow PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early from prison despite the overwhelming recent public outcry.

"It is simple: if Andrew's killers were convicted today, they would receive life sentences due to the law that was created in his name. They would not be eligible for early release.

"This decision is demoralising for all police officers and our fellow emergency service workers, not just in the Thames Valley, that puts themselves in harm's way to protect and serve their community."

‌



View 4 Images Lissie Harper, the widow of PC Andrew Harper (Image: PA)

Mr Burnham paused plans to release prisoners early in September to ease overcrowding in jails as part of the Sentencing Act. The scheme will now be delayed until October.

The Prime Minister assured the public that offenders will face tighter community supervision, including new GPS monitoring for rapists to restrict their movements. Mr Burnham said he "wanted to go even further", but that was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

Article continues below

Announcing the changes, the Prime Minister said: "We will also be introducing much tougher community measures. There will be a presumption that all offenders are tagged, longer periods of supervision and tough new rules, including restriction zones for offenders."

Earlier, Pc Harper's widow Lissie Harper described releasing killers early as "an affront to justice" and "an utter betrayal". She went on to say: "The level of disrespect the Government are showing to Andrew and other victims – and to their loved ones such as me – is beyond contempt."

News.title: Trump officials accused of £6.7 billion 'insider trading operation' as Iran denies peace talks
News.content:
Trump officials accused of £6.7 billion 'insider trading operation' as Iran denies peace talks

Oil markets have been volatile since the US and Israel carried out joint strikes on several key Iranian sites earlier this year and Iran retaliated by striking sites across the Middle East and closing the Strait of Hormuz

View 3 Images Tehran has reportedly accused US Special Envoy for Iran is Steve Witkoff and adviser Jared Kushner of "abusing" negotiations (file image)

Iran has accused officials from US President Donald Trump's administration of a pattern of oil market manipulation.

‌



A source close to Iranian officials said Tehran has tied the alleged manipulation to Axios reports and Trump administration insiders.

‌



Oil markets have been volatile since the US and Israel carried out joint strikes on several key Iranian sites earlier this year. Iran retaliated by striking sites across the Middle East and closing the critical Strait of Hormuz waterway.

‌



View 3 Images Three boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz, as a plume of smoke rises from an explosion in the background, off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 13, 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Razieh Poudat)

About one fifth of all global oil traded passed through the waterway prior to the war.

The strait has been a focus of peace talks, with the repeated opening and closing disrupting global markets.

‌



Between April and May 2026, a series of oddly timed trades in oil futures markets preceded major Iran war announcements. Each of these instances are alleged to be linked to reporting by Axios.

The source said Tehran has "evidence of a $9 billion insider trading operation," The Hormuz Report wrote in a post on X. At the time of writing, $9 billion equates to about £6.7 billion.

It tied the operation to US Special Envoy for Iran is Steve Witkoff and adviser Jared Kushner.

‌



View 3 Images (Clockwise from bottom R) US President Donald Trump, US Vice President JD Vance, Jared Kushner, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff attend the inaugural meeting of the "Board of Peace" at the US Institute of Peace in Washington, DC, on February 19, 2026 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A senior Iranian official previously told a news outlet that Tehran privately warned US Vice President JD Vance that Mr Kushner and Mr Witkoff were "abusing" negotiations and that they were "more interested in exploiting insider knowledge to profit in financial markets than reaching a deal."

On Monday, August 4, Mr Trump told reporters that talks were "going on right now" and will "go quickly, one way or another".

Article continues below

He warned: "This is the last chance for them to sign a good document."

He repeatedly grew frustrated on Monday after Iran contradicted his claim that talks were ongoing and that a deal had been reached between both sides to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with further talks to take place around Iran's nuclear programme.

Iran's foreign ministry denied it was in talks with the US.

News.title: Teen girl forced into car by men as Essex Police launch manhunt
News.content:
Teen girl forced into car by men as Essex Police launch manhunt

Essex Police are investigating after a teenage girl was forced into a vehicle by men in Harlow and driven for around 40 minutes until she managed to flee to safety

View 2 Images The terrifying ordeal began for the girl in Church Langley (Image: Google)

Essex Police are investigating after men forced a teenage girl into a car and drove off with her.

‌



On Wednesday, August 3 just after 6.50pm a teenage girl, was forced into a vehicle in Church Langley, Essex and driven to Epping. The girl managed to get out the car and flee to safety 40 minutes after the terrifying ordeal began.

‌



Essex Police are now urging members of the public in the areas at the time to come forward with any information. The suspects have been described as "white men who were wearing tracksuits."

‌



View 2 Images A manhunt has been launched for the suspects as police try to locate the men responsible (Image: Essex Police)

An Essex Police spokesperson said: "Detectives are investigating an incident which happened in Harlow this evening (Monday 3 August).

"We were called to a report of a teenage girl being forced into a vehicle in Church Langley and driven to Epping, where she managed to flee the car. The incident started in the Minton Lane car park by Tesco at just after 6.50pm.

‌



"The car drove to Epping and the victim managed to get out of the car in Buckingham Road at the junction with Lower Swaines at 7.30pm and get help.

"The girl is safe with her family and is being supported by specialist officers. Thankfully she has not suffered any serious injuries.

"Investigating officers are appealing to anyone who saw the incident in Church Langley or Epping to contact them urgently. The girl is white and has blonde hair. She was wearing a black top, black shorts and white socks and trainers.

Article continues below

"The vehicle involved is believed to be a black car and the suspects are described as white men who were wearing tracksuits."

Detective Sergeant Paul Marks said: “We know this incident will be concerning to people. We understand and we are working at pace to try and identify the car and the men involved in this incident. If you were at either of these locations this evening please check your dashcam or CCTV.

"If you have any information, CCTV, dash cam or other footage in relation to this incident, then please get in contact with us. Please quote 1362 of 3 August."

News.title: UK wildfires: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales
News.content:
Firefighters are battling wildfires in Shropshire and South Wales, with crews declaring a major incident as they tackle the blaze in the Rhondda Valley

Firefighters in Shropshire are tackling a large blaze near a historic site, while crews in South Wales have declared a major incident as they battle a wildfire close to homes.

The blaze at Battlefield Heritage Park, a country park north of Shrewsbury, broke out on Monday afternoon. It is understood to be a few fields from the site associated with the 1403 Battle of Shrewsbury, fought between King Henry IV and a rebel army led by Henry "Harry Hotspur" Percy.

Meanwhile, crews from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service are battling a wildfire in the Llanwonno area of Rhondda Cynon Taf. The blaze, which began on Saturday afternoon, has already spread across around 150 hectares - roughly the size of 210 football pitches.

No residents have been evacuated from their homes, but Rhondda Cynon Taf Council said a rest centre has been opened at a local sports centre for people affected by smoke and poor air quality.

News.title: 'I came to the UK to help the NHS — but I instead face racism at work'
News.content:
'I came to the UK to help the NHS — but I instead face racism at work'

NHS staff, including radiographer Paul Awah, have told us some patients refuse to be treated by non-white staff — and the professionals say the rise of the far right is to blame

View 3 Images Radiographer Paul Awah says he has seen a worrying increase in racism (Image: provided)

NHS staff have revealed the vile racist jibes they endure amid a surge in abuse from patients.

‌



Staff have seen a disturbing rise in racism from patients over the last 18 months, which emerged in a poll by the Society of Radiographers (SoR). Workers who moved to the UK to help the NHS are forced to deal with daily abuse, which they blame on the rise of the far-right movement.

‌



Figures from the latest NHS Staff Survey, published in March, show 9.26% experienced discrimination at work – a five-year high and up from 7.91% in 2021. The SoR is now calling for the NHS to record incidents of racism and monitor how they are dealt with. The move has been backed by the Royal College of Nursing.

‌



Haverfordwest's first Black mayor forced to get personal security guards after death threats READ MORE :

View 3 Images Paul Awah says he has seen an increase in racism and is "worried" for his children (Image: provided)

Dad-of-three Paul Awah, 43, an MRI radiographer from Nigeria, told The Mirror he had seen a rise in racist incidents.

He said: “I feel worried and very concerned because in the last year to year-and-a-half, the rhetoric has changed because of the increase of the far-right movement. Sometimes you can see they are awkward to be treated by me. I went to put a cannula in and they were screaming for help.

‌



“But someone else comes who is not as experienced as myself and they were more cooperative. This happened two weeks ago.”

Ifeanyi Obike, 28, was born in Nigeria and moved to the UK in 2022, working as a CT radiographer. He said: “I have a positive personality, so it takes a lot to get at me.”

But Ifeanyi admits he was shocked when one patient exited the room and refused to be treated by him.

‌



He said: “I was walking past the corridor and heard the patient loudly ask my healthcare assistant, ‘Is he the one going to do the examination? She responded, ‘Yes, he’s the one who will be doing the examination’. And he said, ‘That’s it, I’m not having it done. I’m leaving this place’. And he just walked out.”

View 3 Images Radiographer Ifeanyi Obike was 'shocked' when a patient saw him and walked out of the room (Image: provided)

NHS figures from earlier this year revealed how some 9.26% of staff in 2025 said they personally experienced discrimination at work in the last 12 months from patients or service users. This is up from 9.25% in 2024, 8.57% in 2023, 8.38% in 2022 and 7.91% in 2021.

‌



Thomas Simons, chief human resources and organisational development officer at NHS England, said: “Racist abuse towards NHS staff is completely unacceptable and has no place in our health service. Our new national staff standards are clear that NHS organisations must take meaningful action to prevent and respond to racism, support affected staff and ensure there are clear consequences for patients who racially abuse or discriminate against NHS staff – including the option to refuse care in non-emergency situations.”

Responding to poll of members of Society of Radiographers, showing rise in racist abuse of NHS staff, RCN Associate Director of Employment Relations, Brian Morton, said:

"These findings are utterly appalling and sadly echo the experiences of nursing staff across the country. Our multicultural workforce, made up of every ethnicity and nationality, is a precious thing that should be celebrated. But if we do not take this disgusting and cowardly racist abuse seriously and deal with it head on, we will let down those who care for us and potentially lose them from the health service entirely.

Article continues below

"It is past time for the NHS to start recording incidents of racism on a national scale. That means a standardised method of recording incidents of racial abuse which includes data on the staff group, work areas and ethnicity of the staff member experiencing the abuse.

"Health leaders will only get a grip on this crisis if they fully understand the scale of this problem. Employers who fail to root out racism against their staff must be held to account, including via the new NHS staff standards."

News.title: PC Harper's mother 'devastated' his killers set for early release under revised plans
News.content:
The mother of PC Andrew Harper has told the BBC she is "devastated" two of his killers remain eligible for early release after the government revised plans to tackle overcrowding.

Prisoners who committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme for England and Wales, the government announced on Monday, in a bid to tackle prison overcrowding.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he "wanted to go even further", but that would not be possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his mother, Debbie Adlam, said: "It feels like we're letting Andrew down again.

"We've been through the justice system, we thought we'd done as best as we could.

"Now we're standing up to fight again... so I just feel really let down, for Andrew's sake as well as ours."

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders who killed the officer could be included in the scheme.

The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not have been eligible.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020, would become eligible for release after serving half of their sentences.

Adlan said she was "devastated" by the government's latest announcement, and vowed to continue to fight for justice. "I could not sit back and do nothing," she said.

She added that Justice Secretary Alex Norris had called her to explain the situation and apologise.

News.title: Breast cancer checks missing most women under 50 who are at risk, says study
News.content:
Breast cancer is a leading cause of death in women under 50 in the UK.

About one in seven women develop breast cancer in their lifetime, yet only 5-10% of cases are linked to inherited genes.

Most cases - 96% - are in women over 40, while 25% are in women over 75.

Men can get breast cancer too, with about 420 new cases every year in the UK.

In England, guidance from Nice recommends GPs ask about family history if a woman is worried that she might have a higher risk of breast cancer, and sometimes if they are over 35 and using an oral contraceptive pill or considering taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

Hormones have been linked to a slightly increased risk of breast cancer, although larger risk factors include alcohol intake and obesity.

The study, by a team from Cambridge University and the Institute of Cancer Research, looks at how to predict breast cancer risk in younger women.

They used a risk calculator called Boadicea that combines factors such as family history, lifestyle, reproductive history and genetic information to give a risk score.

If all women under 50 were to have this done, they estimate about a quarter (26.5%) would be categorised as at above-average risk and referred for further assessment.

This would include a third of women under 50 (34.8%) who develop breast cancer within 10 years.

By comparison, the current Nice criteria would result in 1.4% of women under 50 being referred for further assessment, which would include just 4.4% of those women who develop breast cancer.

A main reason for the disparity, the researchers say, is because three-quarters of women (73%) under 50 who develop breast cancer within a decade have no family history of breast cancer - the key criterion in the Nice guidelines.

News.title: There's a reason child vaccination rates are falling - and it's not social media
News.content:
Twenty-week-old Grayson easily could have become one of the tens of thousands of British babies left unvaccinated against polio.

His mother, Lily, agrees with the principle of immunisation. But overwhelmed by the early weeks of motherhood, and suffering from post-partum depression after a traumatic birth, she was daunted by the prospect of a long journey to a doctor's surgery. "I've been through the trenches, awake all night. You don't want to leave the house, or go to a different town."

Weeks ticked by, and eventually Grayson missed the polio and diptheria jabs he was supposed to get at eight weeks old. By that point he was officially classed by the NHS as "overdue" for vaccination; effectively, he was on his GP's naughty list.

Then Lily realised there was a clinic practically on her doorstep - at a location she hadn't expected.

That clinic - in Keighley, west Yorkshire - runs from a vacant retail unit at the Airedale shopping centre, a 1960s-era precinct that locals say has fallen on hard times in recent years, with plenty of empty, boarded-up units. The staff who created the clinic thought: why not use one of those vacant units to administer vaccines?

"This was an empty shop; there was nothing here, the windows were all blacked out," Flora Jennings, a local charity coordinator, tells me over the sound of a baby's laughter, on the morning I visit the clinic.

News.title: US states sue to block Trump tariffs impacting dozens of countries
News.content:
Twenty five US states sued the administration of US President Donald Trump on Monday over new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners.

The tariffs came into effect in July, targeting countries including the UK and China as well as the European Union, over Washington's contention that they have failed to properly tackle forced labour.

In a legal document seen by the BBC, the coalition of Democratic states said the decision was "arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law."

In response, White House spokesman Kush Desai said: "The US is using its lawful authority" to address practices that burden American businesses.

Desai added that any foreign country's failing to deal with the importation of goods produced with forced labour was "unreasonable" and must be addressed.

The new tariffs were imposed on major trading partners like Japan, Brazil and Taiwan under Section 301 of the 1974 US Trade Act, legislation which is designed to target nations that use forced labour.

The duties cover 99.4% of US imports, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

The lawsuit said the Trump administration "cannot use forced labour as a pretext to continue its illegal tariff scheme."

"The tariffs the USTR imposed are so broad that they defy the USTR's own stated aims and make a mockery of the statute used to justify them," it said.

News.title: Thunderstorms and flash flood risk on final day of UK heatwave
News.content:
The heatwave impacting parts of the UK this week continues into Tuesday with a risk of thunderstorms in some parts.

Pershore in Worcestershire and Cavendish in Suffolk hit three consecutive days of heatwave threshold temperatures on Monday and it is expected more parts of southern and eastern England will reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts, external are in effect across much of England until 09:00 BST Wednesday, with temperatures expected to reach more than 30C in some areas.

The intense heat will be short lived though as a change in the weather pattern is on the way from midweek.

News.title: West Ham co-owner David Sullivan advised to stay away from home matches
News.content:
The recommendation from London Stadium comes after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour. He has categorically denied the allegations.

He stood down as joint chairman of the club shortly before the investigation was broadcast, saying he wanted to focus on fighting what he called "factually incorrect and entirely false, decades-old allegations concerning my personal life". He remains the club's largest shareholder.

The investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for three years due to safeguarding concerns. London Stadium were unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historic allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false and that because he had never met any academy or women's team players "1-2-1" during his 16 years at the club, he accepted what he saw as a "meaningless restrictionâ¦for a quiet life".

West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in May and are due to play their first home game of the new season, a Carabao Cup match against Portsmouth, on Saturday.

Sullivan was a regular attendee at the London Stadium last season, where he was photographed watching games from the directors' box.

A spokesperson for London Stadium, the operator of the publicly owned venue, said that "following media reports at the end of the season regarding a safeguarding matter being managed by the club, London Stadium sought further information to ensure it could fulfil its own safeguarding responsibilities".

It said that West Ham had told it that the "matter was investigated and that the club does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Mr Sullivan attending the stadium".

However it said that, despite this, it had recommended the businessman stay away from games because of the "potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators".

Sullivan has previously faced criticism from fans over his running of the club, with thousands joining a protest in September last year calling for his departure.

West Ham declined to comment. It is understood that the club intends to work with the stadium operators to facilitate Sullivan's attendance at games.

Sullivan has not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, presenter Tony Livesey left BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday after 16 years at the station, the corporation announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against Sullivan. He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

News.title: Analysis: Trump fumes as top allies back down on his personal battles
News.content:
It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of contravening evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

On Friday, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former Fox News host and stalwart Trump ally, moved to drop felony destruction of property charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who federal prosecutors had accused of intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool near the Washington Monument.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted â what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury â provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he groused.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

One of Trump's closest allies â his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche â was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

News.title: Half price rail travel extended to 18-year-olds
News.content:
Eighteen-year-olds will be able to buy half price train tickets for most services when railcard rules are changed later this month, the Department for Transport (DfT) has announced.

It's an extension of the 16-17 Saver railcard which currently expires when the holder turns 18. From 17 August, they will be valid for a full year from the date of purchase.

It means 17-year-olds will be able to buy the railcard up until the day before they turn 18, making it valid until the day before they turn 19.

The existing rule meant more than 70,000 students each year were an average of Â£175 worse off than those in the same academic year who hadn't yet had their 18th birthday, the DfT said.

The 16-17 Saver Railcard costs Â£35 per year and entitles the holder to 50% off most train fares.

Rail minister Lord Hendy claimed this "common sense change" is "exactly what passengers should expect from the railway".

He said the change would "lower the cost of travel at a critical time for teenagers, whether they're pursuing further education, vocational pathways or getting their footing in the jobs market".

Jacqueline Starr, chief executive of industry body the Rail Delivery Group, said the change demonstrates the sector's commitment to "offering better value fares and delivering a more joined-up railway".

Kaynat Ahmad, vice president for further education at the National Union of Students, described the railcard as "essential for young people reliant on trains to get to college, work or training".

Eighteen-year-olds were already entitled to a 16-25 Railcard, but that only entitles them to a third off the cost of travel.

The announcement comes after the government said the cap on most single bus fares in England will be cut from Â£3 to Â£2 next year.

News.title: 'Rape list' part of misogyny girls face at school
News.content:
A group of teenage girls have said they feel "worthless" and "frightened" as a result of the extreme misogyny they regularly experience.

The students, from Tyneside, have spoken out after making a film about the language they endure at school and online.

Many comments are too explicit to share, but they include threats of violence and rape often masked as "banter". One girl described how disturbed she had been after a "rape list" was made by boys in her school.

The government said it was "taking bold and decisive action to halve violence against women and girls", with changes being introduced from September to help teachers challenge misogyny.

The North East has the highest rate of violence against women and girls in England and charities warned unchallenged attitudes could lead to abuse in early relationships.

Misogyny is defined as a contempt for, hatred of or prejudice against women.

One girl told the BBC she felt "worthless" after learning of the "rape list" made by boys in her school.

"Boys ordering girls, who they want to rape the most and then the least," she explained.

"It is frightening because you don't know people's real intentions."

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced that if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Responding to the French government, a Reform spokesperson said: "We will always stand up for British interests and protect our people, whether Emmanuel Macron likes it or not."

The spokesperson added: "Humanitarian missions do not violate maritime or international law."

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: Author La Plante banned from driving for six months
News.content:
The court heard she already had nine points on her licence, from three speeding offences in June 2023 and then June and July 2025.

She told the court she believed she would have to have the dog rehomed if she was unable to drive him to his daily walks, saying: "I think the emotional turmoil of that would truly damn my career as a writer.

"It's very, very solitary and I work exceptionally hard and I would just stop."

La Plante, who is best known for creating Prime Suspect's no-nonsense Det Ch Insp Jane Tennison, admitted driving at 24mph twice, 25mph, 26mph and 27mph in the latest offences, which all happened as she was on her way to take her dog for his daily walk.

Giving evidence, La Plante said she got her dog Theo after suffering the devastation of the untimely death of another dog, Hugo.

Fighting back tears, she said she "lost it" when Hugo died and she "didn't know what to do with [her] life".

She added her new dog had helped her through the grieving process.

News.title: Farage says he discussed return to politics months before general election
News.content:
Nigel Farage has told the BBC he discussed the "potential liabilities" of returning to politics before the 2024 general election.

It comes after The Sunday Times, external reported Farage had negotiated a deal in March and April 2024 with then-Reform leader Richard Tice to return to lead the party.

Farage confirmed he spoke with Tice in spring 2024 to scope out what would happen to Reform's finances if he returned but said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement", adding that talks came "quite some time after" he received a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

Labour said Farage's remarks had "blown a gaping hole" in his argument for not declaring the gift after becoming an MP in July 2024.

Farage has repeatedly argued the Â£5m from British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne was an "unconditional gift", was intended for his personal security, "wasn't political in any sense at all" and he was not an MP when he received it.

Reform's opponents have said he should have declared it in the MPs' register of interests when he was elected to Parliament.

The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating whether Farage broke the rules, but the process was suspended when he stood down as Clacton MP last month to force a by-election.

Farage said he took this decision as the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions". The investigation will be resumed if Farage wins the by-election, which is taking place on 13 August.

Farage left frontline politics in 2021 and embarked on a broadcasting career.

In May 2024, Farage was serving as Reform's honorary president but announced he would not be standing as a candidate in the general election in July of that year.

He reversed this position at the beginning of June and took over the leadership of the party.

Appearing at a press conference on Monday, Farage was asked if he had negotiated a deal on what would happen to Reform's finances if he came back as leader - in light of the report in The Sunday Times.

He replied: "I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position.

"And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial.

"But without Richard, the party wouldn't have even survived, so that was useful for me to know. But it wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back."

He added: "If you want clarification on this, that came quite some time after the gift, which is perhaps the important point."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret Â£5m 'gift' from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared."

The Commons code of conduct states that new MPs "must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election".

The rules say "purely personal gifts or benefits" from family or commercial loans would not normally have to be registered.

The rules also say "both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered", adding "if there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered".
