Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal saga has Newcastle in contention for all-time worst transfer window
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal saga has Newcastle in contention for all-time worst transfer window

Newcastle's chief executive stated a desire to be amongst the best clubs in the world in four years - but a transfer window that has seen their best players leave and their captain wanting out is putting that ambition in question

View 3 Images Newcastle are desperate to keep hold of Bruno Guimaraes as they try to avoid a disaster summer (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Bruno Guimaraes has reported for Newcastle's pre-season camp as talk over his sale continues - and his possible exit would make their summer go from bad to worse.

‌



The Magpies are currently fighting to keep their captain after two high-profile sales at St James' Park and the departure of their manager.

‌



So often poor transfer windows centre around dire recruitment, the expensive signings who fail to work out. But in terms of exits we could certainly be looking at one of the worst summers in the history of the Premier League.

‌



There's no doubt that the hangover from the poor summer of 12 months ago, which centred around Alexander Isak's desire to leave, eventually joining Liverpool on deadline day, has bled into the window we're currently in.

Newcastle's forgettable summer of 2025 set them on a path to a first bottom-half finish in recent years, and that had financial consequences which has seen players jump ship. The ripples are certainly being felt.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Arsenal target Bruno Guimaraes complies with Newcastle requests as midfielder boards flight READ MORE :

Arsenal receive immediate response after finally submitting first Bruno Guimaraes offer READ MORE :

Anthony Gordon's move to Barcelona can be written off as the one major deal that Newcastle were always going to have to sanction to remain financially compliant, especially after they missed out on European revenue. The £70million deal was one the majority could stomach.

Sandro Tonali's £100m switch to Tottenham is one that the balance sheet can live with, but what it says to the rest of the squad is perhaps more damaging than the exit itself. The Italian had been linked with Arsenal in January and given that Newcastle nearly doubled their money on the £55m they spent on him, you think fair play.

The issue is the likes of Guimaraes, who with Tonali alongside formed a midfield partnership that could genuinely be compared to any side in the Premier League. That was the only area where the Magpies could claim they were in the elite bracket, and that's a great foundation to build from.

‌



Instead it could implode. Tonali's departure doesn't send a message of ambition and Guimaraes has expressed a desire to move to Arsenal. Newcastle have stood firm, maintaining their talisman is not for sale.

View 3 Images Sandro Tonali joined Tottenham in a club-record deal (Image: Tottenham Hotspur FC)

The Brazilian's exit would leave Newcastle, entering a new era under Matthias Jaissle, looking more and more like a mid-table side. A number of their blockbuster arrivals under the Saudi Arabian regime will have moved on, and questioned will be asked of the project.

‌



Manchester United continue to track left-back Lewis Hall, who has just enjoyed the best season of his career to date. If Guimaraes were to be sold then Newcastle would be financially able to rebuff any offer that comes in for Hall - and they insist he's not for sale.

Even so, the player's head may well be turned, and a squad full of players who would rather be elsewhere isn't a recipe for success. Newcastle were quick to land a new manager, but he's an uphill task ahead of him.

Much has been made of Newcastle's failure to get deals over the line. James Trafford, Marc Guehi, Hugo Ekitike, Joao Pedro and Bryan Mbeumo have all opted for other Premier League rivals ahead of the Magpies.

‌



View 3 Images Eddie Howe has called time on five years at Newcastle (Image: PA)

Missing out on those names has certainly halted Newcastle's progress, but being able to retain their best players has meant that Howe, when he was in situ, had enough to work with that he could challenge England's best on their day. Consistency remained the problem, but a squad boasting Tonali, Guimaraes and Isak was able to end the club's 70-year wait for a trophy.

That was only 18 months ago and yet it seems like that was in a different era such has been the shift in the way many see Newcastle, even those within their four walls.

‌



Its not to say the club haven't spent money - upwards of £100m has been spent of summer arrivals that include Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Toure and Sean Steur. But the fact their signings have done nothing to mitigate the negative feeling around Newcastle says everything about the magnitude of the players they've let go - and those that could still follow them.

Only last year new chief executive David Hopkinson claimed Newcastle can be “in the debate about being the top club in the world ” by 2030. Make no mistake, four years out from that goal, no club sanctions the type of exits that the Magpies have without heavyweight names coming in to replace them.

Sports.title: Man Utd tell Ralf Rangnick's only signing he can leave permanently after brutal snub
Sports.content:
Man Utd tell Ralf Rangnick's only signing he can leave permanently after brutal snub

Ralf Rangnick could not impart many changes during his fleeting spell as manager of Manchester United, but even one of those is seemingly being rooted out of the club

View 3 Images Ralf Rangnick's only Man United signing has been told he can leave the club this summer (Image: 2022 Manchester United FC)

Ralf Rangnick's only transfer signing as interim manager of Manchester United has been told he is allowed to leave the club. Rangnick took over the Reds on a temporary basis after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was sacked during the 2021-22 Premier League campaign.

The Austrian was in charge during the following transfer window and while the club were linked with many players recommended by him, only one was brought to the club. That player was Toby Collyer, who arrived from Brighton and Hove Albion as an 18-year-old prospect.

Four-and-a-half years later, Collyer has reportedly been informed he is allowed to depart the club permanently, having been left out of Michael Carrick's squad for the recent friendly over Atletico Madrid. His absence would have stung as the substitutes' bench was filled with plenty of young academy stars.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Instead, Collyer featured for the U21s side in a 1-0 defeat to Altrincham Town on Friday evening. Last season, Collyer was loaned to Championship side West Bromwich Albion, before being loaned to Hull City in the following transfer window.

Throughout his time at the club, he has only made 13 senior appearances for the Reds, with ten of those coming under Ruben Amorim. His loan spells with West Brom and Hull were both marred by injuries. Now, according to The Sun, the club have said he is free to leave.

Despite United starting the summer short in central midfield, Collyer always seemed far away from Carrick's plans. They have since strengthened by signing Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos from Aston Villa and Chelsea respectively.

View 3 Images Toby Collyer featured against Altrincham Town when many other United youngsters were included in the squad against Atletico Madrid (Image: 2026 Manchester United FC)

A third midfielder is also expected to be brought in this summer. Meanwhile, fellow academy graduate Tyler Fletcher is believed to be ahead of the ex-Brighton prospect in the United pecking order.

‌



Against Altrincham, he was joined by fellow United U21 team-mates Dan Gore, Jacob Devaney and Chido Obi, who all featured in the friendlies against Wrexham and Rosenborg.

Collyer's loan spell with West Brom came to an end after he suffered an injury during a clash against Birmingham City towards the end of November. He was brought back to United to work on his recovery, before being loaned to Hull.

View 3 Images Michael Carrick has made many big changes at Manchester United since taking over from Ruben Amorim (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

‌



He hoped to be involved in Hull's promotion play-off final clash against Middlesbrough at Wembley but he could not recover from his injury in time. He made 12 appearances for West Brom before the loan was ended and he only made five at Hull.

Collyer's departure would also rip out the last bit of Rangnick's legacy at Old Trafford. The now Austria manager took charge of 29 matches, winning 11, drawing nine and losing nine.

He had been expected to take up a consultancy role at Old Trafford, but this did not transpire as he left the club completely upon the end of his caretaker deal.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan's 'overwhelmed' family issue heartfelt statement and explain funeral plans
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan's 'overwhelmed' family issue heartfelt statement and explain funeral plans

Kevin Keegan died on July 20 following a battle with stomach cancer and his family have now issued a statement to thank those who paid tribute and detail plans for his funeral

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan died aged 75 from cancer (Image: (Liverpool FC via Getty Images))

Kevin Keegan's family say they have been "truly overwhelmed" by the volume of tributes following the death of the football legend. England great Keegan passed away aged 75 last month from cancer.

‌



It was announced on July 20 that the former Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle striker had died following a battle with stomach cancer. The Newcastle hero left behind wife of 51 years Jean and their children Laura Jane, 47, and Sarah Marie, 43.

‌



Tributes poured in from across the heartbroken football world for the double Ballon d'Or winner, who won 63 caps for England and managed the Three Lions, Newcastle, Fulham and Manchester City.

‌



A private funeral has now been arranged by the Keegan family, who have also set up a fundraiser in King Kev's honour, which will raise money for charities close to his heart.

Gianni Infantino's opponents prepared to launch rival competition to force out FIFA boss READ MORE :

Southampton boss Tonda Eckert says he received death threats after Spygate scandal READ MORE :

A statement from the Keegan family, issued by the League Managers Association, read: “Following the devastating news of Kevin’s passing, we would like to thank the vast number of people who have expressed condolences and shared their memories of Kevin in recent days.

“As a family we have been truly overwhelmed by the volume of tributes and are grateful for them all. We will be holding a small private funeral in the coming weeks and request ongoing privacy and respect whilst we navigate this extremely difficult period as a family.

‌



“Details of a memorial service hosted by Newcastle United that will take place at a later date will be communicated in due course.”

The fundraiser states: "The Keegan family are deeply grateful for all the kind words and support received from far and wide. To honour Kevin’s memory, they feel there would be no more fitting gesture than to give.

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan touched the hearts of many

‌



"We are therefore raising money for two causes that were close to Kevin’s heart: The Christie Charity and Football Families for Justice. The Christie were an immeasurable help to Kevin and his family, as they are to many others. Football Families for Justice is a charity being set-up by John Stiles, son of the great Nobby Stiles, to support former players who are suffering from neuro degenerative diseases caused by heading the ball during their football career.

"A sporting superstar, but also a husband, father, grandfather and friend - Kevin gave so much to us all."

Keegan was most loved at Newcastle, where he enjoyed his most successful spell as a manager. "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters," the club said in a statement.

‌



View 3 Images Kevin Keegan was a legend at Newcastle United (Image: PA)

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be. As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

"Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions."

Sports.title: Short guides Welsh Fire to crucial win over Southern Brave
Sports.content:
A superb unbeaten half-century from Matt Short guided Welsh Fire to a six-wicket victory over Southern Brave that takes them level on points at the top The Hundred table.

With both sides still in the hunt for a qualification place and coming off the back of morale-boosting victories, it was the Fire who took the honours in Cardiff to join Trent Rockets on 16 points at the summit of the table.

Opting to bowl, Fire's battery of experienced seamers were immediately into the action, Chris Woakes and Sam Cook reducing the Brave to 2-2 off seven balls as Jamie Smith and Ben McKinney both edged behind to Phil Salt.

The Cook-Salt combo also accounted for Nikhil Chaudhary after he and Marcus Stoinis had sedately taken the visitors to an underwhelming 45-3 at the halfway stage.

Not long after, Rachin Ravindra, getting big turn, snared Tristan Stubbs and Moeen Ali with successive deliveries, the latter caught by Joe Root off a skier.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Moeen Ali goes for a golden duck, leaving the Southern Brave in trouble against the Welsh Fire

The Brave were chugging along at barely a run a ball on a tricky surface but Stoinis added some muscular impetus, going to a 35-ball half-century before hitting Cook, who returned a magnificent 3-14, down deep square's throat.

David Miller hit a couple of late sixes but Short, coming on to bowl for the first time in the final five of the innings, had him caught on the edge.

Jofra Archer hit a first-ball six but was gone second ball and the Brave ended with 115-8, their lowest-ever total in The Hundred, below their 118-8 against the Oval Invincibles in 2024.

With little margin for error, Archer set the tone for the Fire, delighting in getting Phil Salt with his first ball and not conceding a run until his eighth.

But Short and Root kept things moving, knowing that one or two partnerships would be enough, and calmly took the score to 60 off 48 before Root departed, caught by McKinney off Chris Jordan.

Ravindra and Jordan Cox came and went but Tom Kohler-Cadmore kept the scoreboard ticking over as he supported Short - who reached a 37-ball 50 with a scoop off Archer and made good use of the ramp throughout to the short straight boundaries - to see his side home, an anticlimactic two wides finishing things.

Image: Matt Short (left) and Tom Kohler-Cadmore saw Welsh Fire to victory over the Southern Brave

Match Hero Matt Short said: "It was tough early and it was a pretty spicy wicket with some quick bowlers. It was nice to bat second and get a bit of dew and skid off the wicket.

"They came hard with a Test match length but the shine wears off and it gets a bit easier. When we bowled, our guys hit the right length and let the ball do the talking."

Despite having won four of their five games, the Fire have a negative net run rate of -0.081, while leaders Trent Rockets are on +0.760.

The Brave, who have now played more matches than any other side in the men's tournament, fell to a fourth defeat in six and are facing a battle to advance.

Sports.title: Nygren spares Hogh blushes as Celtic begin title defence with win
Sports.content:
Celtic made a winning start to their Scottish Premiership title defence with a 1-0 victory over battling Dundee at Celtic Park.

After Rangers had been held by Dundee United on Friday night and Hearts were beaten at Aberdeen on Saturday, Celtic capitalised on opening-round slip-ups from their rivals thanks to Benjamin Nygren's second-half header.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Benjamin Nygren scores Celtic's first goal of the season with a header from a great cross from Kieran Tierney to give the home side the lead against Dundee

It wasn't all plain sailing though, with goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo required to make a super stop to prevent Dundee sub Ashley Hay heading in a late leveller.

Martin O'Neill's side should have been out of sight by then but had seen club-record £11m signing Kasper Hogh spurn two good opportunities inside the first 13 minutes. He then blew a third good chance of the night on 85 minutes, shooting wide from close range before captain Callum McGregor pinged a right-foot shot against a post.

While Hogh laboured, fellow new attacker Camilo Duran looked lively cutting in from the right but it was last season's top scorer Nygren who came up with the crucial moment from Kieran Tierney's fine cross.

Image: Celtic's Benjamin Nygren celebrates scoring

Dundee boss Steven Pressley had called on his side to be "positive" at the home of the champions and his side were certainly that, with Charlie Reilly clipping the side-netting in a good first half from the visitors and on another night they could have profited from their 11 shots and Celtic's wastefulness.

Celtic's need to strengthen their squad further this summer is clear and they will need to find some more sharpness before the key Champions League qualifier against LASK in two-and-a-half weeks' time. But, unlike their title rivals, they are up and running with three points.

The key moments from Celtic Park

9: MISS! A misplaced pass at the back from Dundee sees Kasper Hogh played into the box - but he skews his shot badly wide of the near post. "That's an awful finish," said Chris Sutton on co-commentary.

13: MISS! Hogh is off target again, failing to divert Benjamin Nygren's shot into the bottom corner.

15: SIDE-NETTING! Charlie Reilly clips the side-netting with Dundee's first shot of the game.

34: SHOT! Owen Bevan has Dundee's first shot on target - but it's an easy stop for Viljami Sinisalo.

38: WIDE! Arne Engels looks primed to head Celtic in front but nods his effort the wrong side of the post.

41: SAVE! Kieran Tierney bursts into the box but his drilled shot is well saved by Owen Goodman - Celtic's first shot on target at the 10th attempt.

52: GOAL! Tierney swings in a cross for Nygren to head in the opener from close range.

67: SAVE! Hyun-Jun Yang strikes from 30 yards but Goodman gets down well to make the save.

82: BIG SAVE! Sinisalo does brilliantly to get down to his right to get a hand to Ashley Hay's header which was going towards the bottom corner.

85: ANOTHER MISS FOR HOGH! Hogh passes up his third good chance of the night, stabbing a close-range shot wide of the post.

85: OFF THE POST! Callum McGregor drives into the D and bends a right-foot shot at goal but the ball pings back off the post.

Hogh: 'I have to adapt to the grass'

Celtic's Kasper Hogh speaking to Sky Sports:

"I have to go to some shooting practice, I had a couple of chances today!

"I was just happy to be on the pitch and to help my team-mates win. It doesn't matter if it's me scoring, we won and that's the most important thing.

"I have to adapt to the grass. That's a different thing for me."

O'Neill critical of Celtic performance - but backs Hogh

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Martin O'Neill backs Kasper Hogh to deliver goals despite missed chances, while addressing Alistair Johnston's future, Celtic's transfer plans and their Champions League ambitions.

Celtic boss Martin O'Neill speaking to Sky Sports:

"It was tough. I didn't think we played particularly well throughout the game, yet amazingly we created some really good chances. Maybe could have scored a number of goals. But overall in terms of play, decisiveness and things, I thought that was lacking from our game. Overall, we can do much better."

On Hogh: "I think he will score goals for us. I always want a centre forward to just get hold of the ball at times, but he's getting to know the players. When he knows everybody's name, including mine, then he'll be an asset to us."

On transfers: "It would be nice if all that transfer speculation went away, which I'm sure it probably won't. It would be nice to go away and nice to get a few more players in, which we're trying to do."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kris Boyd and James McFadden believe Celtic shouldn't let either of Alistair Johnston or Arne Engels go unless they get the right price and have a ready made replacement ready to come in.

Wilson: Better to come from Celtic

Former Celtic defender Mark Wilson on Sky Sports:

"The objective is to get three points and get off to the best possible start.

"I think if you can match it with a performance that's sparkling and slick, then fantastic and you entertain the crowd. I don't think they quite got that, they got it in bits and pieces.

"Second half was certainly better than the first half and they were more adventurous with their passing at times.

"There will be better to come from this Celtic team this season, it's a wee bit transitional for them at the minute."

Pressley proud of Dundee performance

Dundee boss Steven Pressley speaking to Sky Sports:

"I thought we were really brave. Brave in and out of possession. We were aggressive, we had pressure. We showed a lot of composure with the ball against a very good Celtic side, probably their strongest side and I thought our work ethic was incredible as well tonight.

"I think we set real standards for the season tonight with the way we went about the game, so I couldn't be prouder of the group. I said pre-game that the winning of this game for ourselves isn't always the result, it's the performance and we gave it a terrific performance tonight.

"We can't underestimate the gulf in finance between the two clubs.In terms of our heart, our desire, our resilience at times, our bravery, I couldn't be prouder of the way they went about things. They showed those words in abundance."

Sports.title: Serena to resume comeback alongside sister Venus in Cincinnati
Sports.content:
Serena and Venus Williams are set to play at the Cincinnati Open after being awarded a wild card for the women's doubles draw.

Serena made a sensational return to tennis during the grass-court season after almost four years out of the professional game, but the 44-year-old suffered a knee injury during a first-round singles loss which led to her and Venus withdrawing from the doubles at the All England Club.

Serena played doubles in London at Queen's Club and at the Berlin Open - but not alongside Venus on either occasion - as she prepared for Wimbledon.

Venus, who turned 46 in June, has also been given a wild card for the singles draw in Cincinnati. She is seeking a first singles victory of 2026 having lost in the first round of all eight of the tournaments she has entered this year.

Venus has had slightly more success playing doubles in 2026, claiming a sole victory at two of the six tournaments she has entered. She most recently played alongside Britain's Katie Boulter in Madrid and breakout star Alexandra Eala in Berlin.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Judy Murray discusses Serena Williams' comeback to tennis.

Among the other players to be awarded singles wild cards for the tournament were fellow Americans Sloane Stephens and Taylor Townsend.

As a doubles pairing, the Williams sisters have won 14 Major titles and three Olympic gold medals. They last took the court for a doubles match together at the 2022 US Open and will be playing the Cincinnati Open for the first time as a team.

Sports.title: Graham stars as Welsh Fire upset Southern Brave in last-ball thriller
Sports.content:
Welsh Fire turned the form table on its head to defeat The Hundred table-toppers Southern Brave in a last-ball thriller in Cardiff.

Until the last dozen deliveries, it looked like it was to be rinse and repeat for the visitors, putting up what seemed a below-par total before unleashing their formidable bowling attack to squeeze the opposition to defeat - but brilliant cameos from Heather Graham and Niamh Holland at the death saw Fire triumph in an absolute thriller to keep their hopes alive.

Having lost their last two games in addition to being hampered by the loss of their captain Sophie Devine - ruled out of the tournament with a calf injury - Welsh Fire desperately needed a win against the unbeaten league-leaders.

In their previous five wins, Brave had twice defended 126-7 and 140-3, and chased 115 and 117. They are curiously the only team in the men's or women's competition not to have gone past 140.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lizelle Lee looked to have lost control of the ball but regained her composure just in time to stump Ella McCaughan.

Today, their batting misfired again after Sophie Molineux became the first captain to win the toss and bat in this year's women's tournament.

The openers were gone after 16 balls, and Laura Wolvaardt and Jemimah Rodrigues rebuilt in uncharacteristically pedestrian style. Batting was not easy on a turning pitch, and the Brave stumbled to 121-5, Welsh Fire seemingly on top but aware of Brave's bowling threat.

Georgia Voll went past Sophia Dunkley to become the 2026 competition's leading run-scorer but departed for 11 to Tilly Corteen-Coleman's second ball, with young spinner having Ella McCaughan stumped from her fifth.

And when the economical Issy Wong hit Devine's replacement Orla Prendergast's stumps, Brave were squeezing the opposition in habitual style, despite bowling an unusual number of wides.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sarah Glenn takes a great catch to get the first wicket of the innings.

A Lauren Bell slower ball deceived Wareham to leave Fire in real trouble, needing 52 off 38 but an unexpected six-four combo from debutant Grace Thompson, in for Em Arlott, put the cat amongst the pigeons. She was then caught, and it looked like the nous and skills of Molineux and Bell would see Brave home.

But that was to reckon without another young talent in Holland. She swept and drove boundaries to leave three runs needed off two, then Lee should have run Graham out but dropped the ball to leave a single needed off the last ball. And Graham gleefully hit Bell through the infield to spark the celebrations.

Match Hero Graham said: "For Niamh to come in at the end, run really well with me, and get a few boundaries away herself; the win is more for those guys than me. It's always nerve-wracking in situations like that. I've played for a lot of years now and been in plenty of tight games, so you just rely on those past experiences to help get you over the line."

Sports.title: Hearn wants £1m per-year deal for Pollock from Northampton
Sports.content:
England star Henry Pollock is expected to seek a significant pay rise to remain at Northampton after agent Eddie Hearn said he is worth at least £1m a year.

Pollock's current contract with Saints expires next summer and is thought to pay around £150,000 a year.

Since agreeing that deal in December 2024, the back-row forward has made his international debut, toured with the British and Irish Lions and helped Northampton win the 2025-26 Gallagher Prem title.

"He's certainly a seven-figure player," Hearn told Telegraph Sport.

"The way rugby's going and what Pollock is doing, his value over the next couple of years will skyrocket, and I think the value of rugby will."

Sports.title: Eala beats Pegula at DC Open to claim first WTA Tour title
Sports.content:
Rising Filipino star Alexandra Eala came from a set down against Jessica Pegula to claim the first WTA Tour singles title of her career at the DC Open.

Eala had trailed by a set when the match was suspended because of heavy rain on Sunday, but the 21-year-old turned the contest round on Monday to claim a 4-6 6-4 6-0 victory.

The victory made Eala the first Filipino to win a singles title on the tour, completing the same career-defining breakthrough that the Washington tournament once gave Pegula when she claimed her first WTA Tour title in 2019.

"At the beginning of the week, there's no way I would have thought that I would be holding this trophy," Eala said. "Winning a 500 (level tournament) is insane. It's an incredible milestone for me."

Eala's popularity soared during the grass-court season as she beat some of the sport's biggest names on runs to the semi-finals in Berlin and last 16 at Wimbledon.

She has swiftly become a huge star in the Philippines, and the nation's flags were dotted throughout the Stadium Court in Washington as chants for Eala routinely outweighed those for Pegula.

It capped a week in which the rising star transformed the atmosphere around the tournament while reaching her first WTA Tour final in her debut at the hard-court tune-up for the US Open.

The two traded breaks midway through the opening set, with Pegula breaking again at 4-4 and serving out the set at love. The players held through the opening three games of the second set before heavy rain suspended play on Sunday afternoon, with Eala up 2-1.

When they returned on Monday, the momentum belonged to Eala. She stormed back to claim the second set, then swept through the third.

She won each game of the final set of the match to complete the comeback in an hour and 47 minutes of court time.

In the process, she defeated all three of the tournament's top seeds and turned the biggest week of her career into a historic first title.

Eala received congratulations from former eight-division boxing champion Manny Pacquiao, who wrote on social media that her comeback showed the "heart of a Filipino" before calling her "our new champion."

Fritz beats Jodar to men's title

In the men's final later on Monday, third seed Taylor Fritz defeated Rafael Jodar 7-6 (7-2) 6-4.

Fritz broke the Spaniard twice early in the second set and eventually converted his fifth championship point after letting four earlier opportunities slip away.

Fritz lay on the court for several moments after winning the 11th title of his career, then got to his feet with a roll of his eyes as the tension of finally closing out the match gave way.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Mubadala DC Open final between Taylor Fritz and Rafael Jodar.

"It was just relief, like thank God I got it done, thank God the match is over," Fritz said of the moment. "It wasn't so much as like a celebration... I can just lay down for a second."

The victory delivered a first title for Fritz since June 2025, and a first on a hard court since February 2024.

It was the first time the 19-year-old Jodar had reached a final at an ATP 500 event, with his only previous ATP Tour final - and title - coming at the lower-level Marrakech Open on clay in April.

Sports.title: More European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifies
Sports.content:
European countries began turning their backs on Gianni Infantino as moves intensified across the globe to end his crisis-hit tenure as Fifa president.

The Football Association was the highest-profile of several Uefa member associations to drop its support for Infantino’s proposed re-election next year. It will write to Fifa confirming it no longer endorses Infantino for a fourth term in charge after the intense controversy surrounding his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.

Wales and Serbia publicly confirmed that they had withdrawn their backing, following a lead taken by Finland last week. Along with the FA, those federations had all previously written letters in favour of Infantino prolonging his tenure but patience has run out across the continent. The Swedish Football Association, which was one of five European FAs not to write letters of support, issued a statement confirming it would oppose his candidature in the election in March.

The FA had previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the United Kingdom’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.

It is joined by the Football Association of Wales, which said in a statement: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

View image in fullscreen Several Uefa nations are mobilising against the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Pierre Albouy/Reuters

Striking a similar tone, the Football Association of Serbia explained recent events had “seriously damaged the reputation and credibility of both Fifa and its president”, saying a withdrawal was “the only logical and rational step”.

In a sign that consensus may not be easy to achieve, the Swiss Football Association stopped short of abandoning its countryman. Instead it asked for “another personal exchange of views with the Fifa president” and said it would “continue to review the developments surrounding Fifa” before the leadership election.

More countries are, however, expected to withdraw their support for Infantino in what amounts to a vote of no confidence. The intended effect is for the embattled president to resign although some insiders are braced for a drawn-out process. While the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which runs the sport in North and Central America, have both strongly criticised Infantino there has been no move by any of their individual federations to call back letters in favour of his re-election.

Ensuring they do so may be critical to the ongoing efforts to remove Infantino quickly. There is acknowledgement in some parts of Europe that other continents should be seen taking the lead if enough of a groundswell for his departure is to be reached. Only 15 countries have publicly supported Infantino since he shelved the FFE project on Saturday but there is an appetite to form a broad coalition against his re-election quickly.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is a contender to take over if Infantino is deposed. Montagliani is understood to be in consensus with the Uefa and AFC hierarchies that new leadership is needed at Fifa.

View image in fullscreen Victor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after the World Cup final. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA

In another blow to Infantino, lawyers acting for Uefa have ordered him and other staff to identify, locate and preserve all documents related to the FFE scheme. Their letter includes Arsène Wenger, the Fifa chief of global football development, among those obliged to comply with its order. It says Uefa is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan”.

Thrive Eternal, the investment firm that had been expected to lead a group taking a 20% stake in FFE, is believed to have been sent a similar letter. JP Morgan, which was enlisted for an advisory role in the scheme, is also understood to have received an order related to FFE.

On Monday afternoon the US State Department denied reports that Infantino had been scheduled to meet Marco Rubio, the United States secretary of state, in a bid to stoke up support for his continued reign as president.

Sports.title: Charlton up for sale again as US owners look to cash in after three years
Sports.content:
Charlton’s US owners have put the club up for sale just three years after taking over at the Valley. The ownership group is understood to have engaged Oakwell Sports Advisory to find what would be the club’s fifth owner in the past six years.

In a sales deck sent to potential investors, which has been seen by the Guardian, Oakwell describes Charlton as “the last remaining football club upside opportunity in London”. Oakwell also claims that Charlton would provide new owners with an opportunity for five to 10 times equity growth through promotion to the Premier League, commercial expansion and investment in women’s football.

Oakwell did the deal that led to the Bournemouth owner, Bill Foley, buying the Prem rugby club Exeter Chiefs this summer, and is helping the Rugby Football League to secure external investment.

Charlton’s location in south-east London is a plus, while the Valley is a modern stadium with a capacity of 27,000, but the club do not own the ground, which belongs to the hated former owner Roland Duchâtelet. Having considered looking at alternative sites, last year Charlton extended the lease on the Valley until 2040.

Charlton have repeatedly changed hands since the fans forced out Duchâtelet in 2020, when the club had three owners in quick succession. Duchâtelet sold Charlton to East Street Investments for just £1 in January 2020, but the consortium led initially by the former football agent Matt Southall collapsed amid in‑fighting and an acrimonious court case, with the club eventually bought by the Danish-American business Thomas Sandgaard later that year. In 2023, Sandgaard sold Charlton to a group of five US investors called Global Football Partners (GFP) led by Gabriel Brener via their UK subsidiary, SE7 Partners.

Under GFP, Charlton returned to the Championship for the first time in five years in 2025 by winning the League One playoff final at Wembley, while the women’s team were promoted to WSL1 last season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

GFP paid around £15m for Charlton three years ago but, having invested in the stadium and training ground and seen Nathan Jones’s side consolidate the club in the Championship, will be looking for several times that figure. Charlton declined to comment.

Sports.title: Benjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defence
Sports.content:
Benjamin Nygren was quickly back on the goal trail as Celtic began the defence of their Premiership title with a 1-0 home win over Dundee. Before the game, Celtic fans cheered as the captain, Callum McGregor, unfurled the flag which confirmed again a 14th title win in 15 seasons.

It was all a bit flat in a first half with Martin O’Neill’s side struggling to get into their stride as the visitors posed problems. However, the Sweden midfielder Nygren, so prolific last season with 21 goals, struck with a close-range header in the 52nd minute and the goal proved enough to keep the three points in Glasgow as a new season got up and running for the champions.

Celtic supporters continue to call for new recruits to the squad but Camilo Durán, the Colombian striker signed from Qarabag reportedly for £5.5m, and Kasper Høgh, the Denmark forward who cost a club-record £11m plus add-ons from Bodø/Glimt, made their debuts.

Alistair Johnston and Arne Engels, both attracting transfer interest, also started for the champions while the Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman came in for his debut.

Høgh fired wide in the ninth minute after being set up by Nygren, then the Dane redirected an effort from Nygren past a post. Moments later at the other end, as the ball bounced around Celtic’s penalty area, Dundee’s Charlie Reilly hit the side netting with a shot from 12 yards.

View image in fullscreen Celtic's Kasper Høgh (left) reacts after a missed chance against Dundee. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Steven Pressley’s well-drilled outfit were finding joy with the high ball, either crosses or throw-ins and in the 33rd minute defender Owen Bevan got his head to the ball in the box but the Celtic goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo gathered comfortably.

Five minutes later, Engels missed the best chance of the match to that point, unmarked in the visitors’ box, he headed a cross from Kieran Tierney past a post, before the Celtic left-back drew a fine save from Goodman with a close-range drive.

The home side faltered at the start of the second half but when Tierney curled in a cross from the left, Nygren headed past Goodman from inside the box and the growing anxiety subsided.

Quick Guide Celtic to play LASK in Champions League playoff Show Celtic will face LASK in the Champions League playoffs. Martin O’Neill’s side were drawn out first against the Austrian champions. The Linz-based club won the Austrian Bundesliga for the second time last season, finishing two points ahead of the defending champions Sturm Graz. The Hoops avoided a potential rematch with Kairat Almaty, who knocked Celtic out on penalties at the same stage last season following a goalless 210 minutes of action. The first leg will take place on 18/19 August, with the second leg the following week. PA Media Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

O’Neill’s side probed with more purpose, the fans got more excited and the noise levels increased while Dundee’s attacks were more sporadic and less convincing, although the pace of Joe Bevan was cause for concern for the Parkhead defence. In the 67th minute Goodman threw himself down to his right to save a long-distance drive from forward Yang Hyun-jun.

Celtic remained in control but as the second goal refused to arrive and the clock ticked on, some nerves returned. In the 82nd minute, Sinisalo pulled off a terrific save from the Dundee substitute Ashley Hay’s glancing header.

Høgh missed another chance when he slid a shot past a post from six yards before McGregor cracked the upright with an effort from inside Dundee’s penalty area; James Forrest bent the rebound wide of the target.

Sports.title: Newcastle reject first bid from Arsenal for captain Bruno Guimarães
Sports.content:
Arsenal have stepped up their attempt to sign Bruno Guimarães by finally beginning formal transfer negotiations and making an opening offer, which Newcastle have rejected.

Guimarães met Newcastle’s incoming manager, Matthias Jaissle, for the first time on Monday at the team’s pre-season training camp at La Manga after a post-World Cup holiday in Brazil.

There had been suggestions that the 28-year-old midfielder would fly to London for a medical at Arsenal, but instead he boarded a commercial flight to Spain.

Once at La Manga, he was expected to tell Jaissle of his determination to swap Tyneside for north London, but everything hinges on whether Arsenal are prepared to meet Newcastle’s valuation for a player with two years remaining on his contract.

While executives at Arsenal believe Guimarães is worth a maximum of £70m – and a bid in that ballpark was rejected on Monday – Newcastle value their captain at around £80m.

If some sort of compromise seems likely given Arsenal – negotiating, initially, through intermediaries – have spent much of this summer in pursuit of a midfielder at the top of Mikel Arteta’s shopping list, Newcastle are under no pressure to sell.

View image in fullscreen Guimarães has had several battles with Arsenal over the past few seasons. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

Indeed, having sold Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer, they would prefer to offer Jaissle the benefit of Guimarães’s talent and experience as he rebuilds the squad.

The 38-year-old was believed to be keen to assess the Brazilian’s mindset as he begins preparations for the opening Premier League match at home against Liverpool two weeks on Sunday. Although the former Al‑Ahli and RB Salzburg manager is still to be officially confirmed as Howe’s successor, Jaissle has been with his new squad since arriving in southern Spain on Saturday. Newcastle are waiting for the completion of some final paperwork before formalising his appointment.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

One signing completed by Newcastle on Monday involved Lukas Hornicek’s £26m move from Braga. The 24-year-old Czechia goalkeeper is expected to replace Nick Pope as the team’s first choice, with Pope now likely to leave St James’ Park.

Hornicek caught Newcastle’s eye after seven clean sheets during Braga’s run to the Europa League semi-finals last season. At 6ft 6in, he cuts an imposing figure in goal and has been highly praised for the sort of high-calibre footwork that should improve Newcastle’s ability to play out from the back.

Hull had hoped to recruit Hornicek, but he turned down a move to the promoted club last month.

Sports.title: Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may work | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Sometimes what is needed is something different.

There is a long history in football of counterintuitive thinking being successful, of the benefits of creative tension, of adding grit to the oyster to generate the pearl, but even so, the news that talks between Vinícius Júnior and Arsenal on personal terms are progressing comes as something of a shock. Mikel Arteta’s great followers of a blueprint adding a free spirit like the Brazilian? Really?

Vinícius returns to Real Madrid this week after the World Cup with movement on his future expected relatively soon. He has 12 months remaining on his contract and Madrid are keen either to tie him down to a new deal or to sell him while he will attract at least some kind of fee. As their squad rebuild goes on under José Mourinho, Madrid’s position is readily understandable. They have already signed Bernardo Silva, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella and Ibrahima Konaté this summer; removing Vinícius’s £420,000 a week (about $30m/year) basic wages significantly increases their financial headroom.

There’s been a sense since Kylian Mbappé joined Madrid two years ago that having him and Vinícius together left the squad unbalanced. Why would you need two rapid forwards who both prefer to cut in from the left, particularly when Rodrygo, who tended to be consigned to the right before tearing his ACL in March, would also prefer to play from the left? Yan Diomandé is likely to confirm his move to Real Madrid from RB Leipzig this week. Although the Ivorian has said he would rather play on the right, he too has spent much of his career on the left.

More broadly, Vinícius does not seem a natural Mourinho player. His pace and technical excellence are undoubted, but he has never been the most diligent at fulfilling his defensive responsibilities. Mourinho likes a forward who can improvise, and worked successfully with Cristiano Ronaldo at Madrid, but it’s difficult to see how he could indulge more than one such player at a time, and Mbappé will take precedence.

But those concerns about tracking, about the willingness to stick to a gameplan, about the capacity to retain possession are just as relevant to Arteta as they are to Mourinho – arguably more so, as Arteta believes far more in structured attacking planning than Mourinho. Is Vinícius, after years of freedom at Madrid, really going to accept those rigid structures?

It’s been fairly clear since the second half of last season that Arsenal would be looking to strengthen their left side. The sale of Leandro Trossard to Beşiktaş did not come as a huge surprise. The 31-year-old is reliable and played a valuable role last season, starting 21 of the 38 league games and coming off the bench on a further 10 occasions, but there is not much stardust about him. Gabriel Martinelli started 11 league games and came off the bench 19 times, and his pace can be a great asset, but it’s no longer clear that he is at his best on the left. The signing of Eberechi Eze last summer looked like an attempt to add creativity from that flank but his tendency to drift infield when Arteta needs his left-sided forward to stay wide meant that by the end of the season he tended to be used centrally behind a striker.

Vinícius would give Arsenal greater attacking thrust. At his best, under Carlo Ancelotti, he could transform a game in seconds. His pace, dribbling ability and finishing mean that no matter how stale a game seems to have gone, no matter how under pressure his team may be, they are never more than seven or eight seconds from a potential goal. It’s easy to see why Arsenal are tempted by him. He would immediately be their highest-profile player, adding a sense of direction to a summer that, at least from a recruitment point of view, has seemed to be drifting. Arsenal missed out on Morgan Rogers, who joined Chelsea, while Julián Álvarez, who would seem a much more natural fit on the Arsenal left, appears more likely to go to Barcelona, if sufficient financial levers can be pulled.

But the fact Vinícius is not a natural fit may be part of the attraction. It was, after all, the season after signing Erling Haaland, far from a typical Pep Guardiola player, that Manchester City won the treble. A player who does not quite fit, who kicks against the general philosophy, can make a process team less predictable. The friction can produce valuable sparks.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Haaland, it’s fair to say, is a different personality from Vinícius and, as a center-forward, there was never a worry he was going to leave his full-back exposed. Vinícius is a bigger risk. He would certainly be an expensive one, not just in terms of his own salary but the inflationary pressure that could have on wages at the club more generally.

But he would also add a dash Arsenal have lacked that would make the accusation of being dead-ball plodders hard to sustain. And with Trossard gone, there is a left-sided hole that needs filling.

Sports.title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time
Sports.content:
It is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Totti dusted it off for the internet generation at Euro 2000.

It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means. The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.

A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder. Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards, asked the man himself what constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible. Rob Smyth

View image in fullscreen The man himself, pictured earlier this year. Photograph: Björn Steinz/The Guardian

Antonin Panenka, 1976

Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)

This one needs no introduction. RS

Antonin Panenka, 1979

Czechoslovakia 2-0 France

The next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsy with a sensual chip in a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80. RS

Diego Maradona, 1984

Napoli training

Most of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner to ensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d already seen him do it in open play. RS

Eric Cantona, 1989

Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)

In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackle of comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowd and tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot, he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset. Daniel Harris

Gianluca Vialli, 1990

Monaco 2-2 Sampdoria

In the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure: against Genoa in the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90. The first was against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16, the second in the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0 in the final. RS

Michal Bilek, 1990

Czechoslovakia 5-1 USA

It’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976. He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!” RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

Nottingham Forest 1-1 Tottenham

Nobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led to a brief post-match discussion in which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. This one was particularly sweet – the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final. RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

England 1-1 Brazil

A kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearer chuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak, as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record. Jonathan Liew

View image in fullscreen With a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos. Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

Eric Cantona, 1994

Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)

In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final, he’d gently rolled two penalties into the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the way only for the kick to sail over the bar as United lost 6-5. DH

Djalminha, 1995

Guarani 2-1 Internacional

Brazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for his signature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot. The first of many was scored against Sergio Goycoechea, whose elastic penalty saves had taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1996

Sheffield United 0-1 Aston Villa

Dwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule, but Yorke was true to his word and settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.” RS

Gianluca Vialli, 1996

Chelsea 2-4 Wimbledon

There’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. But Vialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line by a very different kind of chip earlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1998

Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal

“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman, who was Panenka-ed on the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called, Yorke sidefooted wide. RS

John Eyre, 1999

Torquay 0-1 Hull City

If only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue as this piece of effrontery floated gently past him. RS

Francesco Totti, 2000

Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)

In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti, whose falling leaf penalty foxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation. John Brewin

View image in fullscreen Francesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century. Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty Images

Mixu Paatelainen, 2001

Hibernian 0-0 Hearts

A last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares. Mixu Paatelainen only took it because Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion. RS

Thierry Henry, 2003

Arsenal 3-2 Newcastle

Five days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner was teased softly down the middle by Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was just trolling Ruud van Nistelrooy. RS

View image in fullscreen Thierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle. Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images

Mickaël Landreau, 2004

Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)

For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka. Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup. Jeff Rueter

Liam Lawrence, 2004

Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)

Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). On the Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.

double quotation mark LL I’m gonna dink it. BH No you’re not. LL I am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final. BH Liam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.

He dinked that ball against the bar – “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.” RS

Helder Postiga, 2004

Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)

Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty, a kick so under-amped it barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp. JB

Peter Crouch, 2006

England 6-0 Jamaica

The then-Liverpool striker scored an England hat-trick as part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ball well over the bar from 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.” Will Unwin

View image in fullscreen Judging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Artem Milevskiy, 2006

Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)

You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it came after 120 minutes of the most soporific football ever played. RS

Zinedine Zidane, 2006

Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)

The nerve to do it in a World Cup final. The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar, past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – until Marco Materazzi and the anger took over. Taha Hashim

View image in fullscreen Zinedine Zidane steps up… Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen … and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA Images

Yann Kermogant, 2010

Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)

To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier, dollied his kick into the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even has his own Bonnie Tyler adaptation. JB

Sebastián Abreu, 2010

Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)

If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one of the first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup. A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions. RS

Andrea Pirlo, 2012

England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)

When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ball wafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successes finishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards. DH

View image in fullscreen Andrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart. Illustration: Matthias Schräder/AP

Sergio Ramos, 2012

Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)

For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-final against Portugal. Bruno Alves missed Portugal’s next kick and Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final. RS

Maicosuel, 2012

Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)

The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenka was saved in a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.” RS

Graziano Pellè, 2012

SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)

Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpah to try a Pellènka? RS

Rogério Ceni, 2013

São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)

No surprise that one of the great goalscoring keepers should beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he was fractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically. RS

Alexandre Pato, 2013

Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)

Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to take one of the worst Panenkas ever seen. RS

Alexis Sánchez, 2015

Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)

It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone. His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – and unlike Czechoslovakia in 1976, they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria. RS

Aaron Ramsey, 2017

Serbia 1-1 Wales

The Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramsey unwittingly did so by scoring a Panenka at the same end of the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one. RS

View image in fullscreen Aaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

George Calintaru, 2017

Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua Bucuresti

A Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger. RS

Fedor Smolov, 2018

Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)

Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend that Fedor Smolov’s opening attempt lacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour. JR

Lionel Messi, 2020

Barcelona 2-2 Atlético Madrid

If you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium, you might as well do it in style. RS

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

Fara Williams, 2020

Reading 3-1 Aston Villa

This unusual penalty from Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority. RS

Ademola Lookman, 2020

West Ham 1-0 Fulham

During his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the game but his feeble chip landed straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare moment of post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.” Yara El-Shaboury

Santi Cazorla, 2021

Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al Sadd

Not many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right foot against Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021. RS

Sergio Agüero, 2021

Man City 1-2 Chelsea

City were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided to chip down the middle; Édouard Mendy almost fell for it but had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüero issued a public apology. WU

View image in fullscreen Sergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty Images

Marta, 2022

France 2-1 Brazil

Birthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against France in sublime fashion.JR

Karim Benzema, 2022

Manchester City 4-3 Real Madrid

A moment of mischief at the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final. RS

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Achraf Hakimi, 2022

Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)

If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final, you might as well do it in style. RS

Gaëtane Thiney, 2023

Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FC

We can’t say for sure that this is the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition. RS

Antoine Mille, 2024

Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)

In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after saving one of the more pitiful Panenkas ever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille. RS

Marta, 2025

Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego Wave

If you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025, chipping in off the underside of the crossbar to secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill. Tom Garry

Alexia Putellas, 2025

Roma 0-4 Barcelona

Even the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenka harmlessly over the crossbar during a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner. TG

Tiaguinho, 2025

Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)

A Panenka is a dish best served cold. RS

Brahim Díaz, 2026

Morocco 3-0* Senegal

Brahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenka was easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding. Then again … YE-S

View image in fullscreen Brahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought… Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Mohamed Salah, 2026

Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)

Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is that Mo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australia was the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream. RS

Sports.title: ‘They are terrified’: Como spark row with fans over controversial new stadium policy
Sports.content:
Como, the surprise package of last season’s Serie A, who qualified for the Champions League for the first time, will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules that have sparked a row among supporters.

The club, coached by the former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fàbregas, said on Monday that supporters “who miss more than three home matches without what it considers a valid reason risk having their season tickets revoked”. Another new rule bans fans from wearing the opposing team’s shirts or scarves anywhere in the stadium except the away section.

“Demand for tickets far exceeds supply and, for that reason, I asked the club to find ways to ensure tickets for the [Giuseppe Sinigaglia stadium] end up in the hands of genuine Como supporters – those who want to be there to back the team,” the chair, Mirwan Suwarso, said in a lengthy statement on Instagram.

“There have been too many occasions when away fans have celebrated inside our home sections, while Como supporters, who would have proudly backed the team, were unable to get a ticket.”

On the ban on wearing rival teams’ shirts, scarves and other symbols outside the away end, the club said the measure was introduced for safety reasons. “Our aim is to make the Sinigaglia the true home of our fans and a fortress for our team,” said Suwarso. “We want to ensure the Sinigaglia remains a place where grandparents feel comfortable bringing their grandchildren, where families can enjoy football together, and where passion never crosses the line into disrespect.”

On social media, many criticised the measures as overly harsh, arguing that work commitments, health issues or family responsibilities can prevent people from attending matches without making them any less loyal to the club.

La Provincia, Como’s local newspaper, said its newsroom had received dozens of calls and emails from concerned supporters. “Some worried about health problems or being unable to attend because of bad weather, as well as people who frequently travel for work,” the newspaper wrote. “They are terrified and all asking the same question: will our season tickets be taken away?”

Italy’s national newspaper, Corriere della Sera, reporting reactions from supporters on social media, quoted one fan asking: “Do we need to be accompanied by our parents when we hand in our excuse, like at school?”
