Political tensions sharpen too, with Zambia days from a general election and a Ugandan treason trial pushing to proceed without the accused opposition figure in the dock.

Sudan — RSF Vows to Retake Capital

Commander pledges new offensive

Rapid Support Forces commander Mohamed Hamdan ‘Hemedti’ Dagalo released a video ordering his fighters to seize Khartoum, as paramilitary assaults spread across Kordofan and Darfur. The promise of a fresh offensive deepens what is already the continent’s gravest humanitarian crisis.

An estimated 500,000 people remain trapped under an RSF siege in El-Obeid, and a reported drone strike on a court in North Darfur is said to have killed dozens. The mood across the country is one of dread, with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.

Nigeria — Oil Money and a Strained Naira

Crude exports bring in trillions

Nigeria earned about 24.02 trillion naira (roughly US$17.6 billion) from 182.2 million barrels of crude exports in the first half of 2026. The figures offer a cautious relief but have not yet translated into a calmer foreign-exchange market.

The naira opened the week near 1,368 to the US dollar on the official market, reflecting persistent demand pressure. The big export haul and the weak currency sit side by side, leaving ordinary Nigerians and businesses watching the rate warily.

Sudan’s war is deepening even as West and East African currencies show cautious stability, leaving governance and security fears outweighing the modest economic good news.

Ghana — Cedi Under Heavy Pressure

Energy demand drains the currency

The cedi traded at 12.30 to the US dollar on 3 August, now down 8.89% year-to-date. This sharp fall reverses much of the 40.7% gain the currency posted in 2025.

Energy-sector dollar demand is outstripping supply, pulling the cedi lower and stirring fresh anxiety among importers and households. The slide threatens to push up living costs just as confidence was tentatively returning.

Uganda — Besigye Treason Trial Adjourned

Prosecution seeks trial in absentia

Prosecutors moved on 1 August to try opposition leader Kizza Besigye without him present after he collapsed in the dock and was admitted to intensive care. The treason case was adjourned to 4 August, when the court will weigh the in-absentia request.

The development has rattled Besigye’s supporters and drawn fresh international attention. The hearing resumes amid a tense atmosphere, with the defence arguing that a fair trial is impossible while the accused is hospitalised.

Kenya — Uhuru Convenes Opposition Talks

Azimio coalition meets

Former president Uhuru Kenyatta convened an Azimio coalition council meeting on 3 August, in what is widely read as a return to active opposition politics. The gathering is seen as an effort to build a united opposition front ahead of the 2027 general election.

The move signals a more combative chapter in Kenyan politics, with the former head of state stepping back into the arena. Ruto’s camp is watching closely, aware that a re-energised opposition could reshape the electoral landscape.

Zambia — Tense Countdown to the Ballot

Hichilema bets on economic record

Zambia holds a general election on 13 August, with President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second term. He is campaigning on his debt-restructuring achievements and a projected 4.3 percent growth rate, while challenger Brian Mundubile argues that ordinary Zambians are not yet feeling the benefit.

The country is in a state of tense anticipation, with the vote widely seen as a verdict on painful but promised reforms. Streets in Lusaka and the Copperbelt are calm but charged, as both sides make their final appeals.

South Africa — Xenophobia Row Tests Diplomacy

Deportations and cancelled visits

Fallout from anti-migrant violence continues after 27 July talks in Abuja, with South African deportations topping 109,000 by end-March 2026. Ghana cancelled President Ramaphosa’s planned August visit in protest, a sharp diplomatic signal.

The row is straining relations between two of the continent’s powerhouse nations. Nigerian and South African officials remain in contact, but the mood is one of frustration rather than resolution.

The Bigger Picture Africa’s security picture is darkening, driven by a resurgent RSF in Sudan that promises to fight its way back into Khartoum while half a million people are trapped under siege. Economic signals offer a mixed picture — Nigeria‘s oil revenue is strong but the naira stays weak, and Ghana’s cedi is sliding again after a promising 2025, as energy imports drain dollar supply. Political tests are piling up: Uganda’s treason trial of a hospitalised opposition leader resumes, Zambia heads to a pivotal election in ten days, and Kenya’s former president moves to rally the opposition.

Africa Intelligence Brief August 3: What We Are Watching

Today – South Africa–Ghana diplomatic tensions over anti-migrant violence remain high.

This week – Uganda’s Besigye treason case resumes on 4 August and Zambia votes on 13 August.

World.title: Recife Honors Luiz Gonzaga, King of Baião, in Second Street Tribute
World.content:
Music & Culture: Recife

Key Facts —Event. The second edition of the Tribute to King Luiz Gonzaga (Tributo ao Rei Luiz Gonzaga) was held on Sunday, 2 August 2026 in the Bairro do Recife, the historic waterfront district of Recife, Pernambuco. —Organizer. It was staged by the Movement in Support of Root Cultures and Pernambuco Artists, known as Rebuliço Cultural, to celebrate Gonzaga and defend traditional forró. —Program. Activities began at 2 p.m. with a gathering at Armazém do Campo on Rua da Moeda, followed by a street procession to Praça do Arsenal and an evening of music at the Bar Teatro Mamulengo. —Lineup. More than 20 artists and groups performed, among them Toinho Vanderlei, Aécio dos 8 Baixos, the 8-year-old accordionist Luna and the all-blind Banda Luar do Sertão. —Context. The date marks 37 years since Gonzaga, the ‘King of Baião,’ died on 2 August 1989.

Recife’s historic Bairro do Recife filled with accordions, drums and dance on 2 August as a grassroots cultural movement staged its second annual street tribute to Luiz Gonzaga, the ‘King of Baião.’

A Street Procession Through Recife’s Historic Waterfront

The tribute unfolded across the Bairro do Recife, also called Recife Antigo, the cobblestoned district where the city was founded in the 16th century. Once a decaying port zone, it has been restored into one of Recife’s main cultural hubs, lined with converted warehouses, bars and museums beside the rivers that ring the old town.

Activities began at 2 p.m. with a gathering at Armazém do Campo, a cultural space and market on Rua da Moeda. From there, musicians and cultural groups set off in a cortejo, or street procession, moving through Rua Dona Maria César, Avenida Rio Branco and the postcard-famous Rua do Bom Jesus before reaching Praça do Arsenal.

A cortejo is a defining feature of northeastern Brazilian street culture: an open, walking celebration that carries music and dance directly to passers-by rather than confining it to a stage. Sanfonas (accordions), zabumbas (bass drums) and dancers turned the district into a moving performance open to anyone who happened to be in the street.

Who Was Luiz Gonzaga, the King of Baião?

For readers new to Brazilian music, Luiz Gonzaga is one of the towering figures of the country’s 20th-century culture. Born in Exu, in the dry sertão backlands of Pernambuco, on 13 December 1912, he learned the accordion as a child under his father, Januário, himself a maker and player of the instrument.

Gonzaga turned the rhythms of the northeastern interior into national symbols, carrying the baião, the xote and the xaxado to audiences across Brazil from the 1940s onward. His songs told of drought, migration and the hardship and pride of sertão life, giving a national voice to a region often overlooked by the country’s wealthier coastal centers.

Classics such as ‘Asa Branca,’ ‘Xote das Meninas’ and ‘Súplica Cearense’ are still sung at Brazil’s June festivals and covered by artists nationwide. Gonzaga died on 2 August 1989; his home, a museum and his mausoleum are preserved at the Parque Asa Branca in Exu, where he is buried alongside his wife, Helena.

Forró, Baião and the Sound of Brazil’s Northeast

Forró is the umbrella name for a family of dance rhythms from northeastern Brazil, traditionally driven by a trio of accordion, zabumba and triangle. It is both a genre of music and a partner dance, and it anchors the São João (Saint John) festivities that sweep the region every June.

The baião, popularized by Gonzaga and the composer Humberto Teixeira in the late 1940s, is the rhythmic backbone of that tradition. For decades it shaped how the rest of Brazil imagined the northeast, and it later fed into movements from tropicália to contemporary Brazilian pop.

Defending the ‘forró tradicional,’ or roots forró, was an explicit goal of the Recife tribute. Organizers framed the event as a stand for the acoustic, community-rooted style against the amplified, pop-oriented forró eletrônico that dominates commercial radio and large festival stages today.

The Lineup: More Than 20 Popular Artists

The program moved in the late afternoon to the Bar Teatro Mamulengo, an intimate venue named for the mamulengo, the traditional glove-puppet theater of Pernambuco. More than 20 artists and groups shared the stage across the afternoon and evening.

Confirmed performers included Toinho Vanderlei, Daniel Bento and his Trio Pé de Serra, Aécio dos 8 Baixos, Wellington Santeiro and Eliezer Cavalcante, alongside the eight-year-old accordion prodigy Luna, billed as a sanfoneira mirim, or child accordion player.

The bill deliberately mixed generations and traditions. It featured the Bacamarteiros da Sobac, a black-powder musket-and-drum group from Cabo de Santo Agostinho, and the Banda Luar do Sertão, an ensemble made up of blind musicians, underscoring the event’s roots in community and popular culture rather than commercial celebrity.

Why the Tribute Matters for Pernambuco’s Cultural Movement

The tribute is organized by Rebuliço Cultural, a movement that supports what Brazilians call culturas raízes, or root cultures, and campaigns for the livelihoods of local artists. Now in its second edition, the event is building toward an annual place on the city’s calendar, as reported by Diario de Pernambuco.

Events like this matter economically as well as symbolically. Grassroots festivals sustain a network of working musicians, instrument makers, dancers and small venues that rarely benefit from big-budget productions, and they help keep the Bairro do Recife active outside the peak tourist season.

They also reinforce a broader civic project. In Pernambuco, the second of August, the anniversary of Gonzaga’s death, doubles as a symbolic day for northeastern culture, and street tributes like this one keep his legacy tied to a living, participatory tradition rather than a museum display.

What Foreign Visitors Should Know About Recife Antigo

The Bairro do Recife is walkable, compact and easy to reach from the city center, making it one of the most accessible entry points into Pernambuco’s cultural life for visitors. Its bars, galleries and the riverside Marco Zero square host frequent events, especially on weekends.

The district is also home to the Cais do Sertão museum, a modern institution dedicated to Gonzaga and to northeastern culture, which sits a short walk from the procession route. For travelers, it offers year-round context on the music that filled the streets during the tribute.

Street processions such as this one are free and open to the public, with no ticket required to follow the cortejo through the district. For foreign residents and visitors, they offer a rare, unfiltered look at living Brazilian popular culture, performed by the communities that created it.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where did the second Tribute to Luiz Gonzaga take place?

The second edition of the Tribute to King Luiz Gonzaga was held on Sunday, 2 August 2026 in the Bairro do Recife, the historic waterfront district of Recife, Pernambuco, in northeastern Brazil.

Who organized the tribute and who performed?

It was organized by Rebuliço Cultural, a movement supporting root cultures and Pernambuco artists. More than 20 acts performed, including Toinho Vanderlei, Aécio dos 8 Baixos, the young accordionist Luna and the all-blind Banda Luar do Sertão.

Who was Luiz Gonzaga?

Luiz Gonzaga (1912–1989) was a Brazilian singer and accordionist known as the ‘King of Baião.’ He turned northeastern rhythms such as the baião, xote and xaxado into national symbols and remains a defining figure of Brazilian music.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Pedra do Sal — the Monday roda de samba Free and open-air at the historic stone steps in Saúde where samba was born. Monday is one of Pedra do Sal’s two flagship nights — arrive around sunset and stay for the crowd.

Tonight at a Glance —Pedra do Sal Free open-air samba roda in Saúde, from early evening. Rio’s classic Monday night; the crowd spills onto the surrounding streets. —Samba do Trabalhador Moacyr Luz’s beloved roda at Clube Renascença, Andaraí. It starts in the late afternoon (around 4:30 pm) and runs into the evening; entry about R$30. —Samba da Gávea Intimate acoustic roda at Da Casa da Táta in Baixo Gávea from about 8 pm; musical couvert around R$30. —Bip Bip Honour-system corner bar in Copacabana with a Monday choro-leaning session from around 8 pm — tiny, local and cheap. —Getting home MetrôRio (R$7.90) runs until around midnight; after that use Uber or 99 door-to-door.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Monday belongs to samba in Rio. Start early if you want Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí, which fires up in the late afternoon and is winding down by mid-evening. From there the night moves to Pedra do Sal, which only really fills once it is dark, and to the intimate acoustic roda of Samba da Gávea from around 8 pm. Round it off with a chorinho nightcap at Bip Bip in Copacabana. Most theatres, big clubs and Lapa’s weekend circuit are quiet tonight — this is a rodas-not-megaclubs kind of evening.

—Meet locals: Samba do Trabalhador at Renascença, a roda with a devoted regular following.

—Date night: Samba da Gávea — acoustic, seated and intimate.

—Chill and conversation: Bip Bip — sidewalk tables and an honour-system fridge.

—Meet other expats: Pedra do Sal draws an international crowd on Monday nights.

Where to Go

Pedra do Sal — Saúde The birthplace of samba: an open-air street roda at the historic stone steps, with a mixed crowd of locals, tourists and music purists. Tonight: Weekly Monday samba roda from early evening. Free entry. Best time: Mondays and Fridays; arrive by 7 pm for a drink before the music starts. Cost: Free — you pay only for drinks and food from the surrounding stalls and bars. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde (Zona Portuária), near Praça Mauá. Getting there: VLT to Parada dos Museus or Praça Mauá, about a 10-minute walk; arrive and leave with the crowd. Good to know: No seating and it gets packed — bring small cash and keep your phone secured.

Samba do Trabalhador — Clube Renascença, Andaraí Moacyr Luz’s Monday institution: a seated, sing-along roda with one of the most loyal crowds in the city. Tonight: Every Monday, starting in the late afternoon (around 4:30 pm) and running into the evening. Best time: Go early — it fills fast and the club has been running at reduced capacity. Cost: Around R$30; half-price for students, seniors and Rio residents. Tickets often via Sympla. Address: Rua Barão de São Francisco, 54, Andaraí (Zona Norte). Getting there: No metro at the door; nearest is Uruguai or Saens Peña (Line 1) plus a short rideshare. Phone: (21) 3253-2322

Samba da Gávea — Da Casa da Táta, Baixo Gávea A small, un-amplified Monday roda with a rotating cast of first-rate musicians — a listening room, not a party. Tonight: Weekly Monday acoustic roda from about 8 pm. Best time: Arrive by 8 pm for a table; the room is small. Cost: Musical couvert around R$30, plus food and drink from the café. Address: Rua Professor Manuel Ferreira, 89, Gávea (Baixo Gávea), Zona Sul. Getting there: No metro in Gávea; easiest by taxi or rideshare. Phone: (21) 2511-0947

Bip Bip — Copacabana A legendary hole-in-the-wall where you grab your own drink from the fridge and tally your tab — low-key and thoroughly local. Tonight: Monday choro-leaning session from around 8 pm. Best time: Early evening; it spills onto the sidewalk once it fills. Cost: Famously cheap, honour-system fridge; no formal cover. Bring cash. Address: Rua Almirante Gonçalves, 50, Copacabana. Getting there: MetrôRio Cardeal Arcoverde or Siqueira Campos (Line 1), about a 10-minute walk.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

—Saúde: Historic port district and home of Pedra do Sal; lively when the roda is on, quiet otherwise.

—Andaraí: Residential Zona Norte; worth the trip on Mondays for Renascença.

—Gávea: Leafy Zona Sul bar hub (Baixo Gávea); compact and easy to move around.

—Copacabana: Always something open; Bip Bip is the local pick tonight.

—Lapa: Rio’s weekend nightlife heart — subdued on a Monday.

Getting Home Safe

MetrôRio runs until around midnight (single fare R$7.90), which covers an early exit from Copacabana or Centro. The samba rodas run later than that, so plan to leave by app rideshare (Uber or 99), which is the local norm and safer than street-hailing. Set the pickup pin to the venue entrance and confirm the plate before getting in — especially in the port area around Pedra do Sal and in Baixo Gávea, where you should ride door-to-door rather than walk to a distant metro.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there anything on tonight (Monday)?

Yes — Monday is one of Rio’s best samba nights. Pedra do Sal, Samba do Trabalhador and Samba da Gávea all run, and Bip Bip has its Monday chorinho.

Is Pedra do Sal free?

Yes. The roda is a free, open-air street party; you pay only for drinks and food from the surrounding bars and stalls.

How late does the metro run?

MetrôRio operates until roughly midnight. After that, use Uber or 99 to get home.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 3, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Ó do Borogodó — Monday samba and choro A tiny, legendary room on the edge of Vila Madalena with a Monday roda of samba, choro and MPB. It seats about fifty, so get there early — and because Monday hours can vary, call ahead on (11) 3814-4087 to confirm tonight’s roda.

Tonight at a Glance —Ó do Borogodó Intimate samba/choro roda in Pinheiros from around 8–9 pm; small room, arrive early. Monday hours vary, so call ahead; couvert roughly R$15–30. —Rabo di Galo Speakeasy cocktail bar inside Rosewood at Cidade Matarazzo with live music nightly from 6 pm; no cover, premium drinks, no reservations. —D-Edge For a late one: the long-running Monday “On the Rocks” rock club night in Barra Funda, from around midnight — check D-Edge’s socials for tonight’s edition. —Piratininga Bar Mellow live jazz and blues in Vila Madalena — the softer, sit-down option. —Getting home Metrô (R$5.40) runs until around midnight; after that use Uber or 99.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

São Paulo’s Monday is quieter than its famous weekends, but the reliable spots are worth the trip. Start with an early live-music drink at Rabo di Galo, the speakeasy inside the Rosewood, then move to the samba and choro roda at Ó do Borogodó in Pinheiros from around 9 pm. Night owls can finish at D-Edge in Barra Funda, whose Monday “On the Rocks” rock night doesn’t get going until about midnight. Prefer something gentler? Piratininga in Vila Madalena keeps a low-key jazz-and-blues flame burning.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba / Choro

Where: Ó do Borogodó (Pinheiros), Monday roda.

Jazz / Live music

Where: Rabo di Galo (Cidade Matarazzo, near Paulista) and Piratininga (Vila Madalena).

Rock club night

Where: D-Edge (Barra Funda), the Monday “On the Rocks” party.

Quiet tonight

Where: The big Fridays-and-Saturdays club circuit — Monday is for these specialists.

Pick Your Night

—Solo and safe: Rabo di Galo — upscale and easy to enjoy on your own.

—Meet locals: Ó do Borogodó, a devoted samba-and-choro crowd.

—Date night: Rabo di Galo’s speakeasy setting behind the velvet curtain.

—Chill and conversation: Piratininga — traditional, low-key live music.

—Late and loud: D-Edge’s “On the Rocks” rock night in Barra Funda.

Where to Go

Ó do Borogodó — Pinheiros A cramped, beloved room on the Vila Madalena border that has hosted São Paulo’s best samba and choro for years. Tonight: A Monday samba, choro and MPB roda, roughly 8–9 pm — but Monday hours vary, so call ahead on (11) 3814-4087 to confirm tonight’s session. Best time: Get there early — about fifty seats and it fills quickly. Cost: Couvert artístico around R$15–30 plus consumption (confirm at the door). Address: Rua Horácio Lane, 21, Pinheiros (edge of Vila Madalena). Getting there: Metrô Fradique Coutinho (Line 4-Yellow), about a 10-minute walk, or a rideshare. Phone: (11) 3814-4087

Rabo di Galo — Rosewood, Cidade Matarazzo An upscale speakeasy tucked behind a velvet curtain at the Rosewood, with live music every night and a serious cocktail list. Tonight: Open from 6 pm with live music; the Monday act rotates — check the Rosewood calendar for tonight’s artist. Best time: Go earlier on a Monday to get a seat; it takes no reservations. Cost: No cover; budget for premium cocktails (roughly R$50–90 each). Address: Rosewood São Paulo, Cidade Matarazzo — Rua Itapeva, 435, Bela Vista (near Av. Paulista). Getting there: Metrô Brigadeiro or Trianon-Masp (Line 2-Green), about a 10-minute walk. Good to know: Smart-casual, first-come first-served jazz-club atmosphere.

D-Edge — Barra Funda One of the city’s landmark electronic clubs, whose Monday residency swaps techno for rock. Tonight: “On the Rocks” — the long-running Monday rock night (progressive, indie, psychedelic), from around midnight. Confirm the edition on D-Edge’s Instagram. Best time: Proper club hours; nothing happens before midnight. Cost: Roughly R$30–40 entry (about R$30 women / R$40 men, or a higher consumption minimum); door prices vary by edition. Address: Alameda Olga, 170, Barra Funda (Zona Oeste). Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro (Line 3-Red) plus a short rideshare — the area is industrial, so ride door-to-door at night. Good to know: Bring ID and dress for a club.

Piratininga Bar — Vila Madalena A traditional Vila Madalena live-music bar for a mellow jazz-and-blues evening. Tonight: Open Monday with a live voice-and-guitar set; a relaxed jazz/blues/MPB night. Best time: From early evening; a good sit-down alternative to a club night. Cost: Couvert artístico plus consumption (Monday couvert not fixed — check on arrival). Address: Rua Wisard, 149, Vila Madalena. Getting there: Metrô Vila Madalena (Line 2-Green), about a 12-minute walk, or a rideshare. Phone: (11) 3032-9775

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

—Vila Madalena / Pinheiros: The city’s bohemian bar heart; Ó do Borogodó and Piratininga are here.

—Bela Vista / Paulista: Central and well-connected; Rabo di Galo sits inside Cidade Matarazzo near Avenida Paulista.

—Barra Funda: Industrial Zona Oeste, home to D-Edge; go and return by rideshare after dark.

—Elsewhere: The big weekend club districts are quiet on a Monday — tonight belongs to the specialists above.

Getting Home Safe

São Paulo’s Metrô runs until around midnight (single fare R$5.40; city buses R$5.30), enough for an early exit. The samba roda and especially the D-Edge club night run past that, so plan to leave by app rideshare (Uber or 99), which is the local norm. Set the pickup pin to the venue entrance, confirm the plate before getting in, and in Barra Funda ride door-to-door rather than walking to a distant metro.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there anything on tonight (Monday)?

Yes. Ó do Borogodó runs its Monday samba-and-choro roda, Rabo di Galo has live music nightly, D-Edge holds its “On the Rocks” rock night, and Piratininga offers a mellow jazz-and-blues evening.

What’s the cheapest way to get around?

The Metrô at R$5.40 a ride until about midnight; after that, Uber or 99.

Is São Paulo dead on Mondays?

Not if you know where to look — the venues above are the reliable Monday-night spots while the big weekend clubs rest.

World.title: Carlton McKoy and baby reportedly injured in shooting near San Ignacio Puma gas station
World.content:
Carlton McKoy and baby reportedly injured in shooting near San Ignacio Puma gas station

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A man and a baby were reportedly injured during a shooting near the Puma Gas Station in San Ignacio Town on Monday night.

Preliminary information identifies the adult victim as Carlton McKoy, who reportedly sustained gunshot wounds to the abdomen and leg. The baby was reportedly struck by gunfire during the incident and was later transferred for further medical treatment, possibly to Belmopan or Belize City.

Initial reports suggest the shooting may have occurred during an attempted robbery and that a security officer fired at the suspected robber. However, the exact circumstances surrounding the incident have not yet been confirmed by police.

The conditions of McKoy and the injured child remain unknown. Police are expected to release additional information as their investigation continues.

World.title: Firestarter: Maskall woman burns down boyfriend’s home after removing all her stuff; Charged for arson
World.content:
Firestarter: Maskall woman burns down boyfriend’s home after removing all her stuff; Charged for arson

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 21-year-old Maskall Village woman has been charged with arson following a fire that destroyed the home she shared with her boyfriend.

Vayda Ashanti August, an unemployed labourer, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, August 3, where she was arraigned on a single count of arson.

Police allege that on Saturday, August 1, August intentionally set fire to a 16-by-24-foot wooden and zinc house belonging to 33-year-old Jose David Recinos. The house and its contents were valued at approximately $35,000 and were completely destroyed.

According to the prosecution’s allegations, August and Recinos were separating, and a man had been hired to help her remove her belongings from the residence. After the items were loaded onto a pickup truck, August allegedly told the driver that she had set the house on fire.

The driver and other persons reportedly attempted to extinguish the blaze but were unsuccessful. August was later detained following a report made by Recinos.

No plea was taken because prosecutors are awaiting instructions from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the case will proceed summarily or on indictment.

August was granted bail of $10,000, along with two sureties of $5,000 each. She was ordered not to contact Recinos or members of his family, remain at least 100 yards away from places he lives, works or frequently visits, and report to the Maskall Police Station every Wednesday.

She must also reside with her mother and notify the court of any change of address. August met bail later that afternoon and is scheduled to return to court on September 23, 2026.

World.title: One detained, another sought after 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez shot dead on Vernon Street
World.content:
One detained, another sought after 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez shot dead on Vernon Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained one man and are searching for another in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez in Belize City.

The shooting occurred at approximately 1:15 p.m. on Sunday, August 2, 2026, while police officers were patrolling the area. The officers reportedly heard a gunshot and responded to Vernon Street, where they found Hernandez suffering from a gunshot wound.

Hernandez was rushed for medical treatment but later succumbed to his injury.

Police said surveillance footage showed Hernandez travelling along Vernon Street and stopping near its intersection with Partridge Street, where he remained seated on his motorcycle. Several minutes later, two men approached him, and one reportedly pulled out a firearm and fired a single shot, striking Hernandez.

A man matching the description of one of the suspects was apprehended shortly afterwards and remains in police custody. Investigators are searching for the second suspect.

Authorities said footage from police surveillance cameras across Belize City assisted investigators in identifying the suspects and directing subsequent police operations. Police confirmed that the detained suspect is known to law enforcement, while Hernandez was not known to police.

The shooting was initially reported near the St. Martin de Porres Swift Hall on Vernon Street. Police have not yet disclosed a possible motive for the murder though some reports allege he was robbed for a chain.

World.title: Man detained after chopping 62-year-old grandmother in Succotz during alleged ‘mental health crisis’
World.content:
Man detained after chopping 62-year-old grandmother in Succotz during alleged ‘mental health crisis’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a 23-year-old man in connection with a chopping incident that left his 62-year-old grandmother seriously injured in San Jose Succotz Village.

The incident occurred at a residence in the village at about 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 1.

The injured woman was rushed for medical treatment and was listed in a stable condition at the time of the police press briefing. Police officers, assisted by community members, later apprehended the suspect and took him into custody.

Police said their preliminary investigation suggests that the man may have been experiencing a mental-health crisis. The woman was reportedly injured when she attempted to assist him.

Initial community reports described the injured woman as the suspect’s grandmother, although police officially referred to her only as a female relative.

The man remained detained as police continued their investigation. No criminal charges had been announced at the time of the briefing.

World.title: Police do not suspect foul play in death of ‘Kimmy Boo’
World.content:
Police do not suspect foul play in death of ‘Kimmy Boo’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say they do not presently suspect foul play in the death of 22-year-old Kimane Rosita Ashanti Garbutt, whose decomposing body was found inside an upstairs room in Belize City on Sunday.

Garbutt, who was also publicly known as “Kimmy Boo,” was discovered at a building at the corner of Vernon Street and Amandala Drive at about 9:30 a.m. on August 2.

Police said Garbutt was last seen alive at approximately 7:00 a.m. the previous day, when she told a friend that she was not feeling well. The friend returned to check on her the following morning and entered the room after repeated calls went unanswered.

Garbutt’s motionless body was found in a seated position and had already begun to decompose.

According to information previously released to the media, Garbutt was in the third trimester of pregnancy, had suffered from epileptic seizures and had reportedly experienced pregnancy complications. She had visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for a prenatal check-up approximately two weeks before her death.

Police said a post-mortem examination will determine the cause of death.

World.title: Orange Walk man Luciano Acosta drowns after canoe capsizes at Honey Camp Lagoon
World.content:
Orange Walk man Luciano Acosta drowns after canoe capsizes at Honey Camp Lagoon

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the drowning of 44-year-old Luciano Acosta after a canoe overturned during an early-morning fishing trip at Honey Camp Lagoon in the Orange Walk District.

Acosta had gone to the lagoon with relatives and friends on Saturday, August 1. At about 3:00 a.m. the following morning, he and 41-year-old Eliseo Escalante reportedly boarded a canoe to go fishing.

The canoe later capsized. Escalante managed to swim to a mangrove patch, where he called for help and was subsequently rescued. Acosta was found several hours later, partially submerged near a mangrove patch in the lagoon.

Police do not suspect foul play and Acosta’s body awaits a post-mortem examination.

Honey Camp Ranch, where Acosta had reportedly offered his support for several years, remembered him as an authentic person who was always willing to share Belize with others.

World.title: Thirty-five young women empowered through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp
World.content:
Thirty-five young women empowered through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp

Thirty-five young women from across Belize strengthened their leadership and entrepreneurial skills through the Girls in Governance Leadership and Art Empowerment Camp, a six-day residential programme hosted by the Department of Youth Services (DYS) in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) at the Kindred Spirit Campgrounds in Belmopan.

Participants took part in sessions on leadership, governance, public speaking, advocacy, digital literacy, media engagement, and entrepreneurship, while developing personal leadership plans to create positive change in their communities.

The camp also featured hands-on creative activities, including designing Belize-inspired tote bags, crafting jewelry, creating eco-art, and learning branding and marketing skills. The initiative reflects the shared commitment of DYS and UNDP to empowering young women through leadership, entrepreneurship, and civic engagement.

World.title: Guatemalan man, Rudy Toj, dies in apparent drowning in Belmopan creek
World.content:
Guatemalan man, Rudy Toj, dies in apparent drowning in Belmopan creek

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the apparent drowning of a 38-year-old Guatemalan national whose body was found in a creek in Belmopan on Sunday morning.

The deceased was identified as Rudy Bernabe Toj, a resident of Otox-Ha Street in Belmopan.

Police were called to the creek in the San Martin area at about 7:30 a.m. on August 2, where officers found Toj’s motionless body. Efforts were made to resuscitate him, but they were unsuccessful.

Investigators also found a transparent bottle containing alcohol at the scene. Police said they believe Toj had consumed alcohol before entering the water, but have not determined whether it contributed to his death.

His body awaits a post-mortem examination as the investigation continues.

World.title: WATCH: Waves of excitement at Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day
World.content:
Crew members of 'Empress' pose with the coveted Yamaha engine prize after winning the Yamaha Engine Race at the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Saturday, August 1, 2026.

Sutania Beckford beamed with joy after her boat crew guided ‘Empress’ to a thrilling victory in the Yamaha Engine Race which brought an exciting close to the 43rd annual Old Harbour Bay Regatta on Emancipation Day.

It was sweet triumph for the crowd favourites and their supporters after losing the marquee event in the six-race boat competition to rival ‘Father’s Day’ last year.

“Every year, people come just to see [Empress] because it’s like we are up against everybody,” Beckford said.

“However, Empress decided this time not to have any boyfriends, she was under proper supervision this time, so she came out victorious,” she added with a smile.

Each Emancipation Day, hundreds of residents and visitors converge at the Old Harbour Bay Fishing Village to participate in what Jason Fuller, the president of the Old Harbour Bay Community Development Association, calls “the premier boat racing competition in Jamaica”.

It was another massive turnout on Saturday, with numbers estimated to be in the thousands.

“They love it, they live for it every year,” Fuller said about the lure of the event. “This is their passion, this is their love. And we just try each and every year to ensure that we improve and make it a memorable one.”

In addition to the races, the residents also unite for food, entertainment, and other competitions – including fish scraping, cook-offs and beer drinking – at the regatta. Due to the event’s massive growth, the organisers introduced live streaming at last year’s edition to share the experience with persons who are unable to physically attend.

“Remember, it’s the largest fishing village in Jamaica. So almost everyone have some interaction with fishing, whether you’re a fisherman, a family of fishermen, or so on,” Fuller said. “So, that is one of the main reason why the regatta means so much to the community.”

Noting that a number of fisherfolk in the community were affected by Hurricane Melissa last October, Fuller said the regatta organisers partnered with sponsors this year to give away nets and other items to help affected persons get back on their feet.

“So, even though they were affected, we are trying our utmost best to make it a seamless transition to getting back to what they were before,” he said.

Social Development Commission’s parish manager for St Catherine, Shana-Lee Archibald hailed the event for the economic activity it generates for small businesses in the community.

“The regatta is a great event, it provides an opportunity for our small businesses to benefit and that’s one of the main reasons the SDC is a part of the activities,” Archibald said.

In the meantime, spectators commended the organisers of the regatta while expressing their satisfaction for the fun and entertainment provided.

“Good energy, good vibes, super lit,” said spectator from Canada who goes by the name “Breezy”.

“I just like the view, the people, the music, it’s very nice,” he said.

– Julian Richardson

World.title: Stronger than ganja!
World.content:
Consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Ganesh Shetty says child guidance clinics are now seeing more children addicted to digital devices than to marijuana. He has sounded an alarm over what he describes as a pattern of “disconnection and misconnection, alienation and addiction” amongst Jamaican youngsters.

“These algorithms are created by behavioural specialists, and they drag you into something more interesting, something more wonderful, so that it will suck you in to addiction. I have more tablet addicts coming to my child guidance clinics than weed addicts nowadays,” Dr Shetty disclosed as he warned minors of the danger courted daily.

There are 23 of these clinics in hospitals and health centres throughout Jamaica, providing mental health and counselling services for clients up to 18 years old. Key services include behavioural assessments, emotional support, and treatment for conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and depression.

It is unclear if the troubling trend has emerged at all of them.

Dr Shetty, who is also acting director, adolescent mental health, in the Ministry of Health, made the disclosure on digital device addiction during last week’s press conference to present findings of the National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children.

He outlined the toll addiction takes.

“We have teenagers who are so disconnected [from] everybody and everything. And this is what happens when you’re disconnected, and misconnected, and addicted: You don’t sleep; you don’t eat; you’re miserable. Next day, nobody can talk to you, including your mom. And sometimes, when you see a lot of shooting and fighting and cutting off head and cutting off fingers on your screen, you get disconnected [from] that human suffering. So somebody gets hit in school [and you are more] interested in taking a video of it and putting it online so it can go viral — not going and assisting that person,” he pointed out.

Dr Shetty noted that the attraction to screens has its genesis in seemingly harmless choices made by parents and guardians during their children’s early years. He cited the example of a mother who gives her two-year-old an iPad when out in public to prevent the child from “running up and down”. The woman is proud of her baby who appears well-behaved and does not cause “discomfort to others and mother”.

The mental health professional then described a scenario in which the mother has two more children at home, absent fathers, and she uses digital devices to fill the gap as she does household chores such as cooking.

“So she has to have the older two watch some TV and the younger one to deal with the tablet. What happens? The child gets disconnected from the human beings around her/him, and gets connected with the machine and, even at this age, can get addicted to the machine,” Dr Shetty outlined.

He said a child’s affinity for his electronic device only grows, becoming a competitor for the time spent on every other aspect of life.

“It can affect you, affect your energy, affect your focus, affect your memory, affect your school grades, affect what you want to become. You can’t become [a success] because you don’t have grades to go to college, but you have just grades enough to go to supermarket and push cart,” he warned.

Dr Shetty is heartened that there is recognition that a holistic approach is needed to tackle the areas of concern outlined in the study, which is said to be “one of the most comprehensive national assessments ever undertaken” on social media use by minors in Jamaica.

“I’m glad that most folks you interviewed think it has to be done together. Government cannot do it alone. Community cannot do it alone. Family cannot do it alone. Young persons have to be involved in it. It is a family and community effort,” he said.

According to the study, nine out of every 10 respondents, or 90.2 per cent, support government regulation of minors’ social media use, while 2.9 per cent expressed opposition. Nearly 84 per cent believe Jamaica should establish a clear national policy framework governing minors’ use of social media.

World.title: Catherine Hall is back!
World.content:
President of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Jason Russell, on his way to winning the Celebrity Cook Off at Saturday’s staging of Montego Bay Jerk and Food Festival.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Local stakeholders are thrilled with the return of activities to Catherine Hall Entertainment Centre, with Saturday’s staging of Montego Bay Jerk and Food Festival, an annual event whose fate was in question after the venue was damaged by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“The feeling of being in this Catherine Hall Entertainment Centre is one of triumph,” president of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Jason Russell, told the Jamaica Observer on the sidelines of the celebrity chef cook-off competition which he later won.

“To see the park back and opened, separate and apart from Jerk Fest, to see the Government fix back the park, it looks good. The grass looks good, the walls are up, the fences are up. It gives me a real warm feeling and MoBay is really back,” he added.

Catherine Hall was among the hardest-hit sections of the city when the Category 5 storm struck and the popular entertainment venue was not spared. A section of its perimeter wall was washed away and although it has since been repaired, the venue remained unused for months. Its marquee event, Reggae Sumfest, went to St Ann on July 18 for a one-day event, scaling down the show from the usual seven days.

“They didn’t think that the park would be ready in time and being here we realise that some good work was done,” Russell stated.

Also in attendance at Saturday’s event was Mayor of Montego Bay Richard Vernon, who was equally pleased with the venue’s return.

“It’s good to know that the centre can be used for events. I was always of the view that it could be used ever since the hurricane, just needed to do a little work to get it back in order to ensure we can host events of this size. Today is testament to that thought process back then and we intend for the regular activities in this area to return,” he said.

The facility is owned and operated by the Urban Development Corporation (UDC), which the mayor said had been working diligently to restore the venue. He also commended organisers of Saturday’s event for successfully taking on the challenge of hosting a major event after the hurricane.

Promoter John Lindo admitted there had been significant concerns when organisers first assessed the venue which on Saturday was still being powered by generators. They decided to go ahead with the show, he said, as they did not want to disappoint regular patrons and they know how important the event is to the city.

“Montego Bay Jerk Festival is the people’s show. For 17 years we have been doing it and we must be doing something good. It is a clean, nice show. We do things straight and we do things right and so I guess that is why… the sponsors… are always coming back on board,” he said.

Several sponsors, he added, have thrown their support behind the usual plan to give back to the community by helping individuals connected to the festival and are Hurricane Melissa victims.

Lindo said once arrangements are finalised, organisers will identify the beneficiaries and determine the level of assistance to be provided.

For Mayor Vernon, however, the benefits of the festival were already evident Saturday, particularly for vendors operating both in and outside the venue.

“Events like these they provide spin-offs to other businesses and that is why they are so important. We work closely with promoters to give them as much support as possible to have these types of events,” he asserted.

“Some of them have houses damaged, they’re still fixing and at the same time, you have to send children back to school so they have to deal with that, so I am happy for this opportunity for them and I am happy for this opportunity for the city of Montego Bay,” he stated.

The festival attracted thousands of patrons despite an earlier threat of rain. Attendees enjoyed a wide variety of food, drinks and activities that culminated in a stage show featuring performances by songbird Alliance and several other artistes.

World.title: Pick up a book
World.content:
Kinloss Primary and Infant School teacher Shernette Brooks packing away books she received from Blue World Travel’s Festival at Sea delegation at the Falmouth Port last Wednesday.Horace Hines

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Regional director at the Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Odette Dyer is urging Jamaican children to spend less time on tablets and rediscover the joy of reading, describing books as one of the greatest investments that can be made in a child’s future.

“Please put away the tablets a little bit. That’s not your only avenue for learning and understanding the world. Open your minds to reading a book because when you read, it prepares you for learning, achieving and doing your schoolwork that much better,” Dyer urged students attending a ceremony where 1,000 children’s books were among items donated to 15 schools across Trelawny, St James, and St Elizabeth.

School supplies were also presented to the institutions through a partnership involving Blue World Travel — one of America’s leading travel companies for African American travellers — JTB, and local charity Sarah’s Children. The handover was done at the historic Falmouth Port during the arrival of Celebrity Cruise Lines’

Reflection, which was carrying a delegation from Blue World Travel’s annual Festival at Sea.

Dyer described every donated book as “an opportunity to spark imagination, encourage learning and inspire the dreams of a young Jamaican”. Recalling her childhood, the tourism player said books introduced her to the world long before she had the opportunity to travel.

“I am a testament to reading and loving books. Back then we didn’t have technology, and books sparked my curiosity to explore different cultures. Later, I experienced the world first-hand and was not disappointed,” she said.

Welcoming the visitors, Dyer thanked Blue World Travel President Patricia Nicholson Yarbrough and the team for once again selecting Jamaica as the beneficiary of the annual book drive.

“Tourism is at its best when it creates meaningful connections between people,” Dyer said, noting that initiatives such as the donation demonstrate tourism’s ability to enrich communities long after visitors have returned home. She also commended Festival at Sea passengers who packed books and school supplies before boarding the cruise.

Blue World Travel, a San Francisco-based agency that created Festival at Sea, America’s original African-American cultural cruise, has incorporated children’s book drives into the annual programme for more than three decades.

Yarbrough said the 34th Festival at Sea continued a tradition that began during the cruise’s second year.

“Our passengers are the ones who actually bought all of these books for the schools and libraries. We wanted to give something back to the islands that host us,” she said.

Former Los Angeles School District administrator Peggy Taylor Presley said about 85 per cent of the donated books feature Afro-centric characters, giving students the opportunity to see themselves reflected in the stories they read.

“You can be anything you want to be,” Presley told the students.

Sarah’s Charity Founder Janet Silvera said the donation was particularly meaningful in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, which damaged schools and learning resources across western Jamaica.

“For some institutions, rebuilding a library has become just as important as rebuilding a classroom,” she said, adding that every book has the potential to unlock imagination, build confidence and change a child’s future.

Among the beneficiaries was Kinloss Primary and Infant School in Trelawny.

Teacher Shernette Brooks said the donation would help establish a reading corner for the infant department while expanding the school’s library.

“The child-friendly books will support our younger learners, while the remaining books will benefit the wider student population,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Meanwhile, Dyer thanked the visitors for their generosity, friendship and belief in the potential of Jamaica’s children and encouraged them to experience Jamaica beyond the cruise port.

“Go out, explore the destination and engage with a Jamaican,” she urged.

World.title: From viral buzz to bigger ambitions
World.content:
Tielo Lanez.

When Tielo Lanez released Greedy, the song quickly found a home on social media, introducing the emerging dancehall artiste to a growing audience and earning him early recognition in the genre. Now, almost two years after making his debut on the musical landscape with TikTok trending songs Muk Truck and Bless, dancehall artiste Tielo Lanez has released his debut EP titled The Rebellion.

According to the 21-year-old, The Rebellion represents his musical direction.

“The EP is called The Rebellion because it’s a representation of what I need to become to achieve what I want,” Tielo Lanez told the Jamaica Observer recently.

“I somewhat write as if I’m creating an album each time I create a record,” he explained. “I believe it was only a matter of time before I dropped a project. I don’t think I was getting the singles out fast enough, and so this is a way to get all the songs out without it becoming overwhelming.”

The EP features StairDiWay produced Undecided, and the DJ Mac-assisted Blow and Code Up by Extended Play Records.

The track Shootah Dem (remix) features Kkrytical, while Worship is a collaboration with Ayetian.

Other producers who contributed their talent include MXSSIVH, Alva Music, Kutti Music, Temple Boss, Slyngerz Music, Prod 14, and Doneknowkello.

The project took two months to complete.

The artiste noted that he wrote every song himself and remained fully involved throughout the production.

“The song on this project I believe will surprise people the most is Bad Bunch. It’s my newest sound, created on accident. The instrumental is also a skeleton, which is something very new to me as well.”

The project’s emotional centre, however, is the title track, Rebellion, which the artiste recommends listeners hear first.

“Rebellion is about finding yourself, being yourself and living your truth,” he said, explaining that the song carries a message of honesty and self-discovery that he believes many people will relate to.

Originally from St Thomas, Tielo Lanez (real name Jevaughn Smith) attended Morant Bay High School and later Signal Hill Secondary in the parish.

He shared that music has been his calling since his high school days.

“I’ve been doing music professionally for less than two years and the journey has been challenging. However, the lesson learnt along the journey is to be yourself and to live your truth,” he disclosed.

Putting the EP together also gave the entertainer a clearer understanding of his own creative instincts.

“A lesson that stood out to me while putting this EP together is I’m a jack of all trades when it comes to creating different types of music.”

The artiste experiments with multiple sounds on the project, hoping to better understand both himself as an artiste and the audience discovering his music.

“What I want the audience to understand about Tielo Lanez is that he is more than capable of dominating different styles of music and is ready to make a name for himself,” he said, outlining that his willingness to experiment became one of the defining characteristics of the project.

Rather than chasing trends, Tielo believes the project’s greatest strength lies in its authenticity.

“This project distinguishes itself and me with its sound and energy behind each record. No trends were followed — just music for the soul and pure creativity,” said the artiste.

As he braces himself for fan reactions to the project, the entertainer also sets his sights on finding that one breakthrough record he hopes will elevate his career to the next level.

Tielo Lanez made his debut in the United Kingdom in May, when he performed before at City Splash, which reportedly saw more than 20,000 patrons in attendance. Also sharing that bill were Beres Hammond, Aidonia, and Elephant Man.

World.title: No quarrel with the courts
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) and president of the Jamaican Bar Association (Jambar) Tenneshia Watkins (second right) celebrate Jamaica’s first female Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn (left) and former Jambar President Ian Wilkinson, both King’s Counsel, who were honoured Friday night during the association’s annual banquet.Joseph Wellington

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, whose legal team on Friday lost an appeal to block the disclosure of certain files in his battle with the Integrity Commission (IC), later that evening reaffirmed the importance of an independent judiciary. While speaking broadly about his Administration and not directly referencing his legal issues, Holness stressed that he has no quarrel with the application of the law — even at times when it “constrains the actions of the executive”.

On the contrary, he stressed that “a strong and independent legal profession is indispensable to the rule of law”.

“It provides citizens with representation, assists the court in administering justice, scrutinises public authority, and helps ensure that rights are protected and obligations enforced. Jamaica has a constitutional order built deliberately on the separation of powers, and that separation will, from time to time, produce tension between the branches of the State. I say that as I see others smiling. I do not regard such tension as a defect in our democracy. I regard it as evidence that our democracy is working,” the prime minister declared.

He was speaking to an audience of leaders and other members of the justice system during the 2026 Jamaican Bar Association’s (Jambar) Annual Banquet.

It is essential, the prime minister said, for the judiciary to provide checks and balances.

“When the courts constrain the actions of the executive, they do not obstruct the work of the Government; they discharge the very duty the constitution assigns them. An executive that is never checked is an executive that has forgotten the source of its authority. And let me say that this executive has never forgotten the source of its authority,” added Holness.

He spoke of the importance of a judiciary that is impartial, and displays “principled application of the law” for all Jamaicans, not just some.

“We also expect this for all our citizens who seek access to the courts. That is what secures the confidence of our citizens in our Government and institutions, and this is what keeps us free as we pursue major reforms and investment in security, infrastructure, and the economy,” the prime minister said.

Critics have frowned upon Holness’s decision to take the IC to court. However, his proponents have consistently argued that it is his right — as it is for any other Jamaican — to seek legal redress.

The prime minister was granted leave by the Supreme Court in 2024 to apply for judicial review of the IC’s report on his statutory declarations, challenging processes engaged by the IC and its Director of Investigations Kevon Stephenson.

Holness has maintained that he has not broken the law since the tabling of the report that contained recommendations that the Financial Investigations Division (FID) and Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) examine his financial dealings.

He sought a declaration that the commission acted unfairly and unlawfully in its conduct of an investigation into his statutory declarations, with his lawyers arguing that the issues were of critical importance to the overall fairness of the proceedings. It was revealed, Friday, that their bid was unsuccessful.

Hours after, the prime minister spoke of the importance of a system of justice that is beyond reproach, framing his comments within a national context.

“Confidence in our legal system is essential. Investors and citizens must trust our laws, contracts, and institutions,” he told the audience of legal professionals from bench and bar.

During the banquet, Jamaica’s first female Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn, and former Jambar President Ian Wilkinson, both King’s Counsel, were honoured. Wilkinson is also president of the Jamaica Chess Federation. The prime minister paid tribute to them both.

“They have demonstrated that excellence at the Bar requires much more than technical knowledge. It demands discipline, preparation, courage, integrity, and an abiding respect for institutions,” said Holness.

He also acknowledged a select group of legal stalwarts who were being honoured for individually giving five decades of service to the profession.

“Fifty years of advocacy, 50 years of counsel, 50 years of mentorship — most important — but 50 years of service! You have trained generations, preserved our traditions, and helped shape our institutions we rely on today. Jamaica owes you a debt of gratitude,” Holness said.

Reflecting on her journey from a young child to the peak of her profession as a public servant, Llewellyn was adamant that she would have it no other way.

“I learned from very early that when you have positions in life and you have to serve the people, do not levitate up into the clouds. Stay on the ground, serve the people, they will always know when you are sincere,” she urged young professionals present.

Wilkinson, for his part, emphasised the importance of hard work and mentorship to the craft while urging young professionals to aim for maximising their contributions to the legal arena and country, rather than seeking to line their pockets.

World.title: PRIDE & JOY
World.content:
In this August 6, 2022 file photo, Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls celebrate the semi-final netball win over New Zealand during the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, England. The Sunshine Girls lost to New Zealand in the 2026 Commonwealth Games final in Glasgow, Scotland, on Sunday .Photo: Naphtali Junior

DESPITE coming up short in consecutive Commonwealth Games netball finals, Jamaica’s Latanya Wilson says they are proud they got into position to challenge for the gold medal.

The Sunshine Girls battled gamely but were defeated 48-56 by world number two-ranked New Zealand Silver Ferns at Hydro arena in Glasgow, Scotland, on Sunday.

The Jamaicans had also lost to the Silver Ferns in the preliminary stage, going down 48-53 last week.

But they entered the final high on confidence after pulling off an emotional, nail-biting 46-45 win over 2022 champions Australia in the semi-finals on Saturday.

“I’m very proud that we put ourselves in this privileged position to be out here to actually play the finals,” Wilson said after the match. “I’m a bit disappointed in the loss, but I’m still proud of the girls.”

Wilson, who played wing defence for the full 60 minutes of the game, said she thought they did not get off to a fast start like they did in the semi-final.

“I think it’s a number of things [for falling short]. I feel we started really slow, and I felt like in that second quarter we came back into it but I feel we just kind of let the momentum swing a bit for them. But yeah, I’m still proud. It was a good match. New Zealand is a top team, and we knew that they were going to come out here and put on a strong performance,” the Jamaican netballer said.

Wilson said Coach Sasher-Gaye Henry Wright had urged them to dig deeper during a talk at half-time, at which point they had been trailing by three goals.

“[We had to] just try and get something. We weren’t winning any balls, so it was very important for us to try something different and just give it a prop. Because at [that time] we were done, so we needed to give it a try,” she said.

Jamaica were off to a sluggish start, and despite tying up the scores twice in the third quarter, New Zealand always appeared in control. The Silver Ferns were led by a magnificent shooting performance from goal shooter Grace Nweke who had 48 goals from 54 attempts.

New Zealand led by 16-13 after the first quarter and held on for 28-25 margin at half-time, before increasing the advantage to 41-36 at the end of the third quarter. They led by as many as 10 goals in the fourth quarter before coming out winners by eight goals.

Romelda Aiken-George, who was oftentimes defended by two players when she got the ball, led Jamaica with 32 goals from 36 attempts, while Shanice Beckford scored 16 goals from 18 tries.

Despite the loss, Wilson said she was satisfied they had done their best and that their fans appreciated their effort.

“I think they’re super proud of us, whether we win or lose. I feel like they would be proud of us, and I know that all our fans in Jamaica would be cheering us on, and even here, like it’s amazing. It’s a privilege to be in this position. I know Australia would love to be in this position, so to be able to get this privilege and to be here, it’s good job to us,” she reasoned.

The second-place finish on Sunday earned Jamaica a fifth medal in netball at the Commonwealth Games, as the country finished with 19 medals (10 gold, four silver, five bronze) overall in Glasgow. The other 18 medals came from track and field competitions which ended on Saturday.

In the bronze-medal game that preceded the final on Sunday, four-time champions Australia defeated England 68-50. It was the first time Australia were not contesting the gold-medal game in the history of the Commonwealth Games.

World.title: Drought busters
World.content:
This youngster seems fascinated by this impressive head of cattle on display at Denbigh Agricultural Show on Sunday. Garfield Robinson

DENBIGH, Clarendon —With the country bracing for drought, the National Irrigation Commission (NIC) has given an assurance that it is adequately prepared to provide water to farmers in need should the current dry period persist.

“We are seeing where the water levels are falling, especially in the surface systems [rivers]. But we are monitoring it and we are working closely with the Water Resources Authority, which is the regulator, to ensure that we stay within the guidelines to be able to manage what we do,” said NIC director of engineering and technical services Rohan Stewart.

He was speaking with the

Jamaica Observer, Saturday, on the margins of Denbigh Agricultural, Industrial and Food Show held at the Denbigh Showground in May Pen, Clarendon.

The Meteorological Service of Jamaica is projecting prolonged dry conditions stretching into this October. Last Thursday, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda put the country on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

On Saturday, Stewart assured commercial farmers that the NIC has measures in place to ensure that their thirst for water is met. Outside of irrigation, he explained that NIC has trucks that are used predominantly in the St Elizabeth and Trelawny areas to supply farmers with water.

“That service is in significant demand now, but there are a few weeks’ backlog because the demand is so great in that area; but we are working on it,” he assured.

In addition, he said, there is also a water filling service where individuals may purchase water and truck it to their farms.

“If the drought intensifies, we will have rotation where farmers would get water at different times. Currently, farmers can get water on demand, but if the dry period progresses into a drought where we will have to do some restrictions, then farmers will be notified and they will be given water on a scheduled basis,” Stewart explained.

“With the best plans, sometimes things go awry but we are agile. We are seeing an increase in persons coming for water. Some people would have been dormant or not utilising all of their lands, so some of those persons are coming on to the system. Also, with the new Essex Valley and Parnassus irrigation systems, we are also seeing persons coming on for connection and we are prepared to supply those areas,” he added.

However, Stewart urged farmers to put their own contingency plans in place to weather conditions that are expected to pose a challenge for an extended period.

“Despite where we are now in the dry period, it is not too late for farmers to start planning and implementing those plans. Farmers are encouraged to use water efficiently and we are also saying, ensure you utilise crop cover which will reduce your evaporation and water loss. Also, do mulching and look into planting drought-tolerant crops to achieve the objective of efficiency for the system, success for you as the entrepreneur, and food security for Jamaica,” he urged.

World.content:
Manchester’s Heron House building is the site of a new No.10 North, dubbed the “situation room for growth” by the PM. Burnham has vowed to work from the building regularly, alongside other Cabinet ministers.

When its inaugural meeting took place with regional mayors, the PM (who is married and has three kids, remember) said this might be the “best day of my life.” In a sign that Burnham’s living his best life, there’s even a gold “The Queen Is Dead” disk on the wall from Manchester indie legends The Smiths.

“It’s definitely gone down well here,” says University of Manchester academic Robert Ford of Burnham’s regular references to the city.

Burnham holds a National Economic Council meeting at No. 10 North in Manchester on July 24, 2026. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

“It’s a clever bit of messaging, because it signals to people up here, where he remains very popular, that he hasn’t forgotten about the city that he’s just departed from, and is continuing to place it at the heart of everything.”

From Buckingham Palace to … the Salford Lads’ Club?

World.title: Greece’s Mitsotakis: EU needs new tools to fight back against weaponized migration
World.content:
Recent events at Europe’s borders, most notably in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, are the latest reminder that migration is no longer just a humanitarian issue or management challenge. In some cases, it has become a tool of geopolitical coercion.

The EU has made important progress on this issue with its Pact on Migration and Asylum. It has introduced mechanisms to manage migratory pressure, including flexibility in its procedures and solidarity among member countries. But these tools are designed for situations that remain, at their core, manageable. They do not adequately address scenarios in which migration is weaponized, or where flows are engineered, amplified or facilitated in a way that creates a de facto hybrid challenge.

To be sure, we don’t yet know what caused the situation that unfolded in Ceuta last week. But scenarios like these are not unprecedented.

Greece faced a similar situation at its land border with Turkey in Evros in 2020, as did Lithuania, Poland and Latvia at their borders with Belarus in 2021. What we are witnessing in these cases is not a gradual increase in arrivals but the sudden, massive and often coordinated movements of people — sometimes in the tens of thousands within just a few days — that overwhelm national capacities and test the EU’s resilience as a whole.

In such extreme circumstances, the immediate and full application of standard asylum and reception systems for all arrivals is not simply difficult — it is often impossible. Systems risk paralysis, public trust erodes and the very functioning of Schengen is put under strain.

Europe needs to acknowledge this gap and act decisively.

World.title: EU ministers to back Spain as Ceuta crisis pushes migration up the agenda
World.content:
The groundwork for Tuesday’s meeting was set on Monday when EU ambassadors held talks that lasted around two and a half hours. The Spanish envoy gave Madrid’s account of the Ceuta crisis, during which more than 70 people died, and reprimanded some capitals for spreading disinformation, according to one of the diplomats. The ambassador was asked for verification of Madrid’s figures on returned migrants and for the situation to be closely monitored, two other diplomats said.

Concerns were also raised that Spanish government policies may have been used by people-smugglers and gangs to encourage the events in Ceuta.

“There’s a concern that … the legalization of a million irregular migrants, that it’s been possible [for people-smugglers] to use that to give the impression that the door was open,” said one diplomat from a country that has been critical of Spain.

Italy called for the EU to immediately establish migrant deportation hubs in non-EU countries, one of the diplomats said. The plans follow the approval of a law granting EU capitals the power to set up centers in non-EU countries for processing migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the bloc — so-called return hubs.

But the Spanish ambassador criticized Italy for amplifying false claims about the migrant regularization program, such as Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani’s suggestion on social media that it automatically grants EU citizenship. The program provides legal residency to eligible migrants but does not confer Spanish nationality.

Rallying to support Spain

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set the tone of conciliation on Monday by writing to Sánchez to praise Spain and Morocco for their handling of the crisis and calling for a united European response. She said the episode showed the need for stronger controls at the EU’s external borders, closer cooperation with partner countries, better early-warning systems, action against smuggling networks and more effective returns.

World.title: Europe wants to kick its Palantir habit
World.content:
“Let's be honest, Palantir’s product is very good and addictive, it's pretty much like the sugar in Coca-Cola,” said French digital sovereignty advocate, Philippe Latombe. “Palantir can treat massive amounts of data with great precision and with their experience, they had time to improve their algorithms with many clients and adapt them to many use cases.”

Still, the drive to break free from Palantir is sweeping around the continent, from Madrid, where the government of Pedro Sánchez has instructed state-backed companies to block Palantir from future public procurement contracts, to France’s domestic intelligence services (DGSI) selecting French company ChapsVision over Palantir. In Britain, the next test may come in February 2027, when the new Labour government of Andy Burnham will face a choice of whether to cut off Palantir’s £330 million National Health Service Federated Data Platform contract.

Last month’s decision by the French and German intelligence agencies to choose ChapsVision was a double-blow for Palantir’s leadership. CEO Alex Karp showed little patience for the sudden turn away from his company’s wares, declaring that he wasn’t worried about European competitors. “We have a model of what doesn’t work," he quipped last week on Fox Business. "It’s called Europe.”

Palantir CEO Alex Karp visits "The Claman Countdown" at Fox Business Network Studios. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, ChapsVision’s chief executive, told POLITICO that his company has benefited from what he calls a “visceral rejection of Palantir” in Europe.

But he also cautioned that he did not want ChapsVision reduced to an anti-Palantir way out. Digital sovereignty, he argues, will remain an empty phrase unless governments turn it into industrial policy. “We need more public procurement,” Dellenbach said.

Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, Romania, the Netherlands and Canada have already shown interest in the French Army’s Artemis AI, according to Patrick Moreau, one of the architects of the solution built by French aerospace and defense company Thales.

World.title: Poland appeals €1.3B Pfizer vaccine ruling
World.content:
Warsaw says the end of the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine upended the deal.

Poland on Monday appealed a Brussels court judgment ordering it to take delivery of roughly 64 million unwanted Covid-19 doses and pay Pfizer about €1.3 billion. Warsaw also asked judges to freeze the ruling’s provisional enforcement while the challenge is heard.

“The decision of the court of first instance does not take into account all the relevant factual and legal circumstances of the case,” the Health Ministry said in a statement. It added that Poland would use “all legal means of defense,” but declined to disclose its arguments or evidence, citing the need to protect the state’s interests.

The ruling which Poland appealed relates to a 2021 agreement the European Commission negotiated with Pfizer on behalf of EU countries. Poland stopped accepting vaccine deliveries in 2022, citing collapsing demand and the impact of Russia's war against Ukraine. Pfizer sued Poland and Romania the following year. In April 2026, a Brussels court ruled that Warsaw remained bound by the contract and ordered it to pay roughly €1.3 billion, plus interest and legal costs, for the undelivered doses.

Pfizer defended the Belgian judgment, which it told POLITICO reflected “the importance of the contractual obligations that underpinned a successful European pandemic response, built on the principle of solidarity between Member States.” The company said it was taking “appropriate steps” to ensure compliance through “established legal enforcement mechanisms,” adding that those efforts followed “years of discussions and significant flexibility to accommodate Member States' circumstances.”

World.title: Parisians are now flying above the Seine on electric surfboards
World.content:
Parisians are taking to the Seine on a new type of electric surfboard that lifts riders above the water, creating the sensation of flying.

 

Known as an e-foil, the board combines an electric motor, a submerged hydrofoil and a rechargeable battery, allowing it to glide above the river's surface once it gains speed.

"It's got a board to climb on, and it's got a mast that's fitted with a motor at the back. It's got a wing, like an aircraft wing, and that's the surface we're going to use to 'fly'. Then you put the battery inside, and this battery will give you two hours of autonomy. So you'll be able to cover 30 to 40 kilometres with it. And as you can see, everything is set up in 10 seconds," says Nicolas Pernodet, co-founder of Foil in Paris.

Pernodet believes the activity offers a new way to experience the French capital, and says the sport is easier to learn than many people expect.

Participants say the experience is unlike any other water sport. "The feeling you're after is that of rising up above the water. It's pretty rare. Personally, I've never come across a sport that lets you come out of the water while staying balanced. So it's quite unique — and what's more, it's in Paris," says Lilian, who works in finance.

Architect Patrick Dakessian agrees: "As soon as you're flying, especially when you're over the water, then, when you're flying, the feeling is incredible."
