World.title: 82-year-old charity cyclist dies day after last heroic ride
World.content:
The celebration of a grandfather's mammoth charity bike ride across Australia for motor neurone disease (MND) has taken a tragic turn.

Bob Montgomery has died a day after completing what he called "One Last Ride", a six-week journey that covered almost 5,300 kilometres from Broome in Western Australia to his home town of Bowral in the New South Wales Southern Highlands.

The 82-year-old and his 18-year-old grandson, Tom Malcolm, were welcomed home on Sunday by dozens of family, friends and wellwishers.

MND NSW chief executive Liam O'Meara said Mr Montgomery experienced a medical episode on his way home from a function at Sydney's Rose Bay on Monday.

"Tom, Bob's grandson, decided to push the extra 150-odd kilometres from Bowral to Sydney yesterday and we all got together to greet him," he said.

"It was a lovely afternoon. We had [former South Sydney Rabbitohs player and MND sufferer] Jai Arrow in attendance … Bob was just elated.

"I received a text last night at 9 o'clock to say he has passed away, which was shocking."

The pair's cross-country effort was an idea pitched by Bob Montgomery (left) and timed to coincide with grandson Tom Malcolm's (right) university break. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Mr Montgomery's wife of 59 years, Jen, told the ABC in a statement that his death was "very peaceful".

"He was surrounded by his friends and family and got all of the credit that he absolutely deserved over the past 48 hours," she said.

" So we're really, really pleased his last few days on earth were some of the best. "

Speaking to ABC Illawarra Drive on Monday morning, Mr Montgomery said he was still processing his achievement and the support shown by the community at the finish line.

"It was just an amazing afternoon [on Sunday]," he said.

"They put on a fantastic feed and the speeches were wonderful.

"It was very memorable, for sure."

Bob Montgomery's family shed tears of joy from the finish line on Sunday. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Massive stalwart, MND advocate

Mr Montgomery clocked up five charity bike rides for MND awareness and research since the death of his cousin from the condition 12 years ago.

He raised more than $300,000 for the cause, including a growing $90,000 from his latest venture.

"It can't be understated what he has achieved for many years, not just on this ride," Mr O'Meara said.

"He's been a massive advocate and stalwart for the MND community.

" He didn't have to do any of this. He chose to do it. And I think that's just the mark of the man. "

MND NSW is now looking to award Mr Montgomery a posthumous accolade and establish a memorial ride in his honour.

"He absolutely deserves it and we want to honour his memory," Mr O'Meara said.

World.title: Inquiry told actions of pro-Palestinian protesters in Sydney were 'appalling'
World.content:
The head of a peak Jewish body has criticised the "appalling" conduct of protesters at a pro-Palestinian rally organised in the wake of Hamas's attack on Israel, prompting a tense exchange with lawyers for Palestinian advocacy groups at the antisemitism royal commission.

The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN) and the Palestine Action Group were given leave to appear to question witnesses at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Tuesday.

The inquiry is examining how police respond to protests, using as examples the pro-Palestinian protest between Town Hall and the Sydney Opera House on October 9, 2023 and a neo-Nazi rally outside the NSW Parliament on November 8, 2025.

Jewish Board of Deputies president David Ossip said he first learned about the October 9 rally on the evening of October 7, shortly after Israelis were killed and taken hostage in an attack by terrorist group Hamas in southern Israel.

Mr Ossip says the actions of pro-Palestinian protesters were "appalling". (Supplied: Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion)

Mr Ossip said he believed the rally, organised by the Palestine Action Group, would initially be confined to Town Hall, and later learned protesters would march to the Opera House.

The monument was to be lit blue and white in solidarity with Australian Jews and Israelis, with members of the community intending to hold a vigil on the evening of October 9, 2023.

Police contacted over safety fears

The commission heard the Community Security Group NSW (CSG NSW) had communicated with NSW Police about security concerns associated with the protest.

Mr Ossip said on the advice of police, the Jewish Board of Deputies subsequently told the Jewish community to avoid Town Hall and the Sydney Opera House on the night of the protest, and exercise vigilance if they were in the broader Sydney CBD area.

"The fact that two days after October 7 a community which was highly traumatised and in mourning was told the CBD was not safe for them, had profound psychological impacts," he said. "I can't recall any group … ever being provided advice that they should avoid their own city's CBD for their own safety and wellbeing. "It was effectively the police saying, 'We can't keep your community safe'. In my view it was effectively the police transferring control of the CBD to the protesters."

The commission heard a number of protesters were heard chanting "where's the Jews?" and "f*** the Jews", with an Israeli flag set on fire during the October 9 rally.

Additionally, the commission heard a subsequent inquiry into the rally, including a forensic analysis of 200 hours of CCTV footage, could not find evidence of claims some had chanted "gas the Jews".

'I thought their conduct was appalling'

The inquiry heard Jewish people were advised to avoid Town Hall and the Opera House during the pro-Palestinian protest. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Under cross-examination by counsel representing the Palestine Action Group Dominic Toomey SC, Mr Ossip said he struggled to understand the motivations of the protest organisers.

"Your clients effectively called for a protest at Town Hall on the evening of October 7 whilst the attacks in Israel were still occurring," he told Mr Toomey.

"I still don't understand why they thought calling a protest in such circumstances was necessary. I thought their conduct was appalling.

"It was a scene of international disgrace and infamy. It is amongst the clearest examples of antisemitism we have seen over the past few years."

There was some back and forth about the timeline of the Hamas attacks and the Israeli military's subsequent response.

"You are aware aren't you that Israeli Defence Force fighter jets began conducting air strikes in the Gaza strip around 5:30pm Sydney time on October 7?" Mr Toomey put to Mr Ossip.

US Jewish leader's warning for Australia The leader of one of the world's most high-profile Jewish organisations says Australia faces a crucial test on how it tackles the rise of antisemitism.

Mr Ossip appeared to become frustrated with some of the cross-examination.

"This is a royal commission on antisemitism … I'm a bit confused about why we are getting caught up in the minutia of the timeline of a foreign military," he said.

Commissioner Virginia Bell interjected.

"If the line of questioning falls outside matters that are properly before me, I will rule the question inadmissible. I have not made that ruling," she told Mr Ossip.

Mr Toomey put to Mr Ossip that a number of the protesters who demonstrated at the Opera House were not involved in the initial rally at the Town Hall, and organisers had distanced themselves from those who chanted offensive slogans.

"Do you agree … that they [protest organisers] roundly condemned the actions of those people whose actions you have identified?" he put to Mr Ossip.

Mr Ossip said the condemnation was "welcome".

Counsel appearing for APAN, Ragni Mathur SC, pressed Mr Ossip on comments he made about the timing of the Sydney Opera House protest.

"In the context of your earlier evidence that you found it insensitive that a protest should be called on the 7th [of October] … you appreciated that Palestinian Australians were likewise filled with deep fear with respect to what the future held for those in the occupied territory?" Ms Mathur put to Mr Ossip.

"I think it's important for all of us as citizens of Australia to show kindness and respect and understanding and sensitivity to others," he said.

"Notwithstanding any trauma those Palestinian Australians were feeling, I feel like if they were involved in organising this rally at a time when such grievous acts of violence were being committed against Israeli citizens, I think that showed a lack of sensitivity."

Senior officer addresses inquiry

The commission also heard from NSW Police Acting Deputy Commissioner Peter McKenna, who discussed the police response to the October 9 protest.

The inquiry heard two people wearing Israeli flags were arrested for breach of the peace and issued move on notices, and a flare was launched over the heads of police during the rally.

Acting Deputy Commissioner McKenna said police were in control of the Opera House rally. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said at no point did officers on the ground feel the protest was at risk of getting out of control.

"There is no doubt that watching this on television, watching this on the news, it looked terrible … because of that backdrop of the Sydney Opera House, there were lots of people there, the flare," he said.

"But when I speak to police officers on the ground, they did not have concerns about this protest getting out of control.

"We are talking hours of a protest that has been reduced to seconds or minutes on a news grab that has probably conflated it to make it more significant than what we say it was, as far as public safety goes.

"I'm not talking about the intention behind it or how it might make the Jewish community feel."

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said the October 9 protest continued to have an impact, almost three years on.

"I've been to the Supreme Court to stop protests from going to the Opera House since this particular one occurred," he said.

World.title: New Zealand climbers rescued from Solomon Islands' highest mountain
World.content:
Two New Zealand men stranded on Solomon Islands' highest mountain have been rescued.

Keanu Isaksson, 25, and Luca Zylstra 19, were airlifted out of a steep ravine on Tuesday morning, where they had been trapped for the last six days.

Mr Isaksson's mother, Denise Holl, told the ABC a clear window of weather allowed a rescue helicopter to reach the pair, who were located 1,828 metres up Mount Popomanaseu in central Guadalcanal.

Mount Popomanaseu is a volcanic mountain on the Solomon Islands island of Guadalcanal. (Supplied)

It is understood the helicopter dropped food and a radio to the men, who were then able to clear space for a cargo net to be lowered.

"They instructed the boys to fell some trees to create some space for the helicopter," she said.

"The boys had their own equipment with knives that could do the tree work and they were able to climb the net and get flown back to Honiara."

Ms Holl said she was able to speak with the two men, describing them as both nonchalant and emotional.

"My son and Luca have done lots of adventures together and are very close, and they would have taken very good care of each other," she said.

Keanu Isaksson is an avid climber and has previously visited Mt Everest. (Supplied)

"I'm sure they've got quite a bit of footage and quite a few stories to tell."

Mr Isaksson and Mr Zylstra travelled to Solomon Islands in search of a remote climbing adventure and as preparation for an upcoming trip to the Amazon.

Mount Popomanaseu is a 2,335-metre mountain, taller than mainland Australia's tallest peak, Mount Kosciuszko, which stands at 2,228 metres.

Ms Holl said the friends had summitted with the aid of guides from a local tribe, but those guides could not take the men back down because the descent path crossed into a different tribal area.

During their descent, Ms Holl said torrential rain made the steep terrain "impossible" to traverse, forcing them to camp on a rock overlooking a waterfall for six days.

Reaching the summit of Mount Popomanaseu is a rugged multi-day expedition that requires local guides and custom clearances from local tribes. (Supplied: Visit Solomon Islands)

"They're extremely lucky that the rivers didn't rise any higher because it would have just washed them over the waterfall," she said.

Initial attempts to reach the pair were unsuccessful, with one search party forced to turn back because of heavy rain.

The rescue helicopter meanwhile did not have access to a winch and was unable to land where the men were stranded.

Ms Holl said the past week had taken a huge emotional toll on her family, but they could now rest easy knowing the men were safe.

"We're ecstatic, and I'm shaking right now and just decompressing," she said.

"We're just really happy that this didn't go on any longer."

World.title: How the Reflecting Pool saga saw Trump sour on hand-picked prosecutor
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused a federal prosecutor he appointed of folding "like an umbrella" after she moved to drop charges against a three-time Olympian accused of vandalising the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

He told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, "made a mistake" and "choked" by abandoning the case.

It comes as rumours circulate that Mr Trump is weighing an attempt to oust her from the role she has held for little more than a year.

Here's what to know about the emerging feud.

First, catch me up

This spat relates to the months-long drama over Mr Trump's plagued Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation.

Back in April, the president ordered a multi-million-dollar renovation of the monument, which aimed to fix leaks and turn the pool a colour he called "American flag blue".

No-bid contracts were awarded to two businesses Mr Trump had personal ties to, bypassing a legal requirement to seek competing bids by citing urgency to get the job done in time for Independence Day celebrations.

Ducks swimming in the Reflecting Pool after an algal bloom turned the water green. (Reuters: Ken Cedeno)

Just days after the pool was refilled on June 4, an algae bloom turned the waters bright green.

Park workers were at one stage seen emptying jugs of hydrogen peroxide into the water in an attempt to clear the algae.

By June 9, the newly installed blue lining at the bottom of the pool had begun to peel.

Without providing evidence, Mr Trump later alleged vandals had poured "corrosive and destructive chemicals" into the pool.

A National Park Service worker dumping bleach into the water on June 16. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

On June 19, David "Davey" Hearn, who canoed for the United States at the 1992, 96 and 2000 Olympics, stopped by the pool during a 102-kilometre bike ride and reached into the water to examine the peeling coating.

Mr Hearn, who owned a company that made composite materials for watercraft, told the Associated Press he briefly touched a chunk that was still attached to the side of the pool, then let go when a park worker told him to.

National Guard troops and Park Police then detained him for five hours, and he was later indicted for "maliciously" damaging the lining.

In July, Mr Hearn pleaded not guilty to one felony count of property destruction, and a trial was scheduled to begin on September 28 in the DC Superior Court.

What happened with Hearn's case?

Prosecutors ultimately decided to drop the case.

In court papers filed by Ms Pirro's office on Friday, the prosecution said it had received new information that undermined the charges laid against Mr Hearn.

Trump officials admit Reflecting Pool work was 'botched' The US Department of Justice has moved to drop a criminal case charging a three-time Olympian with deliberately damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Here's why.

The filing cited documents provided by the Department of the Interior, which showed the damage to the pool's sealant was the result of a "botched installation" by a contractor and the "rush to complete the project".

A recent visual inspection also revealed damage throughout the pool, including in the middle, where prosecutors say a vandal would not likely have attempted to peel the lining.

"Given all of this newly discovered information, it is difficult to attribute the widespread damage to the Reflecting Pool to vandalism, let alone to establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt," the filing, which asked a judge to formally dismiss the case, said.

The move to dismiss the charges against Mr Hearn was an embarrassing setback for the Department of Justice and marked a rare moment during Mr Trump's second term of an aide or political appointee openly defying him.

And Trump wasn't happy?

He was not.

The president took to Truth Social on Saturday to voice his displeasure over the move, saying he "100%" disagreed with Ms Pirro.

"I don't know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM, that included the grass, which had a big 86 47 emblazoned in giant letters on it, and other elements of the surrounding area," he wrote, linking the damage to an incident where numbers were found emblazoned onto a nearby lawn.

"There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!"

He later shared webcam video of the Reflecting Pool that showed some passers-by dipping their hands into the water, accusing them of cutting the sealant with "a knife or box cutter, for all to see".

Mr Hearn was never accused of cutting the sealant, but of "forcefully and violently" pulling the liner "with both hands".

Jeanine Pirro had previously accused David Hearn of "maliciously" pulling at the sealant. (Reuters: Cheney Orr)

Mr Trump was still fuming two days later, discussing the matter with reporters in the Oval Office for several minutes on Monday.

"Frankly, I think [Ms Pirro] choked because the judge was really vicious," he said.

"Instead of going after the people that did it, the judge went after her and went after her department, and I guess she choked. I don't know what the hell happened.

"I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed."

What about the rumours?

Two unnamed sources familiar with the president's thinking told CNN it was "highly likely" Ms Pirro would be removed from her job, with one adding that Mr Trump felt "blindsided" by her filing.

Mr Trump was asked whether he was reconsidering Ms Pirro's role while speaking with reporters on Monday but didn't answer directly.

"I don't know what", he said, before sledging the journalist who had asked about the rumour.

"You're fake news. Don't ever talk again."

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was drained again on July 10. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

On Monday evening, Ms Pirro was seen walking into the White House. Also spotted was Department of the Interior secretary Doug Burgum, who has been outspoken in defending the president's suggestions that vandalism was to blame.

Sources told CNN Ms Pirro was not fired during the meeting, nor did she resign.

ABC/AP

World.title: Ben Carroll names ministry, adds new artificial intelligence portfolio
World.content:
New Victorian premier Ben Carroll has announced the make-up of his cabinet, including a new ministry dedicated to ethical and responsible artificial intelligence development.

Ally of former premier Jacinta Allan, Jaclyn Symes, has lost the treasury to Colin Brooks, who will also take on industrial relations.

Mr Brooks said it was an honour to be appointed as treasurer.

"I grew up in small business household," he said.

"Mum worked in a retail ladieswear shop on a main street where I grew up and so it's fantastic to be able to put those principles that she taught me and my dad taught me around budgeting and simple things you can do running a business into place in terms of running the state."

Rebuilding the relationship with business will be a key focus, he said.

Colin Brooks has been elevated to treasurer in the new Carroll government. (ABC News)

Ms Symes has been moved to energy and resources, the State Electricity Commission, climate action and environment, while remaining the leader of the government in the Legislative Council.

Sonya Kilkenny, who at one stage looked to challenge Mr Carroll for the leadership, remains attorney-general and planning minister, but will also become the new minister for prevention of family violence.

Anthony Carbines hands over the police ministry to Paul Edbrooke, who will also add emergency services, crime prevention and the multicultural affairs portfolio to his swag.

Anthony Carbines will become the minister for the new portfolio of artificial intelligence and digital economy. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

That allows Mr Carbines to take on the new ministry — artificial intelligence and digital economy.

Mr Carroll said Mr Carbines's role would include focusing on ensuring AI developments are ethical and responsible, as well as promoting innovative digital investment.

"Artificial intelligence is the biggest transformation going through society and the economy right now," Mr Carroll said.

"My government will be focused on workers.

"Artificial intelligence is a great opportunity but it also needs guard rails and regulatory reform so I want a voice at the cabinet table on that."

He said data centre developments would be part of Mr Carbine's remit.

"Everything needs to be considered on its merits, it needs to be considered wisely — its economic impact, its environment impact, its amenity impact and what is best for that Victorian community," Mr Carroll said.

As part of Mr Carroll's plan to reduce to size of frontbench, Mr Carbines remains the racing minister and leader of the house while taking on major events, medical research and economic development.

New police minister Paul Edbrooke says he will focus on community safety and police resources. (ABC News)

Mr Edbrooke said as the new police minister, he would focus on community safety and police resourcing.

"My first phone calls will be to some of my colleagues in The Police Association, police command, the chief commissioner, to get the information we need to go forward and support the premier's agenda."

Transport infrastructure dumped in new cabinet

A big exclusion from Mr Carroll's government is the transport infrastructure ministry.

The department has been a focus of the Labor government for several years, overseeing Victoria's major rail, road, public transport and freight projects including the Metro Tunnel, the Level Crossing Removal Project and the Suburban Rail Loop.

It has previously been filled by Jacinta Allan and most recently by Gabrielle Williams, who became deputy premier under the leadership change.

Tim Richardson (left), was promoted to Premier Ben Carroll's cabinet on Monday. (ABC News)

Ms Williams will be responsible for women and gender equality, skills and training and First Peoples.

She also takes the education portfolio from Mr Carroll as the disruptive industrial relations dispute with the state's public school teachers continues.

Ahead of being sworn into her new ministries at Government House, Ms Williams said her highest priority was to work with the union to try to come to an agreement.

"I will be rolling my sleeves up as soon as we're out of here today to make sure that we get on and progress those negotiations so that we can get a solution that everybody can be happy with and ultimately respects the work of our hardworking educators and education support staff," she said.

New addition to the cabinet Tim Richardson will be the minister for local government, consumer affairs and renters.

Minister Portfolio Ben Carroll Premier Gabrielle Williams Deputy Premier Education Skills and Training First Peoples Women and Gender Equality Jaclyn Symes Energy and Resources State Electricity Commission Climate Action Environment Lizzie Blandthorn Children Disability Colin Brooks Treasurer Industrial Relations Anthony Carbines Artifical Intelligence and Digital Economy Major Events Medical Research Racing Economic Development Steve Dimopoulos Sport WorkSafe and TAC Equality Paul Edbrooke Police Emergency Services Crime Prevention Multicultural Affairs Enver Erdogan Finance Government Services Casino, Gaming and Liquor Regulation Luba Grigorovitch Youth Carers and Volunteers Paul Hamer Roads and Road Safety Melissa Horne Jobs Industry and Advanced Manufacturing Defence Industry Ports and Freight Sonya Kilkenny Attorney-General Prevention of Family Violence Planning Tim Richardson Local Government Consumer Affairs Renters Michaela Settle Water Rural and Regional Development Agriculture Ros Spence Youth Justice Corrections Victims Support Community Sport Nick Staikos Housing, Building and Precincts Homelessness Seniors Ingrid Stitt Health Mental Health Ambulance Services Special Minister of State Natalie Suleyman Trade, Tourism and Investment Small and Family Business Veterans Vicki Ward Public Transport Creative Industries Nina Taylor Cabinet Secretary

Mr Carroll said his ministers would take the government in a new direction.

"A government that will fight every day for working people, a government that will fix things," he said.

He denied the dumping of the transport infrastructure portfolio was a precursor to cancelling the Suburban Rail Loop project.

He also defended abolishing the portfolio dedicated to reducing cost of living.

"Every portfolio will be driving down cost of living, whether it's in education, whether it's in energy and resources," he said.

"We are running a smaller government, a more efficient and more effective government where it extracts the best value for taxpayers.

"I've considered this very carefully, whether it's the public transport minister being in charge of both infrastructure and services, whether it's the roads minister being in charge of both roads and infrastructure."

There is also no longer a minster for men and boys.

Jess Wilson says Ben Carroll is trying to distance himself from major construction project scandals. (ABC News)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Ben Caroll was simply "shuffling the deck chairs on the Titanic".

"The same faces that have been around the cabinet table for years endorsing decisions by Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan," she said.

She accused Mr Carroll of eliminating references to the Big Build to try to distance Labor from allegations of corruption in the construction industry.

World.title: Alan Jones told 17yo 'there are no rules' at his home, court hears
World.content:
A man accusing Alan Jones of indecently assaulting him has detailed in court a night at the broadcaster's farm, where he said Mr Jones demanded he have a shower and come out wearing "a robe and nothing else".

Mr Jones, 85, is facing an indecent assault and sexual touching trial in the Sydney Local Court, which is hearing evidence from the first of six male complainants.

He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his defence lawyer told the court on Monday the case was actually about media rivalry and treachery from colleagues.

Complainant J began giving evidence on Monday that Mr Jones took an interest in his early sporting career, and gave him a phone, a car and weekly payments during a time where it is alleged the broadcaster kissed or touched him several times.

In court on Tuesday, Complainant J detailed a stay at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Falls farm in 2004, where he said he and the veteran broadcaster spoke over dinner and a glass of wine.

He said Mr Jones told him: "You've got to remember, there's only one rule here … there are no rules."

Mr Jones told the then-17-year-old to go and have a shower, the court heard.

"The defendant told me to go and have a shower and come back in a robe and nothing else," he said.

"It was very, very direct.

"It was, '[J], come back in a robe and nothing else.'"

The court heard Mr Jones told the complainant there were "no rules". (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

The man alleges he wore underwear under his robe, and said his "heart was racing" as he sat on the couch next to Mr Jones, who he alleges rubbed his genitals on the outside of his robe.

"I almost knew what was going happen, based on what happened in the car," the complainant said.

"He wanted me to come out in the nude so he could just undo [the robe], just easy access, he's going to touch me."

'I was completely frozen'

The court then heard more graphic allegations about further indecent assaults, where Mr Jones allegedly pulled the complainant towards him, kissed him, and their naked genitals touched.

There was a further alleged incident on the bed, where Mr Jones and the complainant allegedly masturbated at the same time.

Asked why he did that, the man said: "I thought it was the quickest way to get it over and done with."

"It was another trapped moment.

"I was completely frozen."

Stay up to date with The Case Of podcast The Case Of podcast will bring you all the key updates from the court hearings in Alan Jones's case.

In describing for the court what Mr Jones was allegedly doing with his hand, Complainant J said he was touching his own penis.

Complainant J said he went back to the farm another time, but only because his family was there.

On another occasion, the complainant agreed to stay at Mr Jones's Circular Quay apartment but said he planned to "stand up" to him and tell him to stop the behaviour.

The court heard Mr Jones gave the complainant another "chomping motion" kiss to the mouth without consent before bed.

He told the court he froze in the moment and was still disappointed with himself he did not stand up to Mr Jones.

"Thought that was the time I was going to put a complete end to it all," he said.

"I was prepared to stand up to him and I didn't.

" If I did stand up to him I would then have to lose everything again. "

'The right thing to do'

The court previously heard Complainant J was receiving between $450 to $600 a week from Mr Jones for several years, who said it was to help him with training and so he did not have to get a job.

Complainant J said he received an email from Mr Jones's financial team in 2012, advising him that the payments were coming to an end and also stated that he had received an estimated $110,000 from the broadcaster since 2004.

The complainant told the court he decided to report the allegations to NSW Police in 2024 when he saw on the news that Mr Jones had been arrested in relation to a historic assault investigation.

Asked why he decided to speak out after so many years, he told the trial he did not want compensation for what happened and instead he believed it was "the right thing to do".

"I'm a father now and I'm a proud dad I want to teach my daughter right from wrong," he said.

"What the defendant was doing was wrong I know it was wrong … if there were other people out there, I need to come out.

"I don't want money. I don't want anything out of this … I just wanted justice for what happened."

The trial is expected to last several weeks.

World.title: Solo parenting wasn't for me, so I'm co-parenting with my sister
World.content:
As the hospital hummed with antiseptic quiet and Kathy's fingers gripped mine, I thought about how strange it was to be there at the very beginning of someone's life — a baby who was both mine and not mine.

But let's start back in 2019, when I was faced with a decision to have a baby of my own with one of my partners, and I decided not to.

I've always loved babies and kids — I had lots of younger cousins growing up, and my first job as a teenager was babysitting the kids down the road.

Yet having a kid of my own at the time didn't feel right for me. And that realisation sank me to the bottom of the sea.

Could I parent alone?

Fast-forward to 2021, and I was hyper-focused on the prospect of solo parenting instead.

After careful consideration, Eli Sutherland realised solo parenting was not for them. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

I spent countless hours researching pregnancy and parenthood, intra-uterine insemination (IUI) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF), hospitals and home births, lactation cookies and swaddling techniques.

It was the perfect solution — everything on my own terms and timeline.

I spent $15,000 and submitted to a handful of painful tests, got the sperm delivered, and had the procedure. As soon as it went ahead, though, I knew it didn't feel right.

I didn't want to have biological children in that way, by myself, at that time. The procedure didn't take.

Solo parenting, it turns out, wasn't for me. But the process of discovering that also came with weekly phone calls with my sister, Kathy.

"I realised something," she said one day.

"It's funny how you're younger than me, but sometimes you lead me to realisations. I want to be a mum. I think I want to do IVF."

Do you have a unique co-parenting story to share with us? We'd love to hear from you.

Kathy came out as asexual and aromantic a few years ago and had maintained a stance of child-free-by-choice for years before that. Partly because babies meant a partner and sex (nope!) and partly because she's a primary school teacher, and that's enough kids to deal with on the daily.

Eli with their brother, Andrew, and sister, Kathy. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

But accompanying me on my reproductive journey flicked a switch for Kathy — what became visible, became possible.

So we embarked on our own adventure

I'd been thinking about what it might mean to hold a child who isn't mine.

As a non-binary person, the label "maternal" fit me like a left shoe on a right foot, while "paternal" made me seasick.

Still, the pull was undeniable.

Kathy and I spent months planning what it would look like for me to move back to Perth/Boorloo from Melbourne/Naarm for the first six months of my nibling's life (for those who haven't heard of this term, nibling is a non-gendered combination of niece or nephew with sibling, i.e. a child of one's sibling).

Eli and their sister Kathy at the hospital. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

We also had some gentle (and sometimes less than gentle) conversations with people about our decision.

We explained, time and again, that:

"No, we're not a lesbian couple, we're siblings."

"I won't get paid parental leave, but I'm still taking six months off work to be the secondary co-parent."

"They'll have plenty of positive masculine role models, thanks."

"All this for a child that's not my own? Yes, I'm sure."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

It was sometimes exhausting having to justify why our family looked different to others — a pregnant asexual woman, accompanied through birth and the newborn phase by a non-binary queer sibling.

But mostly it was wonderful to have conversations with people about what family means to them, and how that differs (and aligns) with what it means to us.

The moment that changed me

By August 2022, my sister and I were gowned in matching blue hospital attire, face masks and hairnets.

The gurney wheeled Kathy down the fluorescent-lit hallway towards the delivery room, her stomach stretched as far as it would go, holding a tiny human safe inside.

Eli with Kathy and their bub shortly after birth. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

And what a privilege it was to be in that delivery room. To be the first person to see, to hold, to kiss my nibling.

When she was finally placed on Kathy's chest, I felt something shift inside me.

Maybe that feeling is what parentalism means: a continual rebirth of the self, the family, the love we offer and lose.

Storm-grey seas revived to deepest blue.

In the years since, we've had four Christmases, dozens of trips to the beach, countless bubbles, and a whole lot of Bluey. Add to that the sleepless nights and bottle feeds, trips back and forth between cities, a few more IVF rounds, and now a baby brother heavyweight champion of chubby cheeks.

Eli and their nibling relaxing on the couch. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

Kathy will always be Mum to these two gorgeous kiddos, and I'll be something flowing in-between. Mostly I'm "Unty" (a gender-neutral mix of uncle and aunty), and sometimes just Eli.

But maybe the word isn't what's important.

Maybe what's important is just that I'll always be there with them.

Eli Sutherland (they/them) is an award-winning poet and writer living on Wurundjeri Country, and is the festival director of Trans Book Festival.

World.title: 'Cocaine dealer' on Mahmood Fazal's Four Corners episode says she did it as 'an acting role'
World.content:
Further concerns over the accuracy of reporting by sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal have been raised on Media Watch, including that a hire car was used to mislead viewers in the profile of a purported cocaine dealer.

Fazal's employment was terminated after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year, ABC managing director Hugh Marks confirmed at a Senate estimates hearing in May.

Since then, two episodes of Four Corners, Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, have been removed by the ABC due to accuracy concerns.

On Friday, a Background Briefing audio program titled "Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer" was also removed.

Loading...

In both the Background Briefing program and Cocaine Nation episode, Fazal interviewed Remy, a masked figure who is a purported cocaine dealer to Sydney's elite.

Now, Media Watch has reported that self-styled Sydney rapper Charissa Habkouk claims that she played the role of "Remy" as a favour to Fazal and that the core of her story in both programs was invented.

Ms Habkouk told Media Watch she considered Remy "an acting role and a favour to Mahmood".

"All of that … is a complete fable … there’s no validity to [it] … [Fazal] knew I could play the part and look the part," she told Media Watch.

Media Watch has alleged "Remy" was a role played by self-styled Sydney rapper Charissa Habkouk. (ABC: Four Corners)

She added that Fazal had approached her initially on Instagram, saying the story was "his shot to secure his work with the ABC".

In a response to Media Watch, Fazal rejected Ms Habkouk's claims and said he was "already contracted by the ABC on a permanent ongoing basis".

"The suggestion that I needed this story to 'cement' my position at the ABC is false," he said in a statement.

He added that he stood by the "integrity of my reporting and the editorial processes that underpinned both programs".

"I reject the suggestion that I fabricated, staged or knowingly published information that I believed to be false," Fazal said.

Mahmood Fazal was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing before his Four Corners role. (ABC)

Mercedes-Benz misleading in program

Media Watch reported Ms Habkouk alleged a Mercedes-Benz seen in the Four Corners episode was not hers, as the program implied, but hired by the ABC.

In the episode, a masked Ms Habkouk tells Fazal: "I’ve got us some nice wheels, a driver, take you to a few spots around Sydney."

She has since alleged the ABC "hired it, just to make it look like I was being driven around in it and there was an image".

Four Corners’ former executive producer Matthew Carney told Media Watch if Ms Habkouk's allegations "can be verified, then this is disappointing and troubling".

"If this information had been disclosed to me, the program would not have been broadcast," Carney said.

Ms Habkouk's claim cannot be immediately verified.

The ABC did not respond to Media Watch's questions.

Four Corners withdraws episodes The ABC has withdrawn the Four Corners programs Meth Highway and Cocaine Nation by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

She also told Media Watch that her previous claims, made on social media, that she had been paid for the Four Corners appearance, were false, leading the program to say that her accounts of events should be treated with caution.

"I didn’t get paid for the role. Not by Mahmood or the ABC," she told the program.

The ABC has previously said Fazal's episodes were removed "following concerns identified about the veracity of sources used in the three programs".

"The ABC Ombudsman is already conducting an independent review of whether the Four Corners programs complied with the ABC's editorial standards," it added in a statement.

Fazal alleges reporting heavily scrutinised

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, is an award-winning journalist specialising in crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

ABC withdraws third story by Mahmood Fazal The ABC has withdrawn a third story by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

Prior to joining the ABC, he worked for VICE as a senior staff writer and host of the series Violent Times.

His reporting has appeared in The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

After the Four Corners episodes were removed, Fazal said in a statement posted to social media that he was “shocked” by the decision.

"I believe the process ABC is following and its decisions so far set a worrying precedent for the organisation's independent [sic] and commitment to public-interest journalism," he said.

In another lengthy video statement, Fazal claimed he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, with that proximity later used to remove him from the organisation.

He said his reporting was heavily scrutinised during editorial standards and production meetings.

Charissa Habkouk says she played drug dealer Remy as a favour to Mahmood Fazal. (ABC: Four Corners)

"If there were questions about a source or a fact, we hashed it out internally at the time and made a call," Fazal said.

"And it wasn’t me making the call. Confidentiality doesn’t mean there was no oversight."

The withdrawals come at a turbulent time for the broadcaster after the sudden departure of news director Justin Stevens in May.

Mr Marks confirmed he and Stevens disagreed about the direction of the organisation and announced a replacement, Reuters executive editor Simon Robinson, the following day.

World.title: Three money habits that can keep you stuck financially
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingMoney psychology Opinion Three money habits that can keep you stuck financially Paridhi Jain Money contributor August 4, 2026 — 2:09pm

August 4, 2026 — 2:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you’ve hit a ceiling in your financial growth, today’s column is for you. Maybe you’ve been trying to increase your income or business revenue for a while, but it’s not happening. Perhaps you’ve been diligently saving or investing, but eventually something always sets you back. You just have that feeling that no matter how hard you try – the numbers don’t seem to budge. Today, I’m sharing some of the unconscious patterns that I commonly see and work through with my clients who are struggling to break past a financial ceiling. There’s a lot more to happiness than just how wealthy you are. Simon Letch Fear of being seen (or judged) as greedy What this looks like: You worry that people might judge you for having or wanting more than you “need”. You don’t want to be the odd one out. You might already be embarrassed by, or feel bad about, having more than others. You also might see some rich people in the spotlight doing unethical things and think: “I don’t want to end up like them”.



How this holds you back: If you have a negative perception of what it means to have more wealth, then you will keep finding ways to stay at a level that feels comfortable. Why would you want to become something that you think is bad, wrong, unethical or negative? You wouldn’t. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m in my 60s and well-off. So why am I so reluctant to spend money? Paridhi Jain Money contributor How to start to move past this: First, start to understand where you developed this negative perception from and why. Then, start to gently question the limitations of this perspective. Is it true that all people with significant wealth are greedy? Can someone be poor and greedy, or rich and generous? Does more money for you really mean less money for someone else? Do you actually think you would be greedy – or are you just scared of other people’s judgment? Attachment to frugality What this looks like: You got to a certain level of financial comfort through frugality. Now, it’s more than just a habit or a lifestyle; it’s a personality. You second-guess small purchases. You constantly look for the cheapest option. You don’t buy anything you don’t really “need”.



How this holds you back: There’s a saying: “What got you here won’t get you there.” Frugality can help at the start of your financial journey, but after a point, it can hold you back. If you’ve trained yourself to live within your means and not desire more, you may now have no real incentive to take the risks that would lead to greater growth. In the short term, this might not be the most lucrative path – but it will be the more sustainable path, long-term. You’re not even spending the money you do have, so why would you need more? Your strategy has been to train yourself to want less, instead of increasing your capacity to create more. How to start to move past this: You’ll want to start slowly expanding your capacity to enjoy spending money. This will be an uncomfortable transition to make because it’s going to feel like you’re moving in the wrong direction. However, as you start to enjoy spending money, you will also find yourself more inspired to want to create more wealth.



Chasing growth to ‘prove’ Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting Men control 60% of household finances. Here’s why they shouldn’t Victoria Devine Money columnist What this looks like: You’ve got a little chip on your shoulder, or something to prove. You want to prove – to yourself or to others – that you can achieve X milestone. Maybe you’re doing it to make your parents proud, or there’s someone in your family who you’re trying to compete with. Perhaps you were underestimated and now want to show what you’re really capable of. How this holds you back: Wanting to prove something can be a compelling driver, but it often has a ceiling because you’re not driven by what feels inherently fulfilling and meaningful to you, personally. You’re being driven by what you think someone else will be impressed by. This increases the likelihood of picking a path that isn’t really aligned to your natural talents, strengths and interests – but rather the one that you think will produce an impressive outcome. Eventually, this path might start to feel like a hard slog, which is difficult to sustain long-term.



How to start to move past this: First, you want to start noticing when and why you started feeling the need to “prove” anything at all. Here, you’ll discover the unresolved “wounds” that might need addressing. For many people, somewhere in their past, they learnt to earn love, praise, attention or validation through performance. Through this process, start to ask yourself: how do you cultivate enough worth, safety and validation, internally, so that you have nothing to prove? Then, start the process of discovering. What is the path that would feel meaningful and fulfilling to you, regardless of the outcome? In the short term, this might not be the most lucrative path – but it will be the more sustainable path, long-term. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant tells court he feared he owed $110,000 to 2GB broadcaster
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the second day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

On day one, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court of the second day of his criminal trial. Sam Mooy

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him in the car as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls property. He said he was fearful at the time of speaking out because he didn’t want to “lose everything”.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, after completing his evidence-in-chief.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Tourist charged $1200 reservation fee at Brisbane fine-dining establishment
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandRestaurants Tourist charged $1200 reservation fee at Brisbane fine-dining establishment Julius Dennis August 4, 2026 — 1:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sally Tsai and her family visited one of Brisbane’s most well-known fine-dining restaurants while on a trip from Taiwan, they mostly got what they expected: small, elegant servings and a big bill. But it wasn’t until after her trip that Tsai noticed the bill from Restaurant Dan Arnold – the two-hatted French-meets-Aussie cuisine establishment named after its chef – was even bigger than she thought. The restaurant had charged her a $400 fee three times after she made the booking, with Dan Arnold’s name listed next to each of the charges. Sally Tsai (second from right) with her family in Brisbane. Sally Tsai “It’s not like it’s being spammed … it’s [spaced out] around 13 hours afterwards,” Tsai said.



A booking confirmation email from the restaurant to Tsai, seen by this masthead, states the restaurant does not charge booking fees. Tsai said only one of the payments was deducted from her bill when they dined at the Fortitude Valley restaurant on July 10. A meal had by Tsai and her family at RDA in July. Sally Tsai When she noticed the triple charge, Tsai wrote to the restaurant and their booking service, SevenRooms, requesting a refund. SevenRooms wrote back to say restaurants are responsible for their own charges, but Tsai said the restaurant has not responded to her since.



“Zero word, zero response,” Tsai said. This masthead has also spoken to another Restaurant Dan Arnold customer who said they had similar issues but eventually got their money back. Tsai has logged a complaint with the Office of Fair Trading, which is attempting to facilitate conciliation between her and the restaurant. Arnold said the extra payments appeared to be due to a third-party provider, and the restaurant never received extra money from an “isolated number of affected guests”.



“Upon becoming aware of the issue, we confirmed that the duplicate charges were disputed and the dispute is currently being processed through the relevant payment provider,” he said. “While we have taken the necessary steps on our end, the final processing time is subject to the payment provider and the guest’s financial institution. Dan Arnold has been a fixture of the Brisbane hospitality scene since his return from France in 2018. Markus Ravik “We are aware of Ms Tsai’s inquiry and have been in communication regarding the matter.” Arnold opened the restaurant, also known as RDA, in 2018 to critical acclaim after spending the better part of a decade in France working in Michelin-starred restaurants.



In 2022 Arnold also took over another renowned Brisbane French restaurant, La Cache a Vin, before selling his stake to co-owner Romain Maunier in 2025. Related Article Food Celebrated restaurant Pneuma to close after departure of star chef The next year, he launched Pneuma, with former GOMA Restaurant chef Matt Blackwell in the Brisbane CBD, before that closed in July 2025. Upon his departure from Pneuma, Blackwell, who was the creative force of the restaurant, said he did not agree with the direction the business was heading. “Day to day, it’s all going well … but the direction it’s going is not where I’m wanting to be at the moment. So it makes sense to call it now,” he said at the time.



More than a year later, Arnold finds himself in a legal matter with another Brisbane hospitality identity, Cameron Votan, who previously operated a restaurant in the space where Pneuma later opened and who has taken action against him. That matter was filed in the Brisbane District Court in May, and remains unresolved. Arnold is yet to file a defence. World.title: ‘Bigger things to worry about’: Bombers great Watson weighs in on Lethal spray
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Bigger things to worry about’: Bombers great Watson weighs in on Lethal spray Jon Pierik August 4, 2026 — 1:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Essendon’s coaching exodus has continued with another assistant coach about to leave the club, while Bombers great Tim Watson has taken aim at his former club for “dobbing” in Leigh Matthews for his comments about the club’s coaching process. The Bombers confirmed on Tuesday that forwards coach Cam Roberts would leave the club at the end of the 2026 season, just like football department general manager Dan McPherson, whose departure was announced five days earlier. Essendon great Tim Watson has defended one-time Hawthorn rival Leigh Matthews over his comments about the Bombers’ coaching race. Joe Armao They join senior coach Brad Scott, assistant Ben Jacobs and head of psychology Ben Robbins among those departing the club this year. It was Matthews’ comments about the Bombers’ search for Scott’s replacement that lit a fuse on Saturday. The four-time premiership coach – one of the AFL’s most respected voices – told 3AW he would have “no confidence” to coach the Bombers under the current administration, adding: “If I was a coach, I wouldn’t be going to Essendon”.



The Bombers were privately upset with Matthews’ comments on Saturday when contacted by this masthead, given the Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend is a Brisbane Lions club director, but they went a step further on Sunday when chief executive Tim Roberts sent a transcript of Matthews’ comments to the AFL, as reported by Seven’s Agenda Setters. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser Bombers president Andrew Welsh also contacted Lions chairman Andrew Wellington for an explanation of Matthews’ comments. Three-time premiership great Watson, speaking on SEN on Tuesday, said Matthews, the former Hawks hard nut who clashed against the Bombers in three grand finals in the 1980s, was within his rights to comment. “Leigh is very considered and has powerful conversations from time to time, and he’s very direct in what he has to say,” Watson, the former Bombers skipper, told SEN.



“He’s not somebody that goes out there looking for clickbait, he’s not a hot-taker. There’s enough evidence around to suggest that what he’s saying not completely untrue, either. “I don’t know whether I would have gone to that degree, had I been at Essendon, that I thought, ‘OK, I need to go to the AFL and get some sort of comment from them’.” The AFL will not take action against Matthews, insisting it’s a club-based issue. When asked if there was an insecurity at the bottom-placed Bombers, Watson said: “I think there’s a lot going on at the club at the moment. “They’re staring down the wooden spoon, they haven’t got a coach. I would have thought you’ve got much bigger things to worry about than dobbing someone in about what they’ve said.



“I would think the best thing you can do in this business is point at the scorecard. At the moment, their scorecard looks miserable, but when it looks better you can point at it and say this is where we’re at. But they’ve got a long way to go before they are at that point.” A Bombers spokesman said on Tuesday the club had dealt with the Matthews matter on Saturday afternoon. Andrew Welsh, James Hird and Matthew Lloyd in their playing days at Essendon in 2004. Getty Images Cam Roberts’ stint at Essendon lasted seven seasons, starting as a development coach for the 2020 campaign. “When I first arrived, I simply wanted to contribute and help people improve. To have had the chance to work alongside such committed players, coaches and staff over the past seven seasons has been a privilege,” Roberts said.



Jacobs and Robbins quit in May in solidarity with Scott, while McPherson confirmed last week he would step down at the end of the season. Tim Roberts thanked Cameron Roberts for his contribution. “We appreciate that prior to appointing a senior coach there is always a level of uncertainty at AFL clubs. While we’re disappointed to see him leave, we completely respect his decision and thank him for everything he’s contributed to Essendon,” the CEO said. The Bombers’ hunt for a new senior coach has been reduced to four candidates: club legend James Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis, a former long-time Brisbane Lions assistant.



Caretaker coach Dean Solomon, a friend and former teammate of Hird and McVeigh, will this week have his first formal discussions with club hierarchy about the full-time job. But Solomon has publicly remained tight-lipped on whether he’ll seek the head coaching role. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist Welsh, Tim Roberts, football director Ted Richards, vice president and ex-Victory chairman Anthony Di Pietro and Essendon’s general manager of people and culture, Caroline Monzon, are on the selection panel. Melbourne Victory great and former coach Kevin Muscat, and long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop have supported the panel, challenging the candidates on their leadership credentials and game style. Formal interviews are continuing this week, the Bombers hoping to confirm their appointment by the end of next week as they restructure their football department, including the men’s and women’s programs. World.title: What Matt King’s NSW coaching contract means for Ivan Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLState of Origin What Matt King’s NSW coaching contract means for Ivan Cleary Christian Nicolussi August 4, 2026 — 1:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ivan Cleary may need to wait until 2030 to coach NSW after it was revealed Matt King’s two-year contract includes an option to activate a third year should the Blues beat Queensland in 2027 or 2028. King was officially unveiled as Laurie Daley’s successor as NSW Blues coach at NSW Rugby League’s Sydney Olympic Park headquarters on Tuesday. Loading Joined by his wife Kirsten and three young daughters, King revealed he had missed out on the top job with the Blues two years ago, and said he would call on coaching heavyweights Craig Bellamy, Craig Fitzgibbon, Michael Maguire and Trent Robinson as his unofficial “advisory board”. King also said he had wanted former Storm teammate and current Maroons coach Billy Slater to be the first to hear the news of his appointment, and insisted he was under no illusions about the media scrutiny that is certain to come his way in the role.



NSWRL CEO Dave Trodden confirmed King’s job would be a full-time role and that he would automatically trigger an extension for 2029 if he led the state to Origin glory in the next two years. Panthers coach Cleary will finish up with Penrith at the end of next year and has already spoken about his hopes of coaching at representative level, leading to speculation he would be installed as Blues coach as early as 2028. Matt King was officially unveiled as NSW Blues coach on Tuesday. Getty Images “Ivan is one of the greatest coaches there will be in rugby league, but we needed was a coach for 2027,” Trodden told this masthead. “Ivan wasn’t available, so that was always going to be a real difficulty. “There was the assumption about having a [stop-gap solution coach for 2027], which would almost be giving up next year’s series – and that’s not the way we were thinking. We expect to win next year, we expect to retain the trophy, and Matt King is the very best option to do that.



“He has a two-year contract, and if he wins a series in the next two years, there’s the automatic extension for 2029.” King, who will step down from his role as a Roosters assistant at season’s end after ten years on their coaching staff, said: “If I could pick any job, I’m picking this one. The jumper means so much to me. The players you have at your disposal, and just the contest, it’s incredible what State of Origin does for our country and what it means to people. To know I’m steering the ship, it’s pretty wild.” Matt King poses with daughters Charlie, Willow, Harper and wife Kirsten after his appointment on Tuesday. Getty Images King, the one-time garbo and Melbourne, Warrington, South Sydney, NSW and Australian cult hero known for his wild hair, won a premiership at the Storm with Slater, which explained why he was so eager to reach out to his coaching counterpart. Slater is saved simply as “Bill” in King’s phone, and King, 45, said: “We see each other a lot at footy games because he is a commentator. It’s always a handshake and a cuddle at the same time, and asking how the families are.



Related Article State of Origin Why a former garbo who has never coached first grade will lead NSW’s Origin defence in 2027 “There’s been a real mateship for a long time. I rang him about 9.30pm on Monday, he called me back first thing on Tuesday, and I said, ‘I wanted you to hear the news officially before you heard it anywhere else’. “I’m looking forward to that challenge of going up against Bill. Friendships can co-exist with the fact we’ll compete against each other and go hard against each other.” Maguire memorably accused Slater of living in “glass houses” during the 2024 series – the year King joined the NSW coaching staff – which frustrated Slater. When asked if his good mate actually resided in a “glass house”, King replied: “The last time I went to Billy Slater’s house, he had a little terrace in Richmond. I think he’s upgraded since then. I’d have to see how much glass he’s got.”



As for what he wanted to see from his NSW players? “Be a tough bugger, play with clarity, and go after the moments when your time comes,” King said. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Horror night for Sydney’s emergency departments
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWHealthcare Horror night for Sydney’s emergency departments Rachel Rasker Updated August 4, 2026 — 1:08pm ,first published 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Emergency services across Sydney on Monday recorded one of their busiest winter days, with a record 4100 ambulance callouts and almost 10,000 emergency department presentations. Western Sydney hospitals were among the hardest hit. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the state would see continued presentations for flu-like illness throughout winter. Emergency services in NSW have recorded one of their busiest days on record. James Brickwood “Influenza can also cause complications for people with comorbidities,” he said. “If someone with a co-morbidity gets influenza, the likelihood that they end up in the hospital is far greater than someone who just gets influenza on their own.”



There were about 1000 more emergency department presentations than usual. Related Article Flu season ‘Things are about to kick off’: NSW flu cases spike NSW Health Secretary Susan Pearce said dozens of patients were redirected to various hospitals on Monday to ease pressure on overflowing emergency departments. “The west, south-west, Nepean in particular were very, very busy last night (Monday),” Pearce said, with Park also pointing to Blacktown, Bankstown, Campbelltown and Liverpool hospitals as particular hotspots. Both Pearce and Park apologised to the patients and families who experienced long waits or were treated on the floor of waiting rooms.



It comes despite flu and COVID-19 cases remaining relatively stable – especially compared to last winter. Health authorities expect case numbers to rise now that children have returned to school. There were more than 2500 positive laboratory tests for influenza, the latest weekly surveillance report shows. The real number is significantly higher. Premier Chris Minns told 2GB it would be the worst three weeks of the year for emergency departments and warned people not to attend unless they were experiencing an actual emergency. Australian Medical Association NSW president Dr Fred Betros said telling patients to stay away from emergency departments “is not a health strategy”. “This is not an unforeseen crisis. It is a failure to prepare for predictable demand,” he said in a statement.



Park pointed to the 270 beds across western and south-western Sydney occupied by patients who are medically ready to be discharged but awaiting a federal government-funded place in an aged care or NDIS program. “That is the equivalent of a hospital not being able to be used,” he said, estimating 1300 people were affected. Betros said the state needed more consultant doctors, properly staffed beds, modern industrial arrangements to attract and retain doctors, and serious investment in prevention, general practice and public outpatient care. While he acknowledged the state government was right to press the Commonwealth on aged care and NDIS delays, he said “stranded patients cannot be blamed for every failure in our hospitals”. NSW Health chief health officer Dr Kerry Chant said influenza can “be that straw that broke the camel’s back” for people with underlying health conditions, including diabetes and lung disease, and urged the community to ask their GP about preventative health advice.



“It’s not too late in the season to get vaccinated,” she said. “In previous years, the pattern of when these respiratory viruses peak changes. Last year we saw quite a late peak of influenza … into that December period, which was quite unusual. So it’s not too late.” She said early indications have shown that this year’s flu vaccine is a better match for the influenza strain that’s currently circulating, predominantly H3N2 subclade K. World.title: Spaghetti aglio e olio with crispy chicken
World.content:
Step 1 Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Pat the chicken skin dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Add the chicken, skin side down, and cook for 4-6 minutes or until the skin is deep golden and crisp. Turn and cook for a further 4 minutes or until cooked through. Transfer to a plate, cover loosely with aluminium foil to retain heat and leave to rest before slicing thickly crosswise.

Step 2 Place 2 tablespoons of the remaining oil and the garlic into a large, deep frying pan over medium-low heat. Season with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3-4 minutes or until fragrant and lightly golden.

Step 3 Meanwhile, cook the pasta in a large saucepan of boiling salted water for 6-8 minutes or until al dente. Reserve ½ cup of the pasta cooking water, then drain.

Step 4 Add the drained pasta, reserved cooking water, chilli flakes, parsley, half the lemon zest and half the lemon juice to the garlic oil. Toss vigorously over low heat for 1-2 minutes until the liquid emulsifies into a glossy sauce that coats the pasta. Season to taste.

Step 5 Whisk the remaining olive oil, lemon zest and lemon juice together in a bowl to make the dressing. Toss the baby spinach with the dressing in a separate bowl.

How to start to move past this: First, you want to start noticing when and why you started feeling the need to “prove” anything at all. Here, you’ll discover the unresolved “wounds” that might need addressing. For many people, somewhere in their past, they learnt to earn love, praise, attention or validation through performance. Through this process, start to ask yourself: how do you cultivate enough worth, safety and validation, internally, so that you have nothing to prove? Then, start the process of discovering. What is the path that would feel meaningful and fulfilling to you, regardless of the outcome? In the short term, this might not be the most lucrative path – but it will be the more sustainable path, long-term. Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the second day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

On day one, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court of the second day of his criminal trial. Sam Mooy

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him in the car as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls property. He said he was fearful at the time of speaking out because he didn’t want to “lose everything”.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, after completing his evidence-in-chief.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Tourist charged $1200 reservation fee at Brisbane fine-dining establishment
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandRestaurants Tourist charged $1200 reservation fee at Brisbane fine-dining establishment Julius Dennis August 4, 2026 — 1:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sally Tsai and her family visited one of Brisbane’s most well-known fine-dining restaurants while on a trip from Taiwan, they mostly got what they expected: small, elegant servings and a big bill. But it wasn’t until after her trip that Tsai noticed the bill from Restaurant Dan Arnold – the two-hatted French-meets-Aussie cuisine establishment named after its chef – was even bigger than she thought. The restaurant had charged her a $400 fee three times after she made the booking, with Dan Arnold’s name listed next to each of the charges. Sally Tsai (second from right) with her family in Brisbane. Sally Tsai “It’s not like it’s being spammed … it’s [spaced out] around 13 hours afterwards,” Tsai said.



A booking confirmation email from the restaurant to Tsai, seen by this masthead, states the restaurant does not charge booking fees. Tsai said only one of the payments was deducted from her bill when they dined at the Fortitude Valley restaurant on July 10. A meal had by Tsai and her family at RDA in July. Sally Tsai When she noticed the triple charge, Tsai wrote to the restaurant and their booking service, SevenRooms, requesting a refund. SevenRooms wrote back to say restaurants are responsible for their own charges, but Tsai said the restaurant has not responded to her since.



“Zero word, zero response,” Tsai said. This masthead has also spoken to another Restaurant Dan Arnold customer who said they had similar issues but eventually got their money back. Tsai has logged a complaint with the Office of Fair Trading, which is attempting to facilitate conciliation between her and the restaurant. Arnold said the extra payments appeared to be due to a third-party provider, and the restaurant never received extra money from an “isolated number of affected guests”.



“Upon becoming aware of the issue, we confirmed that the duplicate charges were disputed and the dispute is currently being processed through the relevant payment provider,” he said. “While we have taken the necessary steps on our end, the final processing time is subject to the payment provider and the guest’s financial institution. Dan Arnold has been a fixture of the Brisbane hospitality scene since his return from France in 2018. Markus Ravik “We are aware of Ms Tsai’s inquiry and have been in communication regarding the matter.” Arnold opened the restaurant, also known as RDA, in 2018 to critical acclaim after spending the better part of a decade in France working in Michelin-starred restaurants.



In 2022 Arnold also took over another renowned Brisbane French restaurant, La Cache a Vin, before selling his stake to co-owner Romain Maunier in 2025. Related Article Food Celebrated restaurant Pneuma to close after departure of star chef The next year, he launched Pneuma, with former GOMA Restaurant chef Matt Blackwell in the Brisbane CBD, before that closed in July 2025. Upon his departure from Pneuma, Blackwell, who was the creative force of the restaurant, said he did not agree with the direction the business was heading. “Day to day, it’s all going well … but the direction it’s going is not where I’m wanting to be at the moment. So it makes sense to call it now,” he said at the time.



More than a year later, Arnold finds himself in a legal matter with another Brisbane hospitality identity, Cameron Votan, who previously operated a restaurant in the space where Pneuma later opened and who has taken action against him. That matter was filed in the Brisbane District Court in May, and remains unresolved. Arnold is yet to file a defence.
