World.title: ‘Bigger things to worry about’: Bombers great Watson weighs in on Lethal spray
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Bigger things to worry about’: Bombers great Watson weighs in on Lethal spray Jon Pierik August 4, 2026 — 1:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Essendon’s coaching exodus has continued with another assistant coach about to leave the club, while Bombers great Tim Watson has taken aim at his former club for “dobbing” in Leigh Matthews for his comments about the club’s coaching process. The Bombers confirmed on Tuesday that forwards coach Cam Roberts would leave the club at the end of the 2026 season, just like football department general manager Dan McPherson, whose departure was announced five days earlier. Essendon great Tim Watson has defended one-time Hawthorn rival Leigh Matthews over his comments about the Bombers’ coaching race. Joe Armao They join senior coach Brad Scott, assistant Ben Jacobs and head of psychology Ben Robbins among those departing the club this year. It was Matthews’ comments about the Bombers’ search for Scott’s replacement that lit a fuse on Saturday. The four-time premiership coach – one of the AFL’s most respected voices – told 3AW he would have “no confidence” to coach the Bombers under the current administration, adding: “If I was a coach, I wouldn’t be going to Essendon”.



The Bombers were privately upset with Matthews’ comments on Saturday when contacted by this masthead, given the Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend is a Brisbane Lions club director, but they went a step further on Sunday when chief executive Tim Roberts sent a transcript of Matthews’ comments to the AFL, as reported by Seven’s Agenda Setters. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser Bombers president Andrew Welsh also contacted Lions chairman Andrew Wellington for an explanation of Matthews’ comments. Three-time premiership great Watson, speaking on SEN on Tuesday, said Matthews, the former Hawks hard nut who clashed against the Bombers in three grand finals in the 1980s, was within his rights to comment. “Leigh is very considered and has powerful conversations from time to time, and he’s very direct in what he has to say,” Watson, the former Bombers skipper, told SEN.



“He’s not somebody that goes out there looking for clickbait, he’s not a hot-taker. There’s enough evidence around to suggest that what he’s saying not completely untrue, either. “I don’t know whether I would have gone to that degree, had I been at Essendon, that I thought, ‘OK, I need to go to the AFL and get some sort of comment from them’.” The AFL will not take action against Matthews, insisting it’s a club-based issue. When asked if there was an insecurity at the bottom-placed Bombers, Watson said: “I think there’s a lot going on at the club at the moment. “They’re staring down the wooden spoon, they haven’t got a coach. I would have thought you’ve got much bigger things to worry about than dobbing someone in about what they’ve said.



“I would think the best thing you can do in this business is point at the scorecard. At the moment, their scorecard looks miserable, but when it looks better you can point at it and say this is where we’re at. But they’ve got a long way to go before they are at that point.” A Bombers spokesman said on Tuesday the club had dealt with the Matthews matter on Saturday afternoon. Andrew Welsh, James Hird and Matthew Lloyd in their playing days at Essendon in 2004. Getty Images Cam Roberts’ stint at Essendon lasted seven seasons, starting as a development coach for the 2020 campaign. “When I first arrived, I simply wanted to contribute and help people improve. To have had the chance to work alongside such committed players, coaches and staff over the past seven seasons has been a privilege,” Roberts said.



Jacobs and Robbins quit in May in solidarity with Scott, while McPherson confirmed last week he would step down at the end of the season. Tim Roberts thanked Cameron Roberts for his contribution. “We appreciate that prior to appointing a senior coach there is always a level of uncertainty at AFL clubs. While we’re disappointed to see him leave, we completely respect his decision and thank him for everything he’s contributed to Essendon,” the CEO said. The Bombers’ hunt for a new senior coach has been reduced to four candidates: club legend James Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis, a former long-time Brisbane Lions assistant.



Caretaker coach Dean Solomon, a friend and former teammate of Hird and McVeigh, will this week have his first formal discussions with club hierarchy about the full-time job. But Solomon has publicly remained tight-lipped on whether he’ll seek the head coaching role. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist Welsh, Tim Roberts, football director Ted Richards, vice president and ex-Victory chairman Anthony Di Pietro and Essendon’s general manager of people and culture, Caroline Monzon, are on the selection panel. Melbourne Victory great and former coach Kevin Muscat, and long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop have supported the panel, challenging the candidates on their leadership credentials and game style. Formal interviews are continuing this week, the Bombers hoping to confirm their appointment by the end of next week as they restructure their football department, including the men’s and women’s programs. World.title: What Matt King’s NSW coaching contract means for Ivan Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLState of Origin What Matt King’s NSW coaching contract means for Ivan Cleary Christian Nicolussi August 4, 2026 — 1:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ivan Cleary may need to wait until 2030 to coach NSW after it was revealed Matt King’s two-year contract includes an option to activate a third year should the Blues beat Queensland in 2027 or 2028. King was officially unveiled as Laurie Daley’s successor as NSW Blues coach at NSW Rugby League’s Sydney Olympic Park headquarters on Tuesday. Loading Joined by his wife Kirsten and three young daughters, King revealed he had missed out on the top job with the Blues two years ago, and said he would call on coaching heavyweights Craig Bellamy, Craig Fitzgibbon, Michael Maguire and Trent Robinson as his unofficial “advisory board”. King also said he had wanted former Storm teammate and current Maroons coach Billy Slater to be the first to hear the news of his appointment, and insisted he was under no illusions about the media scrutiny that is certain to come his way in the role.



NSWRL CEO Dave Trodden confirmed King’s job would be a full-time role and that he would automatically trigger an extension for 2029 if he led the state to Origin glory in the next two years. Panthers coach Cleary will finish up with Penrith at the end of next year and has already spoken about his hopes of coaching at representative level, leading to speculation he would be installed as Blues coach as early as 2028. Matt King was officially unveiled as NSW Blues coach on Tuesday. Getty Images “Ivan is one of the greatest coaches there will be in rugby league, but we needed was a coach for 2027,” Trodden told this masthead. “Ivan wasn’t available, so that was always going to be a real difficulty. “There was the assumption about having a [stop-gap solution coach for 2027], which would almost be giving up next year’s series – and that’s not the way we were thinking. We expect to win next year, we expect to retain the trophy, and Matt King is the very best option to do that.



“He has a two-year contract, and if he wins a series in the next two years, there’s the automatic extension for 2029.” King, who will step down from his role as a Roosters assistant at season’s end after ten years on their coaching staff, said: “If I could pick any job, I’m picking this one. The jumper means so much to me. The players you have at your disposal, and just the contest, it’s incredible what State of Origin does for our country and what it means to people. To know I’m steering the ship, it’s pretty wild.” Matt King poses with daughters Charlie, Willow, Harper and wife Kirsten after his appointment on Tuesday. Getty Images King, the one-time garbo and Melbourne, Warrington, South Sydney, NSW and Australian cult hero known for his wild hair, won a premiership at the Storm with Slater, which explained why he was so eager to reach out to his coaching counterpart. Slater is saved simply as “Bill” in King’s phone, and King, 45, said: “We see each other a lot at footy games because he is a commentator. It’s always a handshake and a cuddle at the same time, and asking how the families are.



Related Article State of Origin Why a former garbo who has never coached first grade will lead NSW’s Origin defence in 2027 “There’s been a real mateship for a long time. I rang him about 9.30pm on Monday, he called me back first thing on Tuesday, and I said, ‘I wanted you to hear the news officially before you heard it anywhere else’. “I’m looking forward to that challenge of going up against Bill. Friendships can co-exist with the fact we’ll compete against each other and go hard against each other.” Maguire memorably accused Slater of living in “glass houses” during the 2024 series – the year King joined the NSW coaching staff – which frustrated Slater. When asked if his good mate actually resided in a “glass house”, King replied: “The last time I went to Billy Slater’s house, he had a little terrace in Richmond. I think he’s upgraded since then. I’d have to see how much glass he’s got.”



As for what he wanted to see from his NSW players? “Be a tough bugger, play with clarity, and go after the moments when your time comes,” King said. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Horror night for Sydney’s emergency departments
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWHealthcare Horror night for Sydney’s emergency departments Rachel Rasker Updated August 4, 2026 — 1:08pm ,first published 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Emergency services across Sydney on Monday recorded one of their busiest winter days, with a record 4100 ambulance callouts and almost 10,000 emergency department presentations. Western Sydney hospitals were among the hardest hit. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the state would see continued presentations for flu-like illness throughout winter. Emergency services in NSW have recorded one of their busiest days on record. James Brickwood “Influenza can also cause complications for people with comorbidities,” he said. “If someone with a co-morbidity gets influenza, the likelihood that they end up in the hospital is far greater than someone who just gets influenza on their own.”



There were about 1000 more emergency department presentations than usual. Related Article Flu season ‘Things are about to kick off’: NSW flu cases spike NSW Health Secretary Susan Pearce said dozens of patients were redirected to various hospitals on Monday to ease pressure on overflowing emergency departments. “The west, south-west, Nepean in particular were very, very busy last night (Monday),” Pearce said, with Park also pointing to Blacktown, Bankstown, Campbelltown and Liverpool hospitals as particular hotspots. Both Pearce and Park apologised to the patients and families who experienced long waits or were treated on the floor of waiting rooms.



It comes despite flu and COVID-19 cases remaining relatively stable – especially compared to last winter. Health authorities expect case numbers to rise now that children have returned to school. There were more than 2500 positive laboratory tests for influenza, the latest weekly surveillance report shows. The real number is significantly higher. Premier Chris Minns told 2GB it would be the worst three weeks of the year for emergency departments and warned people not to attend unless they were experiencing an actual emergency. Australian Medical Association NSW president Dr Fred Betros said telling patients to stay away from emergency departments “is not a health strategy”. “This is not an unforeseen crisis. It is a failure to prepare for predictable demand,” he said in a statement.



Park pointed to the 270 beds across western and south-western Sydney occupied by patients who are medically ready to be discharged but awaiting a federal government-funded place in an aged care or NDIS program. “That is the equivalent of a hospital not being able to be used,” he said, estimating 1300 people were affected. Betros said the state needed more consultant doctors, properly staffed beds, modern industrial arrangements to attract and retain doctors, and serious investment in prevention, general practice and public outpatient care. While he acknowledged the state government was right to press the Commonwealth on aged care and NDIS delays, he said “stranded patients cannot be blamed for every failure in our hospitals”. NSW Health chief health officer Dr Kerry Chant said influenza can “be that straw that broke the camel’s back” for people with underlying health conditions, including diabetes and lung disease, and urged the community to ask their GP about preventative health advice.



“It’s not too late in the season to get vaccinated,” she said. “In previous years, the pattern of when these respiratory viruses peak changes. Last year we saw quite a late peak of influenza … into that December period, which was quite unusual. So it’s not too late.” She said early indications have shown that this year’s flu vaccine is a better match for the influenza strain that’s currently circulating, predominantly H3N2 subclade K. World.title: Spaghetti aglio e olio with crispy chicken
World.content:
Step 1 Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Pat the chicken skin dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Add the chicken, skin side down, and cook for 4-6 minutes or until the skin is deep golden and crisp. Turn and cook for a further 4 minutes or until cooked through. Transfer to a plate, cover loosely with aluminium foil to retain heat and leave to rest before slicing thickly crosswise.

Step 2 Place 2 tablespoons of the remaining oil and the garlic into a large, deep frying pan over medium-low heat. Season with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3-4 minutes or until fragrant and lightly golden.

Step 3 Meanwhile, cook the pasta in a large saucepan of boiling salted water for 6-8 minutes or until al dente. Reserve ½ cup of the pasta cooking water, then drain.

Step 4 Add the drained pasta, reserved cooking water, chilli flakes, parsley, half the lemon zest and half the lemon juice to the garlic oil. Toss vigorously over low heat for 1-2 minutes until the liquid emulsifies into a glossy sauce that coats the pasta. Season to taste.

Step 5 Whisk the remaining olive oil, lemon zest and lemon juice together in a bowl to make the dressing. Toss the baby spinach with the dressing in a separate bowl.

World.title: Chlöe Swarbrick kicked out of House after challenging Speaker's 'double standards'
World.content:
The Greens co-leader has been kicked out of the House, after challenging what she called the Speaker's "double standards".

Chlöe Swarbrick says there's a specific issue with the Speaker's treatment of the Green Party compared to the "Right Honourable Winston Peters".

The opposition used Question Time on Tuesday to canvass both the Prime Minister's comments about small businesses, as well as his handling of Foreign Minister Winston Peters after he told Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to where you've come from" during a tirade in Parliament last week.

Peters came under scrutiny by Labour leader Chris Hipkins, questioning Christopher Luxon.

At one point Hipkins suggested Helen Clark "quietened him down when she dumped him from Cabinet." Peters then rose, requesting Hipkins withdraw the comments because it was a "lie".

The Speaker Gerry Brownlee said he would take a look at the Hansard and "come back to the House" on the issue.

Chlöe Swarbrick then requested a point of order, seeking guidance from the Speaker on the use of the word and accusation of a "lie".

"You have punished me - personally - multiple times for the use of that word.

"I'm seeking your guidance as to whether this rule applies universally, or there's one rule for us and another for him" she said, pointing at Peters.

Brownlee said every situation was different, and he would consider the issue later.

Speaker Gerry Brownlee. VNP / Phil Smith

But later in Question Time, Swarbrick asked her own questions of the prime minister regarding official advice he'd received about the impacts of AI data centre.

She continued with questions about whether the "Data Grid AI centre" would raise electricity prices, and whether the government had commissioned cost-benefit analysis on the consenting of AI data centres.

Luxon said the advice the government had had was that "it won't put an upward pressure on electricity prices" and they were taking more advice on the issue regarding a cost-benefit analysis.

Finally, Swarbrick asked:

"How many hyperscaled AI data centres does he understand might be consented before we receive the official cost-benefit analysis and understanding of impact on our energy grid and electricity prices?"

Luxon responded saying there were "around about 60 data centres in New Zealand today" and three expected to "come on stream".

During the answer, Swarbrick heckled the prime minister, asking if he knew the difference between a data centre and an AI data centre.

The Speaker interrupted, saying she had already asked her question.

"You can raise it in a different way, but don't do it across the floor of the house," Brownlee said.

Brownlee was about to move onto the next question, when a number of MPs raised their voices and he interjected again.

"Everyone is making far too much noise in here, and then turning around expecting me to interpret what a whole 123 people are saying - it's ridiculous!"

Swarbrick then raised another point of order, and said "respectfully, the problem is your double standards".

Brownlee responded by saying "the member will leave the house".

'Winston Peters is being treated differently to everybody else'

Speaking to reporters after she left the house, Swarbrick stood by her comments saying it was "well documented".

She said the Greens had written to the Speaker and met with him "multiple times" about the "demonstrable fact" there was uneven standards being applied, "particularly in the context of the Green Party, and when it comes to the behaviour of the Right Honourable Winston Peters."

Swarbrick gave the example of Peters being "allowed off the hook" for accusing the other side of lying.

"This is something which Gerry Brownlee has consistently told me that I have to stand up, withdraw, and apologise for, and a standard that he's also applied to Labour members of the House."

She acknowledged the Speaker had a "difficult job", but the "baseline thing" he can do was "apply the same standards to members across this house".

"Winston is so frequently heckling when people are asking questions.

World.title: Hipkins puts pressure on Luxon over his 'parent-child mentality' comments
World.content:
The Prime Minister has come under pressure in Parliament over his comments about New Zealand businesses, with Labour leader Chris Hipkins using question time to ask Christopher Luxon if he stands by them.

It comes after Christopher Luxon apologised on Monday for comments deemed "out of touch" by some, after he told an audience at a Rotorua Business Chamber event last week that some businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and too often looked to the government for help.

Hipkins asked Luxon if he stood by his view that "small business owners who are struggling through tough economic conditions, have created a parent-child mentality"?

Luxon responded by saying he'd addressed those comments "extensively and publicly yesterday," and apologised.

Hipkins then referred to actions by the Prime Minister's office over the weekend, ahead of the apology, which stated Luxon had been "mischaracterised".

"Was he correct on Sunday when his office said that his comments disparaging small business owners had been mischaracterised, or was he correct yesterday when he himself said that he was disappointed with how his comments had been reported, or was he correct hours later when he apologised if he defended anybody?"

Luxon said he'd addressed the issue in his previous answer.

Hipkins then quoted from senior ministers in Luxon's cabinet, firstly, National's Erica Stanford.

"Does he agree with Erica Stanford that his comments have caused a lot of hurt and upset? If so, why?" Hipkins asked.

Luxon again said he'd addressed the comments in his earlier answer, but then said he was "very proud" of the government's investment boost programme.

The centrepiece of last year's Budget, the boost, allows businesses to deduct 20 percent of a new asset's value from taxable income on top of normal depreciation.

Luxon then asked whether Hipkins would support the policy going forward.

Hipkins challenged this, telling the Speaker "I know we're three years into this, but the Prime Minister's job is to answer questions, not ask them".

Hipkins said Luxon hadn't addressed the question, referring to Stanford's comments, and the Speaker suggested Luxon might want to "add more".

Luxon then repeated a similar answer, suggesting Hipkins was "trying to politik" and again asking if the Labour leader he would support Investment Boost.

Hipkins then quoted the deputy prime minister, asking if Luxon agreed with David Seymour who said "there are some people who call themselves business people yet always have their hand out to the government."

Hipkins added, if Luxon did agree, "which businesses does he think fall into that category?"

Luxon's response began with him saying he was "actually very proud of New Zealand businesses".

"I, unlike the member, I get to see many of them each and every week. I actually get out of the bubble of Wellington and go meet with them and understand what their needs are," Luxon said.

He then listed a range of policies the government had focused on, such as opening up new trade deals, advocating for investment boost, RMA reform and fast track, "things that that member's opposed."

Again, Hipkins challenged the response, telling the Speaker Luxon hadn't addressed the question, and again the Speaker suggested the Prime Minister could "say a bit more".

Luxon then said he won't speak for the deputy prime minister, but for himself to say "I'm very proud of New Zealand's small businesses across this country. They do an incredible job."

"They're the lifeblood and the backbone of New Zealand, we care about them in this government."

He said that was why the government got the "settings right" so businesses can grow incomes, jobs and wages, "that's what we want them to be doing".

Hipkins then quoted Luxon himself, telling the Business Chamber audience that the "last person I wanted ever to talk to as a CEO was the government".

"Was he referring to his time as the chief executive of a government-owned airline, or his time as the chair of the Prime Minister's Business Advisory Council?"

Luxon responded saying, "that's what led me to politics, my friend, having seen how rubbish the government managed things in the last lot, it got me here very quickly."

Hipkins then asked if Luxon thought being a manager at a large multinational company, and earning a large salary, was comparable to running a small business in New Zealand.

Luxon responded saying he was Prime Minister of New Zealand, "that's my current job."

Finally, Hipkins referred to older comments by the prime minister, asking "which reflects his view of business in New Zealand, that they: Have a 'parent-child mentality', that they are 'C-listers', that they are 'weak, whiny, and inward-looking', or that they are 'soft'?"

Luxon didn't refer to any of those statements, saying instead "what I believe is a government should empower and enable businesses."

He said there was a very big difference between Labour "running Covid" and "our government running a fuel crisis".

World.title: What you need to know about complaining when things go wrong
World.content:
The leg of a ladder that buckled, a bath screen that shattered and icecream with pieces of metal in it were some of the problems New Zealanders have encountered in the past two years with items they've purchased.

The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's latest Consumer Survey shows that just under half of all consumers reported having a problem with a product or service in the past two years.

"While 44 percent of consumers have experienced a problem in the past two years, the survey also shows that when problems occur, consumers who understand their rights are more likely to take action and achieve a resolution," consumer services manager Simon Gallagher said.

A quarter of consumers said they had been deceived by a business.

The most common problems were related to the quality of a product or service, or the product or service not being what was expected.

The largest number related to motor vehicles bought from private sellers, followed by groceries and rest home real estate.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Gallagher said people who took action when they had a problem were often able to resolve it.

"Three-quarters achieved a resolution, while awareness of dispute resolution services increased compared with 2024.

"It's also encouraging to see that awareness of consumer protection laws remains very high, with 95 percent of New Zealanders aware that consumer protection laws exist. Additionally, a record 61 percent agree New Zealand has adequate laws to protect consumers from being misled or cheated by businesses.

"The survey highlights an important gap between awareness and understanding. While most consumers know these protections exist, only half say they have a moderate or good understanding of their rights, and tested knowledge of consumer rights has declined since 2024."

Thirty percent said they did not take action because they did not think it would solve the issue.

"Kiwis get better outcomes when they know their consumer rights… it's an interesting system where people actually develop their capability sometimes by having the issue. The real challenge for us is that tested knowledge has declined. So we'll be focusing some effort into there about building that capability and helping consumers feel confident raising their issues with businesses and understanding that there is persistence required but also understanding there are resolution pathways available to them.

"We will be using the results to work with our partners like the Commerce Commission and others in consumer sector organisations, to continue improving the information and tools we have available," Gallagher said.

Less than half of consumers said they would trust that the information given by salespeople was fair and accurate.

What can you do if you have a problem?

Gallagher said anyone who had a concern should complain to the business involved in the first instance.

He said people should understand their rights under the Consumer Guarantees Act, which requires businesses to sell products that are of acceptable quality, fit for purpose, match the description, are reasonably prices and delivered on time.

Services must be carried out with reasonable care and skill, have to be fit for a particular purpose, carried out within a reasonable time and charged at a reasonable price.

Businesses can remedy a problem by repairing or replacing a product with an identical model, or providing a refund. This has to be provided at no charge and, again, within a reasonable time.

Consumers who are not able to get resolution from the business within a reasonable time can have the fault fixed elsewhere and request a reasonable payment to cover their costs.

If there is no remedy available, the customer can ask for a refund or replacement or keep the faulty item but get compensation for the difference in value.

Consumers can also make a claim for compensation for any additional loss or damage suffered because of the failure, such as food that spoiled if a fridge stopped working.

Businesses do not have to give a remedy if a customer changes their mind, uses a product more than is reasonable, damages a product, misuses it, knew about the fault, took an unreasonable amount of time to get it fixed or went to another repairer before contacting the original sellers.

Gallagher said the CGA relied on consumers exercising their rights first.

He said if people "hit a roadblock" with the initial business, there were other remedies available to them such as the disputes tribunal or other consumer-based complaint systems. "It's actually the confidence to take action is the bit that needs to be continually reinforced."

World.title: Why New Zealand won't be getting an earthquake warning system any time soon
World.content:
Quake experts discusses NZ’s alert system and preparedness Morning Report Download MP3 4m

New Zealand won't be getting an earthquake early warning system any time soon, Earth Sciences says.

Countries like Japan, which suffered a large quake last week, use technology that can alert the public before damaging tremors happen.

New Zealand has been hit by multiple earthquakes in the past 10 days beginning with the first of two quakes in Te Anau, on 25 July, followed by a strong 5.9 quake in Taumarunui on 26 July. A 5.7 earthquake struck Te Araroa on the East Cape on 2 August.

Earth Sciences principal scientist Bill Fry told Morning Report the technology used to warn people seconds before an earthquake struck, relied on two basic principles - that shaking radiated away from the source and that the first shake wouldn't be the strongest.

"So based on these two things, the Japanese and others, have found ways to look at earthquake waves very close to the source and give some seconds of warning."

He said sensors close to the source of the shaking could help predict the strength and direction of the tremors, while other technology used light shaking to predict stronger shaking at a single point.

Fry said instead of an early alert, New Zealand focused on a rapid response.

"There are other lower-hanging fruits. We've decided to use the same technology as earthquake early warning to try to give us a rapid understanding of places that might have experienced strong shaking and shaking damage."

He said that information would feed into the emergency response.

In places that had early warnings - like Japan - systems existed to shutdown infrastructure such as high-speed trains and machinery, Fry said, but the prospect of implementing something similar in New Zealand raised many questions.

"A lot of those questions are in the social science. If we could deliver some seconds or tens of seconds warning, how would that be taken by people and how would they take appropriate action to ensure their safety?

"How would it be used?"

Fry said researchers were actively trying to answer those questions.

He said to date, the country had the science and technology to understand earthquake waves and their effect on the ground.

World.title: Willie Walker named new Fijiana XV head coach
World.content:
Blues Women's team mentor Willie Walker has been appointed to lead the Fijian Women's 15s side.

Walker, who has led the Blues Women to three consecutive Super Rugby Aupiki titles in 2024, 2025 and 2026, was announced as the head coach of the Fijiana XV at a news conference in Suva on Tuesday.

The Fiji Rugby Union said Walker has a "proven record of success in New Zealand women's rugby" and is set to steer the national women's rugby programme.

Walker is the latest New Zealand rugby mind to take charge of a Fijian side, following former All Blacks assistant coach Brad Mooar's appointment as Fijian Drua head coach less than a fortnight ago.

"Walker's appointment will complement the outstanding work that has already been undertaken over the past decade in the growth and development of women's rugby in Fiji," Fiji Rugby said in a statement.

"His role will be to build on that strong foundation by contributing to the continued development of a high-performance women's programme, strengthening coaching pathways, establishing robust systems, and helping create an environment that supports long-term success across all levels of the women's game."

In a Facebook post, the Blues said Walker's influence extended far beyond silverwhare.

"It's in the culture, the standards, the relationships and the belief that have become the foundation of who we are."

Speaking on his vision for the team, Walker told local reporters they have "a good plan set up" on the levels they want the Fijiana XV to reach.

"We got good targets and we've good to build on the success that has been established over the last few years," he said.

"Off the back of a reasonable World Cup performance there's a lot of growth to be had in terms of some technical and tactical knowledge and awareness.

"I think it's about building those pathways and the depth for Fijiana rugby so we can continue with that success."

The Fiji national women's rugby team is currently ranked 13th in the world.

At the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup, the Fijiana XV did not advance past the pool stage after two losses and a win.

They were led by Welshman Ioan Cunningham, who stepped down at the end of the tournament.

Meanwhile, the Fijiana XV will host the Springbok Women in a two-Test Series this month under interim head coach Mike Legge.

World.title: Aussie swimmer out of leadership group after reported drinking session
World.content:
Australian swimmer Isaac Cooper has stepped down from the Dolphins's leadership group after a drinking session at the Commonwealth Games.

Cooper was reported to be out drinking when he was expected to be supporting teammates at Glasgow's Tollcross International Swimming Centre last Wednesday night.

Cooper was also seen drinking at the Australian team hotel during that day, the report said.

"Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow, which is in conflict with team expectations," a Swimming Australia statement said.

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

"Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team's athlete leadership group."

Cooper was scheduled to race the 100m backstroke final that night but withdrew from the event after qualifying eighth-fastest.

Swimmers were expected to support teammates at the Glasgow Games when not racing, while Cooper also missed the team meeting that night.

The 22-year-old won gold at the Glasgow Games as a member of the 4x100m medley team after swimming in the heats.

He also finished sixth in the 50m backstroke final, an event he won a silver medal at the 2024 world championships.

Cooper will next compete at the Pan Pacific championships in the United States starting August 12.

AAP

World.title: Blues announce King as new Origin coach after Daley steps down
World.content:
Former NSW State of Origin player Matt King has been named the new head coach of the Blues.

King was announced as the new coach on Tuesday after predecessor Laurie Daley stepped down from the role on Monday.

Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach The NSWRL pays tribute to Blues "hero" Laurie Daley as the coach stands down from his role after this year's series win over Queensland.

King played nine times for the Blues from 2005-2007, and over 200 first grade matches for Melbourne, South Sydney and Warrington across the NRL and Super League in England.

"I'm very clear on what it looks like to be the head coach of NSW," King said.

"I have a true understanding of what it means to lead this great state of ours and I can't wait for that opportunity.

"The one true rugby league love of my life has been the NSW Blues. To know now that I have the opportunity to guide the team moving forward, to lead the program over the next little period, means the absolute world to me."

The 45-year-old has been a long-time assistant coach under Trent Robinson at the Sydney Roosters, and has been part of the Blues' coaching staff since 2024.

Daley stepped down as Blues coach on Monday after guiding NSW to a series win this year.

The Blues sealed the series with a 30-12 triumph in the decider at Lang Park, just the fourth time NSW has won a deciding Game III in Brisbane.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said in a statement on Monday.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

World.title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
World.content:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

World.title: Infantino could face UEFA lawsuit as he scrambles for FIFA presidency support
World.content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and says potential evidence should not be destroyed.

Mr Infantino on Saturday dropped a secretive proposal to raise $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) from investors, including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner, days after media reports revealed it, provoking a global furore.

UEFA led the backlash and its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.

Now UEFA's lawyers have informed FIFA that the European body is "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints … arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters".

The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Mr Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke Two of football's major bodies launch stinging rebukes of FIFA boss Gianni Infantino after his failed privatisation ploy.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Meanwhile, the Swedish football federation confirmed that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.

On Saturday, UEFA signalled it wants to end Mr Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world football and that "no option should be off the table".

Hours earlier, Mr Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.

The FFE spin-off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the football body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.

It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement that said staff felt deceived by their boss Mr Infantino.

FIFA COO Kevin Lamour has made clear his opposition to Gianni Infantino's plan. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

Legal proceedings are "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

UEFA has been outspoken against its former employee Mr Infantino, while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF also made strong statements opposing Mr Infantino's plan.

Mr Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.

Gianni Infantino is reportedly seeking support from Donald Trump in his FIFA presidency battle. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Mr Infantino's path to stabilising the presidency he has held for more than 10 years was unclear. A report yesterday claimed he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally US President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Mr Infantino and there is no call this morning," Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.

The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Mr Infantino had pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.

Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe, with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.

The candidate deadline is November 18 for an election four months later in Morocco.

World.title: 'Lot of nonsense': Dearden clears air on Cowboys future
World.content:
North Queensland co-captain Tom Dearden has cleared the air about his future and given the club a boost as he targets returning from injury to inspire a finals run.

At the end of the 2023 season Dearden, 26, signed a five-year contract extension through to the end of 2029.

But multiple reports in recent weeks linked him to an early exit for personal reasons due to his pregnant partner, Millie Over, living in Sydney.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Dearden fronted the media to refute the reports due to the impact they were having on his personal life.

"There's been a fair bit of speculation getting around at the moment. There's been a lot of suggestions that I wanted to move or leave the club," Dearden said.

"That's not the case at all. I don't feel like I should have to get up here and explain myself against speculation.

"It's just been a whole lot of nonsense. I've got my private life with a partner who's pregnant and I'd like for that all to be kept private.

"I'm committed to the Cowboys until the end of 2029 and I think it's a bit silly that you have to get up here and speak to a bit of nonsense that's going around."

Dearden made it clear that he was "not recommitting".

"I've always been committed to the Cowboys and none of that has ever changed, so it's a bit disappointing that my partner and family have had to deal with a lot of questions," he said.

Maroons dealt massive blow Queensland selectors have been forced to cope with the news one of their best playmakers will miss up to eight weeks with his ankle injury.

"It's had an impact on the personal life. I've got a pregnant partner and I think when there's speculation getting around like that, people are reading that and it gives them questions to ask and you always have to answer to people."

Dearden has played just once since suffering a syndesmosis and ankle fracture in round 10.

The injury ruled him out of the State of Origin series and he returned against the Dolphins in round 20 only to tear a muscle in his shin on the other leg.

Dearden played through the match but during the following week discovered the issue.

"It's been a frustrating year having to sit out because I love representing the Cowboys," Dearden said.

"It's a bit of a weird injury but it's tracking pretty well and hopefully I've only got a few more weeks [on the sidelines]."

Dearden and the club have targeted the round 26 home clash with Wests Tigers in Townsville as his return date, after the Cowboys' round 25 bye.

North Queensland is in ninth position and plays Gold Coast away on Thursday night before an away clash with Parramatta without its influential half.

AAP

World.title: Former Sea Eagle, ABC radio personality John Gibbs diagnosed with cancer
World.content:
Former Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles halfback and ABC Sport rugby league commentator John Gibbs has been diagnosed with cancer.

Gibbs, 70, has been part of the ABC Sport team since 2016 and has been a popular personality among listeners.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

He was on the ABC Sport call with Andrew Moore and Matthew Elliott on Sunday afternoon when the Parramatta Eels defeated Wests Tigers.

"Gibbsy", who played 81 first grade games for the Sea Eagles and represented New South Wales and Australia, announced his diagnosis on Monday, and that he would be stepping away from broadcasting to focus on his health.

Moore, ABC Sport's lead rugby league caller, said his friend Gibbs wanted listeners to know he was prepared for his upcoming treatment on NRL MONDAY.

"John Gibbs called me this afternoon to confirm something he had been fearing for a while. He's been diagnosed with cancer — Hodgkin's lymphoma," Moore said.

"He knows he's in for a fight, but he wants you to know he's up for it.

"We are family and, as I discovered a year ago, the wave of support from the ABC team, it's significant, it's powerful, it's amazing and it helps.

"Like so many of you, he's ready to kick cancer to the kerb and beat the mongrel."

The former international has been a constant on Sydney radio since the 1980s as a commentator, presenter, and host for 2UE, 2GB and ABC Sport.

World.title: Young Tiger banned as gut-punch crackdown continues
World.content:
Richmond defender Luke Trainor has received a one-match ban for striking as the AFL's crackdown on gut punches continues.

Trainor will miss the Tigers' trip to face Adelaide at Adelaide Oval on Saturday after punching West Coast forward Jack Williams in the stomach as the two were jostling in the goal square at the MCG on Sunday.

Williams dropped to the turf while Trainor jogged off.

Coach Adem Yze had hoped Trainor would only be fined for the second-quarter incident in the 11-point win over the Eagles.

But the match review officer took a dim view of the incident, assessing it as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which draws a one-match ban.

It leaves Richmond short of a tall defender against Adelaide's powerful forward line headlined by Riley Thilthorpe.

AAP

World.title: Wallabies to battle heat, typhoon in Japanese Test
World.content:
The Wallabies are not concerned Japan's searing heat and lingering typhoon will play a part in their preparation or Test match as they look to face old foes in Les Kiss's debut as coach.

Australia will take on Japan in the first of two Tests on Saturday night at Hanazono Rugby Stadium in Osaka, although conditions are not expected to be easy to play in.

Temperatures are tipped to stay in the high 20s to mid-30s degrees Celsius all week as the country grapples with a heatwave.

To make matters worse, Typhoon Dolphin is bringing wind gusts of up to 216kph and heavy rainfall ahead of hitting the Southern Japanese Ryukyu Islands on Friday, about 1,500 kilometres south of Osaka.

Wallabies thrash Italy as Schmidt era ends in triumph The Wallabies record a convincing 57-10 victory over Italy in Perth, as Joe Schmidt's coaching tenure finishes on a winning note.

But Queensland hooker Josh Nasser is treating the conditions as just another day in Australia.

"Obviously it's pretty warm over here, but I grew up in Brissy. We get some pretty hot summers as well. So humidity's up, temperatures up, but it's no different to some of the conditions we get back home," he told reporters on Monday.

"In the wet, the ball gets slippery, things tighten up a little bit. But I think we've got a big focus on just still trying to express ourselves.

"We play a fixture in Fiji each year, which we get pretty extreme conditions for.

"We're really not hyper-focused on it. We're just accepting that it will be hot, and then sticking to our processes."

Wallabies assistant coach Scott McLeod also warned of another typhoon that could affect Australia's clash.

"Is that Eddie Jones?" he joked when a journalist asked about Typhoon Dolphin.

Jones, who led Australia to a dismal Rugby World Cup showing in 2023 before resigning, will coach his second game against the green and gold with the Brave Blossoms.

Former Wallabies coach Eddie Jones will face Australia for the second time as Japan's coach. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

Nasser expects his presence to add extra spice to the fixture, especially as the master agitator took over the Japanese side just six weeks after resigning and was forced to deny that he had been in talks with Brave Blossoms officials during the World Cup.

Jones will not be the only Australian on the opposition, with former Queensland lock Harry Hockings along with Ben Gunter, Jack Cornelsen, Dylan Riley, Michael Stolberg and Tiennan Costley all options to play.

The Wallabies have been humbled by Australians featuring for different national teams in the past, most notably Canberra-born Mack Hansen when he scored a stunning first-half hat-trick to help Ireland win 46-19 last November.

"They'll be fired up to prove a point against us, I'm sure. [There's] nothing too strange about seeing them there, but it'll be a good battle," Nasser said.

"A couple of them are my good mates. Harry Hockings is one of my best mates.

"[I haven't spoken to him] on the rugby front, but I'm sure I'll catch up with him for a beer after the game."

The reunions will all culminate in Kiss's first match in charge of the national team since Joe Schmidt departed following the Wallabies' rousing 57-10 victory over Italy on July 18.

AAP

Tech.title: The studio behind Pokémon struggles to find its voice in Beast of Reincarnation
Tech.content:
You have to imagine that the team at Game Freak is bursting with ideas. The studio puts out new mainline Pokémon adventures with a machinelike precision. But every so often it launches a curious experiment, whether it’s an action title about a militarized elephant or turning horse races into a card game, showing that it’s capable of more than the latest generation of pocket monsters. That’s part of what makes the idea of Beast of Reincarnation so enticing. Here is an established studio breaking free of the franchise it has become known for to make its take on a blockbuster action game. Unfortunately new ideas are in short supply in Beast, and aside from its slick action, there’s little that hasn’t been done before.

Beast of Reincarnation takes place exactly 2,000 years in the future in a postapocalyptic vision of Japan that blends sci-fi and magic. Humans still exist, though many of them transferred their consciousness to robotic golems in order to survive the calamity that ruined the world. The real problem is that a mysterious blight has infected the landscape, turning wildlife into vicious, mutated monsters. Even worse: This seems to portend the return of the titular beast, a powerful creature that, as its name implies, appears to be immortal. You play as a wandering mercenary-type named Emma who has the ability to absorb the powers of fallen mutants, and soon she’s tasked with traversing the world to power up so that she can take down the beast for good.

It’s not a bad setup for an action game, as it gives you a reason to keep moving forward. Emma is constantly on the hunt for the next big creature that she can use to get stronger before taking on her final task. Beast of Reincarnation isn’t an open-world game, but instead is divided into a series of big locations that you travel between as the story progresses.

Image: Fictions

The standout feature of the game is its action. Emma is a speedy samurai type, wielding a blade and various bows. At first, Beast seems like Dark Souls or Elden Ring, a game built around dodging and parrying, with little room for error. But as you unlock new powers, it proves to be something a little different. Emma’s signature ability is that vines and plants can grow out of her hair. This sounds weird, but it’s also incredibly useful; she can build bridges to traverse big gaps, or use her hair like a grappling hook to reach locations up high. She also has an adorable and gigantic magical dog companion who follows her everywhere and provides a hand with combat and tedious chores like collecting loot.

Emma’s powers are especially helpful in battle. Slowly she gains abilities that let her zip around the battlefield, using her hair to quickly gain ground on an enemy, deliver an attack from above, or team up with her powerful pup for a devastating blow. Her hair can even improve your stealth: At one point I unlocked a skill that caused tall plants to sprout wherever I crouched, temporarily giving me some cover before delivering a silent kill. It takes a few hours for things to open up, but eventually Beast’s combat has plenty of room for freedom and creativity.

The same can’t be said for the rest of the experience. Initially, Beast’s postapocalyptic world is compelling because it’s full of mystery. You know almost nothing about the history of the world, but there are hints of interesting dynamics, like the human-infused machines and how they evolved differently from flesh-and-blood people. But Beast pushes the idea of mystery to a frustrating extreme. Everything in this game is mysterious: the landscape, Emma herself, her two human travel companions, her giant dog, the little girl that only Emma can see, the other wandering fighters she encounters in the world. I love a story that is full of secrets and intrigue, but I barely understood what I was even doing in Beast until at least a dozen hours into the game. It doesn’t help that the game hides explanations of many of its key elements in a tutorial menu. And when you do finally get answers to the big mysteries, they’re mostly underwhelming.

Image: Fictions

The story isn’t the only place that feels underdeveloped or uninspired. There are a number of gameplay elements — like the ability to grow your own food, and a weapon upgrade system — that are so simple that it’s easy to forget about them altogether. Meanwhile, the level design is incredibly straightforward, making exploration a bore, particularly when it comes to the dead-simple platforming sections. The game’s skill tree is even a literal tree.

But the real issue with Beast of Reincarnation is that it is full of ideas that already exist elsewhere. The story is like a watered-down version of Nier: Automata’s heartrending postapocalypse, while the boss battles feel ripped out of Monster Hunter (with designs straight from its contemporary Wild Hearts and one specific creature that looks identical to a Stranger Things demodog). Your mobile home base functions much like the one in Death Stranding — you can even shower — and it looks just like an AT-ST from Star Wars. Everywhere you go, there’s something from a different game or movie.

This is especially disappointing because there is so much potential in Beast of Reincarnation. Not only is the combat thrilling, but, as derivative as it is, the game still manages to create an incredible sense of melancholic moodiness through its sound and visuals. But it never delivers on that; I was excited to learn about the strange religions and customs that were developed by isolated groups of golem, for instance, but the revelations were all surface level and quickly brushed aside.

That sums up much of the Beast experience: There are flashes of excitement and intrigue, but mostly you’ve seen all of this before. At least there’s more Pokémon on the way.

Beast of Reincarnation launches on August 4th on the PS5, Xbox, and PC.

Tech.title: Your Fitbit data can now connect directly to Apple Health
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is rolling out an update that will finally allow you to connect your Fitbit workouts, steps, vitals, and other data to Apple Health, as reported earlier by 9to5Mac. With Google Health’s 5.05 update, you can now tap your profile icon, select “Partner apps,” and choose Apple Health to link your data directly.

Previously, you could only import your Apple Health data into Google Health, but not the other way around. That meant using third-party apps — like Power Sync for Fitbit or Fitbit to Apple Health Sync — or some other kind of workaround to connect your Google Health information to Apple Health.

Google Health replaced the Fitbit app in May. The new app had a bit of a rocky rollout after users raised concerns over the new AI health coach, user interface, and other issues, though Google has since addressed some of these complaints.

Along with this update, Google announced that users in the US can use Smart Health Links to share medical records with a provider or family member. You can create a link by heading to the Health tab, choosing the “Medical” section, selecting “Shareable records,” and tapping the “plus” icon. From there, you can choose which data you want to include in the link and share it via a URL or QR code.

Tech.title: Samsung’s discounted smart monitor is $349.99, its lowest price yet
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Samsung makes a variety of TVs and computer monitors, but if want both and you’re limited on space, you might want to consider the M80F. This capable 32-inch 4K panel combines features commonly found on both types of screens, and Amazon and B&H Photo both have it discounted to $349.99, where it’s usually $400 or much higher. In addition to acting as a standard 4K screen for your computer or console, the M80F has a full suite of video streaming apps you’d expect to find on a television, with picture-in-picture support for multitasking, plus a removable webcam for video chats.

The M80F has above-average connectivity for a monitor. In addition to the ports like HDMI 2.0, USB-C for charging devices up to 65W, and USB-A for your keyboard and mouse, you can also connect the Tizen interface to Wi-Fi to directly communicate with your network (it also supports Bluetooth headphones). Speaking of gaming, the M80F supports apps like Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now, letting you pair a controller to the display to play games over the cloud. The VA panel is better suited for work than play, but HDR10 Plus support will help your movies and TV shows pop.

My colleague Cameron Faulkner reviewed a previous version of the M80F and appreciated its versatility, but the $699.99 launch price was a bit off-putting, so a discount on a newer, improved model is definitely worth calling out.

Tech.title: Europe’s AI labeling and transparency rules are now in effect
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The European Union has ushered in some additional rules that aim to make it easier for people to identify chatbots and AI deepfakes online. The new transparency obligations under the bloc’s landmark AI Act came into effect on August 2nd, requiring companies to disclose when people are interacting with AI models, and if content has been generated or altered by them.

The transparency rules differ between providers (companies that develop and market AI systems) and deployers (platforms and services that use those AI systems), though some companies like Meta and SpaceXAI are classified as both.

If enough companies do adopt the EU’s AI icons then labels should look more consistent across online platforms. Image: The European Commission

Providers must design AI systems to explicitly notify users when they’re dealing with AI instead of a human, “unless this is obvious,” and include machine-readable marks on synthetic audio, image, video, and text so that it can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Likewise, deployers are required to label any AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, and video deepfake content that’s designed to look real.

“The rapid development of generative and interactive AI systems is making it increasingly difficult to distinguish AI interactions and AI-generated content from human-created and authentic content,” the European Commission said in its transparency guidelines. “People should know when they are interacting with AI or exposed to AI-generated content. This will help them make informed decisions, calibrate their trust and reliance on AI and avoid misinformation or deception.”

The Commission has also developed a set of AI disclosure labels that tech platforms can adopt in accordance with the AI Act rules, alongside examples of when they should be used. These mirror similar labels that have already been introduced by TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook. The EU-made icons have been introduced to prevent platforms from having to design their own, and while the EU examples are optional to use, the Commission pointedly notes that its labeling requirements “are not.”

Companies that fail to comply with these new transparency rules risk facing fines of up to €15 million (about $17.2 million), or 3 percent of their global annual turnover. While the new transparency rules are enforceable immediately for new AI systems, any models and services that launched before August 2nd have a four-month grace period until December 2nd to comply.

Tech.title: The first-gen Kindle Scribe is a big e-reader and digital notebook that’s $150 refurbished
Tech.content:
The Kindle Scribe is worth considering if you’re heading back to school, as its large 10.2-inch screen can display textbooks and ebooks, or let you jot down handwritten notes during class. Now through August 8th, the first-gen model (with a Premium Pen) is down to just $149.99 with 16GB of storage in refurbished condition at Woot when you apply the promo code KINDLE25 at checkout. That’s $220 off its original launch price from 2022 and even cheaper than the current Kindle Paperwhite, though you’ll only get Woot’s 90-day warranty. Woot doesn’t specify the exact condition of its refurbished devices, but it does offer a brief explanation here of what to expect.

The Kindle Scribe features a sharp 300ppi E Ink display that’s glare-free and supports adjustable color temperatures, making it easy to read whether you’re outside in the sun or studying late at night. Like all other Kindles, the Scribe gives you quick and easy access to Amazon’s massive store of digital books, so you can switch between assigned reading and your favorite novels without carrying multiple books or devices. It’s not waterproof like the Kindle Paperwhite, though, so you’ll want to keep it away from the pool and be careful when it rains.

It’s also a solid digital notebook, with the device offering a variety of pre-made templates for everything from lined paper and planners to to-do lists. After updating the software, the original Kindle Scribe also includes the same AI-powered note-taking features as the newer models, allowing you to jot down notes directly on compatible ebook pages, summarize and refine your handwritten notes, generate AI-powered summaries, and more.

Tech.title: Microsoft is bringing Xbox 360 games to PC
Tech.content:
Building on its recently announced plans to bring original Xbox games to PC, Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC as well, according to a leaked document, seen by The Verge, that was sent to developers recently. Xbox 360 games will be able to run on the next-gen Project Helix console, “Xbox PCs,” and handheld devices, the document says.

Microsoft has already said that Helix will play PC games, so making these older Xbox titles available on PC helps build a broader Xbox library that can travel between devices, similar to what’s already possible with Steam. Creating all these digital licenses also helps set up for a future of consoles without disc drives; Sony has already declared game discs dead, and Microsoft may follow.

With 360 games, developers can opt into making them backward compatible, and they will have control over things like a game’s price and if it’s available on Game Pass. The feature is expected to have a “gradual” rollout between 2027 and 2028 “across next-gen devices.” The “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC is also set for October 2026; the initial program announced in July included just four games.

The document also includes details about a way for players to get a digital version of a game that they already own on a physical disc, which The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on in July. The document says that if a player puts an Xbox One or Series game on disc into an Xbox One or Series X console with a disc drive, they’ll be granted a digital license that’s bound to “that disc and the player’s account.” The license will stay with a player across Xbox devices, but if the disc “changes hands,” the license will transfer to the new person. That should mean that gamers can still trade and sell discs; once the original owner of a disc does so, they can’t play the digital version they got from that disc anymore.

According to the document, a public beta for the disc-to-digital program was set for July with general availability set for August. We understand Microsoft had originally planned to test its disc-to-digital program with Xbox Insiders in July, but the beta was delayed. It’s unclear if the timeline of August general availability is still accurate.

The planned changes follow Microsoft’s major Xbox “reset” announced in July, which included thousands of layoffs and the company selling off four studios.

Tech.title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO.

This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder, because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all.

Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable.

But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop.

That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads.

This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it.

Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of Bluesky. Welcome to Decoder.

Thank you. Thanks for having me.

I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think Bluesky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are.

Bluesky today is really two things. There’s the Bluesky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath Bluesky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And Bluesky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol.

The whole point of Bluesky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app.

There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that Bluesky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of Bluesky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO?

It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why Bluesky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job.

I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. And so I agreed to be interim CEO initially because I was still a general partner at True and it’s a firm I helped build. It’s an amazing firm that I didn’t want to leave behind. But also, at True, we’ve had this model where we’ve moved back and forth between operator and investor. I did that while I was running Automattic.

So I stepped into it. After working on it hands-on for a few months, it just got more and more fun, more and more energizing. You just feel the momentum. Also, True just switched to a new fund. So actually the timing was good where I could say, “Okay, I will switch my true role to part-time, become a venture partner,” which is what I used to be when I ran Automattic, “and I’ll go all in at Bluesky.”

Tell me about the difference between being the interim CEO and the full-time CEO. When you’re the interim CEO, it feels like there are probably some boundaries in what you can do. And then the full-time CEO can obviously do everything that a full-time CEO can do. What did you feel like the boundaries were as interim CEO?

On the inside, it hasn’t felt very different. I actually think the move to drop the “interim” is more important on the outside, especially for the ATmosphere and the AT Proto community, and people building on this platform and in this ecosystem just to say, “No, I’m here for the duration. This isn’t just some interim gig and then somebody else is going to show up.” So I felt like, to the outside, that makes a big difference. On the inside, the job really hasn’t changed much..

So many of my conversations here in Decoder are really about the timescale of decisions. I’ll make the comparison to my newsroom because it’s easy and it’s easy to understand. Our reporters make decisions in like 30-minute increments. A story comes up, they write it, they publish it, they move on to the next thing. I make decisions maybe in like week- or month-long increments. What are we going to cover? Where are the resources going to go?

It seems like in the interim CEO role, the timescale of those decisions is necessarily short or it has the appearance of being short. And then I’m reading your note that you published when you became the full-time CEO. In the very beginning of it, you say we’re at the very beginning of the story with a decade of exciting work ahead. And I’m wondering if the timescale of the decisions you’re making now are a decade.

Yeah. It touches on something really fascinating with this project. In general with decision making, one of the frameworks I really like is the reversible and irreversible decisions. A lot of decisions we make are actually reversible. I like to optimize to just make those decisions quickly and then make sure you can undo the decisions if you need to change them.

And then there are a few decisions that really do have very long-term implications. They’re much harder to reverse. With this project in particular, there are decisions made at this protocol level that we’re going to have to live with for a long time. There’s a part of the company in this community that thinks very, very, very long term. This is a protocol that is going to be around for decades already. It’s in enough use that it’s going to be around for a long time. Those decisions you really need to be careful about. Then it goes all the way to things we try in the product that work or don’t work.

I wasn’t in the interim mindset as much because I am also an investor in the company, so I care very much about the long-term picture. What attracts me to this whole endeavor is that it can have a really important long-term impact. I always think about, okay, how will this play out? Does this truly serve the core mission? It’s okay to make some of these harder decisions now that won’t pay off for a long time because this is going to take a while.

It’s not just one company. It’s already thousands of others that are building together. That’s just a different timeframe and decision-making process than your typical just “go fast, scale as quickly as possible” [methodology]. I like it. I’m comfortable with it.

I just want to stick with Bluesky, the company that is both responsible for the standard and the protocol, and the product that a lot of end users love and sometimes hate. That is the core tension of the company. The user base of Bluesky is or is not interested in the development of AT Protocol, is or is not interested in the wider ATmosphere.
